Learning target:
Upon completion of this module, students command profound knowledge of current topics in Financial Accounting and Financial Analysis, which they are able to apply to complex real-world cases.

Contents:
This course, with varying emphases, acquaints students with current topics in Financial Accounting and Financial Analysis. Topics in Financial Accounting include complex accounting treatments under IFRS that are typically relevant to multi-national firms, e.g., accounting for business combinations and goodwill, impairment testing, accounting for employee benefits and stock options. Topics in Financial Analysis include accounting-based securities valuation and analysis of IFRS financial statements.

Contents:
What is culture and how can we study it? That is the key question that concerns this class, and we will be pursuing this question first and foremost as a theoretical problem. That is, we will be encountering both the work of important voices in the canon of cultural studies theory and practice, and the work of theorists, historians, philosophers, sociologist, etc., who have proved influential in terms of how cultural studies goes about its business. Students will be made familiar with a variety of key theoretical contributions and will also see how these approaches influence what we 'see' when we study a piece of fiction, a film, a tv series, a painting. To this end, each theoretical framing will be accompanied by a practical example.

Contents:
Conspiracy theories are everywhere in recent years - from conversations we overhear at the bus stop to White House press briefings. But contrary to general perception, we are not living in an age of conspiracy theories, as they were far more widespread in the past, both in Europe and the United States.

The focus of this lecture will be on the history of conspiracism in the U.S. from the Puritans to the present. We will investigate why and with what effects conspiarcy theories were for a long time at the center of political discourse, why they were stigmatized after World War II and why they have been (partly) relegitimized in recent years. In addition, the lecture will focus on fictional representations, on how novels, films, and TV shows have articulated, dismissed, or negotiated conspiracist visions since the 19th century. In the last weeks of the semester, we will then look beyond the U.S. and examine the popularity and effects of conspiracy theories in Germany and other regions.

Learning target:
Students will learn

to define conspiracy theories and distinguish them from phenomena such as misinformation or disinformation;

to understand their forms and functions;

about the development of conspiracy theories throughout American history;

about their representation and negotiation in fiction;

and about the role of significance of conspiracy theories in Germany and other regions.

Keywords:
conspiracy theory, conspiracism, populism, stigmatized knowledge, misinformation, American Revolution, Civil War, anti-Communism, anti-Catholicism, Kennedy assassination, 9/11, deep state, coronavirus pandemic, Donald Trump, QAnon.

Literature:
There is non obligatory reading. All texts will be made available on Moodle.

Michael Butter, The Nature of Conspiracy Theories (London: Polity, 2020) offers a general introduction to the topic.

Contents:
The class introduces current research into American literature and culture of the second half of the 19th century into modernism. You may get 3 credit points for attending the lecture and writing three short (1 1/2 page) responses; you can get more CP and a grade for passing an oral exam.

Contents:
In this course we will read and discuss autobiographies by Afro-American authors and explore the resonances of these texts with the activism and politics of their times. Autobiographies open up interesting perspectives on social movements. They offer insight into individual dispositions, value systems and personal experiences, all of which may contribute to political commitment. At the same time, they are also frequently written to frame individual life-stories within political contexts. Therefore, we will in this seminar consider autobiographies in two ways - as private testimony and as a genre to connect the micropolitics of experience with the political agendas of social movements.

Literature:
Rosa Parks, My Story (with Jim Haskins), 1992

Anne Moody, Coming of Age in Mississippi (1968)

Barack Obama, Dreams from My Father (2004)

Contents:
How have the 9/11 terrorist attacks changed the United States? This is the central question we will attempt to answer in this course, 25 years after the attacks happened. We'll set the stage with sessions on Al Qaeda and the U.S. during the 1990s and on the 9/11 attacks themselves. Then we will turn to the immediate responses to 9/11 by both the American people and the Bush Administration. The longer-term consequences of 9/11 revolve around the War on Terror, the wars in Afghanistan and Iraq, as well as the politics of fear in the United States itself (involving anti-Muslim sentiment, immigration, polarization, and the militarization of law enforcement). Ironically, the aftermath of 9/11 opened the door to both Barack Obama's presidency and to Donald Trump's. We will also look into the politics of public memory and 9/11 memorials.

Please note: American Studies Master students can do a project for the Practice Module in this seminar.

Contents:
In this class, we will trace the development of poetry in the 19th C, discussing their shifting aesthetics and cultural functions. We will engage in both close readings, historical contextualizations, and questions of canonization. A specific focus will be on Romanticism, esp. Emily Dickinson and Walt Whitman.

Contents:
In this seminar we will read and contextualize black poetic efforts from Langston Hughes to Natasha Trethewey. Our close readings of the respective poems are supplemented and informed by a set of shifting key semantics (e.g. universalism/particularism; Black Nationalism; Afrofuturism; Afropessimism) from black cultural discourses. These will help put into focus the interplay of aesthetics and politics in this rich lyric tradition.

Contents:
The class will examine both historical and contemporary American social dances. We will develop an understanding of these dances as cultural practices and investigate the location of these practices within the Black Atlantic.

You will be familiarized with the basics of performance studies and contemporary Dance Studies. You will gain an understanding of the theoretical concept and historical space of the Black Atlantic. Finally, you will learn about specific dances, their aesthetics, histories, and social contexts.

This class will include two additional sessions in which we will be dancing ourselves.

Contents:
From promotional videos to genuine art form, music videos are an interesting and influential genre. When MTV first aired The Buggles’ „Video Killed the Radio Star“ in 1981, the tension between the medial affordances of sight and sound were already made explicit. In this seminar we will discuss the history, aesthetics and cultural work of music videos from its predecessors (cf. The Soundies in the 1940s) to the dissemination of in an ever-chancing media environment (YouTube, TikTok, etc.). Is it true that "Internet Killed the Video Star" (Knarf Rellöm)?

We will both theorize the format, contextualize it with help of both media and cultural studies approaches, and take a look at specific examples from a number of different music genres and eras.

Learning target:
Students will be able to understand both the medial affordances and cultural work of music videos as part of popular culture.

Contents:
What happens when societies go wrong? Dystopian fiction imagines worlds shaped by surveillance, authoritarian rule, ecological collapse, or extreme social control and asks what it means to live, resist, and remain human under such conditions.

In this seminar, we will explore dystopian literature to understand how imagined futures reflect historical fears and contemporary debates about power, technology, gender, and politics. Through close reading and discussions, students will learn how these texts create their worlds, develop their conflicts, and offer sharp critiques of our own societies.

Keywords:
dystopian fiction – power and control – surveillance – authoritarianism – resistance – social critique – speculative futures

Literature:
1984 by George Orwell

The Handmaid’s Tale by Margaret Atwood

Parable of the Talents by Octavia E. Butler

Contents:
The maximalist novel is a multi-form and unusually long type of fiction that has gained special cultural significance in postwar US literature. In this class we will take Herman Melville's Moby-Dick as a case study to introduce fictional maximalism, frame it as one mode of the Great American Novel, examine its relation to encyclopedic literature, and establish the genre’s distinctive formal and thematic features—among them its conventional association with masculinity. We will then assess key scholarly definitions of maximalism against extracts from a range of selected novels—some canonised within the maximalist subcategory of US literature, others long overlooked by scholars of this form. We will do so while pursuing two guiding questions: Why has the maximalist novel come to be understood as a distinctly American narrative form in the postwar era? And how might its earlier, conventional definitions be reconsidered from a twenty-first-century standpoint?

Learning target:
Students will develop the ability to critically analyse literature in relation to intersectional issues of discrimination and representation, particularly the association of size—and, by extension, masculinity—with intellectual and national greatness. They will gain a deeper understanding of literature’s role in shaping national identity and the contribution of writers, critics and scholars to either reinforce or challenge dominant power structures.

Keywords:
fictional maximalism, Great American Novel, US identity, gender, literary excess

Literature:
We will read extracts from the following novels (all provided or available online):

Herman Melville, Moby-Dick

Thomas Pynchon, Gravity’s Rainbow

Leslie Marmon Silko, Almanac of the Dead

William Gaddis, J R

Nicholson Baker, Room Temperature

Nicholson Baker, The Mezzanine

Lucy Ellmann, Ducks, Newburyport

David Foster Wallace, Infinite Jest

Karen Tei Yamashita, I Hotel

All primary and secondary sources will be provided on Moodle, along with information on how/when to approch them in preparation for each class. It is warmly recommended that you do NOT read everything before the beginning of the course: these novels are challenging and it will be easier for you to approach them following the guidelines that I will provide and on a weekly basis during the semester.

Contents:
This seminar adopts a genealogical perspective on popular music and popular culture, focusing on innovations and experimentations that emerge in the 1970s and extend into contemporary digital media cultures. Rather than treating historical periods in isolation, the course traces how mediatechnological transformations reshape the evaluation and appropriation of popular music across five decades. The course has a particular focus on the genealogies of pop-cultural figures.

Contents:
The debate over gun control and gun rights continues to divide the United States. Despite frequent mass shootings, Congress remains unable or unwilling to pass more effective gun regulation. In this seminar we will examine both the history of guns and gun control in America and their current importance in terms of American culture and society. Issues we will discuss include the role of the courts and the Second Amendment; the politics of gun control; the role of special interest groups such as the National Rifle Association (NRA); guns and popular culture; and the societal cost of gun violence.

Contents:
This class is geared at first-year students in the B.A. “Interdisciplinary American Studies.” It is independent of the lecture with the same title taught by Prof. Ingrid Hotz-Davies. Do not sign up for this lecture.

Please note that this class consists of the seminar (taught by Michael Butter on Tuesday ) and the tutorial (taught by Hanna Mekanovic on Monday). You need to attend both in order to get credit.

This seminar will introduce you to the theoretical concepts which are foundational for Cultural Studies. We will discuss how such concepts prove useful for the analysis of a broad range of cultural phenomen and apply them to a wide range of examples such as films, images, political writing and various cultural practices. Thus, we will actually “do” cultural studies, and you will gain a first insight into American cultural history.

Learning target:
In this class, students will be introduced to the most important theories, concepts and methods of cultural studies, and practice their application to a broad variety of examples.

Literature:
Michael Butter, From Panem to the Pandemic: An Introduction to Cultural Studies (Tübingen: Narr, 2023) will serve as a textbook for our class. Buy it or download the e-book from the university libary's website.

Contents:
This seminar introduces students to American theater plays from the 1970s to the present, a period of profound social, political, and artistic transformation. We will explore how playwrights have used the stage to grapple with complex issues of race, gender, sexuality, class, and national identity. We will discuss different dramatic forms and their functions, such as the "choreopoem," the hip-hop musical, and the revival of the family drama. A central focus will be on how theater functions as a site for cultural memory, political resistance, and cultural empowerment, and how it offers a space for imagining new futures. We will investigate how plays respond to historical crises, from the AIDS epidemic to deindustrialization and post-9/11 tensions, and how they dissect the American family and its myths.

On selected Thursday nights from 6-8 p.m., we will watch those film(ed) productions of the plays not generally available (e.g., on YouTube). These screenings are mandatory.

Learning target:
Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to

identify and describe major playwrights, plays, and theatrical movements in the United States from the 1970s to the present.

analyze dramatic texts within their broader historical, political, and cultural contexts.

analyze how issues of race, class, religion, and family are represented on the American stage.

develop and refine critical reading and writing skills for the advanced analysis of dramatic literature.

Literature:
Most required texts and material will be available on Moodle.

Contents:
This course examines how queer YA fantasy and superhero fiction engage with social injustice and power dynamics in US society, while reimagining the figure of the “American hero.” The first two classes introduce the historical development and key features of these genres, with particular attention to biases and debates surrounding diversity. Focusing on four contemporary novels by queer authors from different ethnic backgrounds, we will reflect on literature as a lens for understanding US history and culture, as well as on popular fiction as a site of ideological struggle and a means of visibility and empowerment for marginalized communities. We will also explore the possibilities that the genres under analysis offer to develop an intersectional understanding of discrimination related to race and ethnicity, gender and sexual orientation, and neurodivergence.

Learning target:
Students will develop the ability to critically analyse literary texts in relation to intersectional forms of discrimination and representation in contemporary US society, with particular attention to the popular imaginary of the American hero. They will gain a deeper understanding of how literary representation operates both as a site of empowerment and ideological struggle for marginalized groups and as a means of reinforcing dominant cultural models.

Keywords:
contemporary literature, young adults, fantasy, superheroes, race, gender, queer, US history and culture

Literature:
Primary sources:

Moniquill Blackgoose, To Shape a Dragon’s Breath

Aiden Thomas, Cemetery Boys

Ryan Douglass, The Taking of Jake Livingston

TJ Klune, The Extraordinaries (book 1) (relevant extracts from books 2 & 3 or the series will be provided in due time by the teacher)

All secondary sources will be provided on Moodle, along with information on how/when to approch them in preparation for each class.

Contents:
Spanning from roughly 1967 to 1976, from Bonnie & Clyde to Taxi Driver, New Hollywood marked a significant change in the way American cinema worked. A set of new filmmakers unafraid to challenge the conventions, had an ear for the historical transformations of their time, and an eye for filmic traditions other than Hollywood. Directors like Martin Scorsese, Terrence Malick, Alan J Pakula, Elaine May, Francis Ford Coppola helped define new contracts with their audiences about what movie experience could look like. We will analyze a couple of movies from this important period of American movie-making, discuss the aesthetics and cultural work, and speculate about the contested canonization of this period in film history.

Contents:
Ever since the release of the original movie nearly five decades ago, Star Wars has captured the imagination of audiences around the globe. In this class, we will examine the phenomenon from different angles. We will analyze the films and pay close attention to their narrative structures, recycling of myths, and visual tropes, as well as to their negotiation of politics, race, and gender. We will discuss the impact of the films on Hollywood, and how they have, in turn, been shaped by shifts in the entertainment industry. Therefore, we will also examine the expansion of the Star Wars universe in fiction, TV shows and merchandize. Finally, we will investigate how fans have for half a century engaged with the franchise, how this engagement has been encouraged and curbed by the producers, and how it has had an impact on the shape of the overall narrative.

Literature:
All required reading will be available on Moodle. Students needs access to all products of the Star Wars franchise throughout the semester, for example, through a DisneyPlus subscription.

Contents:
Technological utopias are a central concept for understanding US-American political discourses. Technolibertarianism is a political ideology whose proponents believe in unhindered technological development and minimized government. This ideology has its roots in American libertarianism and early Internet culture.

In the last decade this political ideology has moved from being a fringe idea in Silicon Valley to one of the major political influences shaping the current Trump administration's political actions and institutions such as DOGE.

In class we will explore the history of tech utopias and the ambiguous historical roots of the current technolibertarian ideology by examining writings by Ayn Rand and Max More.

We will use our historical contextualization to understand and critique contemporary technolibertarian thought by figures like Elon Musk and ideas like techno-monarchism.

Contents:
In this seminar, we will explore the American Dream in twentieth- and early twenty-first-century American literature and film. Rather than treating the American Dream as the promise of freedom, personal fulfillment, and upward mobility, we approach it as a cultural myth that is shaped by social, economic, and cultural tensions. With this in mind, we will focus on how cultural texts expose the flaws in the American Dream and its pursuit.

By analysing film and fiction from different decades and their respective historical contexts, students will explore how these works represent and critique the American Dream through themes such as disillusionment, conformity and rebellion, immigration, and inequality.

The film screenings are MANDATORY and will take place after the seminar sessions!

Literature:
Fiction:

Arthur Miller, Death of a Salesman

F. Scott Fitzgerald, The Great Gatsby

Film:

Francis Ford Coppola, The Godfather II (1974)

Sam Mendes, American Beauty (1999)

Additional film tba

Contents:
The class will focus on 19th century anti-slavery abolitionist texts and their political and social contexts for the first part of the semester.

We will read key works by authors such as Frederick Douglass and Harriet Jacobs. We will also investigate popular anti-slavery texts such as Uncle Tom's Cabin and trace how such texts can be both anti-slavery and contribute to racist stereotyping at the same time.

In the last third of the semester we will look at later instances of abolitionist writing calling i.e. to defund the police or end the current American prison system and investigate how these more contemporary texts by authors such as Angela Davis might connect to the 19th century tradition.

Literature:
Please buy the following books:

Richard S. Newman: Abolitionism: A Very Short Introduction. New York, NY: Oxford University Press, 2018.

Harriet Beecher Stowe: Uncle Tom's Cabin, i.e. the Bantam Classics edition

Henry Louis Gates Jr.: The Classic Slave Narratives

Contents:
When the movie Black Panther some scholars of 19th Century African American Literature realized that it not only builds on the superhero tradition in film - it also builds on a trope that is well know in stories that are more than 100 years old: a black ideal(ized) community hidden somewhere in Africa or Texas or Georgia. We will have a look at these texts that are sometimes read as Black Science Fiction or Black Utopias. We will discuss these genres and their history and then move into the present to Octavia Butler's Parable of the Sower, for instance. Or Black Panther.

There will be a moodle page with texts for you - for the beginning please read W. E. B. Du Bois' short story "The Comet."

Contents:
This course will provide a basic understanding of the most important parts and elements of the U.S. political system, including federalism, Congress, the Presidency, the Supreme Court, the Constiution, public opinion, and elections. We will pay particular attention to the ways in which the Trump Administration is trying to change the system in the run-up to the 2026 mid-term elections in November.

Contents:
The aim of this course is to help you develop basic insights into the workings of American foreign policy and into the main developments in America's engagement with the world since 1945. Some of the topics we'll examine are: the origins of the Cold War, the interconnections between domestic politics and foreign policy, and the question why the United States ended up fighting a number of wars in this period.

This is the first of three courses IAS students can take to specialize in U.S. foreign policy.

Contents:
The end of the Cold War and the collapse of the Soviet Union seemed to open the door to much-improved relations between the United States and Russia. A democratic Russia in an integrating Europe as the basis for a new, more peaceful world order, seemed to be within grasp. So how did we end up in the current situation? We will pay particular attention to the growth of NATO, nuclear strategy, and Russian attempts to create a sphere of dominance in its immediate neighborhood (including Russian aggression against Ukraine).

Contents:
War photography plays an important role in the development of media and journalism. In class we will be examining the development of war phtography beginning with the Crimean War and discussing questions such as authentictiy, authorship and propaganda.

Contents:
This course invites students to reflect on the range of meanings encompassed by the term "text", through the study of two novels (one in dialogue with its film adaptation), a novella, a memoir, and a play from different historical periods and cultural contexts. We will pay particular attention to the ways in which writing inscribes the body, the body functions as a readable text, and embodiment itself becomes a site and process of meaning-making. The course also foregrounds how the concept of the “body as text” has historically developed within predominantly male literary and critical traditions, often positioning the female body as its object of representation and interpretation. We will read primary texts alongside selected works of literary theory to support critical analysis and discussion. Beyond its central focus on body and text, the course also explores how literature across genres and media engages with concerns of health and illness, and how such concerns shape the ways bodies are imagined, narrated, and interpreted.

Learning target:
Students will learn to think critically about "text" and to analyze how texts engage with issues of health, illness, and embodiment in connection to wider historical and cultural contexts. They will develop the ability to examine how bodies are written, read, and interpreted within different narrative forms, and how such representations participate in processes of meaning-making.

Keywords:
text, body, gender, male gaze, health and illness in literature

Literature:
Primary sources:

Alasdair Gray, Poor Things (novel) + Yorgos Lanthimos's Poor Things (film)

Please consider buying the paperback or hardback 1992 Bloomsbury edition with illustrations (or later printings of this edition, of course. Ebooks probably do not include illustrations and the reading experience with the physical book in this case will be important to our discussion of the novel)

The other primary sources will be provided on Moodle:

Katherine Anne Porter, Pale Horse, Pale Rider (novella)

Carmen Maria Machado, In the Dream House (memoir)

Lisa Kron, Well (theatre play, very short)

Katherine Dunn, Geek Love (novel)

All secondary sources will be provided on Moodle, along with information on how/when to approch them in preparation for each class.

Contents:
This module provides an overview on the basics of international taxation. The taxation of different forms of international investments and the tax effects caused by the financing decisions made on these international investments will be closer looked at. Furthermore the influence of the EU on taxation will be described.

Learning target:
Students assess the enormous impact that changes in transaction structure have on after-tax cash flows and to integrate tax strategies into the bigger picture of corporate decision making. They explain the competitive advantage of certain tax strategies for corporations. As a side effect, students will be faced with basic tax law principles and, thereby, will broaden their knowledge about legal issues.

Literature:
Erickson, Merle/ Hanlon, Michelle L./ Maydew, Edward L./ Shevlin, Terry (2019): Scholes and Wolfson’s Taxes and Business Strategy, 6th edition, New Jersey.

Schreiber, Ulrich (2012): Besteuerung der Unternehmen, 3. Aufl., Heidelberg.

Scheffler, Wolfram (2016): Besteuerung von Unternehmen I, 13. Aufl., Heidelberg.

Contents:
This module focuses on the effects of taxation on essential corporate decisions, namely, investment, financing, acquisitions or the choice of the appropriate legal form. Since specific tax law is not the main part of this approach, the module can be chosen even by students without an in-depth knowledge in tax law. Nonetheless, it provides a broad framework for understanding how taxation affects corporate decision-making. No specific prerequisites are required.

Learning target:
During this course students will obtain an in-depth knowledge in derivatives pricing by using continuous-time concepts of modern finance theory as well as their application to equity and other securities. Having completed this course, students will be able to approach the literature in this field successfully and apply continuous-time techniques for arbitrary derivatives pricing challenges.

Literature:
Hull, J. (2014): Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives, 9th ed., Upper Saddle River.

Shreve, S. (2010): Stochastic Calculus for Finance II: Continuous-Time Models, 2nd ed., Springer Finance.

Contents:
The module of advanced topics in international financial reporting and risk management explains and connects the following concepts: financial scandals, earnings management, agency theory, information asymmetry, IFRS, properties of financial information, role of external auditors, diversifiable versus market risk, market efficiency and crisis. Students will be introduced to the current state of empirical/theoretical literature that links financial reporting and risk management.

Literature:
At the beginning of the seminar students will be provided with three individualized research papers of international journals as an introduction to their respective essay topic. These papers are meant to form a base-line to their research.

Comment:
The examination office has agreed that both courses (Portfoliomanagement and Computational Finance in Python) may be taken.

Learning target:
Students develop in-depth knowledge of advanced finance concepts. They are able to apply these concepts to arbitrary securities classes in the context of modern finance challenges. Having completed this module, students approach the literature in this field successfully and are able to develop, control and evaluate advanced problems in finance.

Learning target:
Participating students will obtain in-depth knowledge of a special topic by carrying out individual analyses and writing a thesis. The ability to critically evaluate these findings is enhanced by presentations and discussions in class.

Contents:
The module initially deals with exchange rates and currency risks as the fundamentals of international financial management. Hedging and speculation as important strategic approaches to exchange rate risk management are introduced and dealt with in depth using numerous instruments. This includes the interaction with investment decisions. The special features of international finance are illustrated using direct investments and various aspects of corporate finance.

Literature:
Breuer, Wolfgang, 2000: "Unternehmerisches Währungsmanagement. Eine anwendungsorientierte Einführung", 2. Auflage, Wiesbaden, Gabler.

Moffett, Michael H., Stonehill, Arthur I. and Eiteman, David K., 2003: "Fundamentals of Multinational Finance", Boston, Addison-Wesley.

Shapiro, Alan C., 2010: "Multinational Financial Management", 9th Ed., New York, Wiley.

Contents:
In this
course we introduce you to sustainability issues and perspectives in the
context of finance and provide hands on skills for sustainable investing.

The
sustainable investments course is designed to give you the skills,
understanding and credentials in this growing field of finance. Global funds
under management are quickly moving to an ESG, responsible, impact or
sustainable investing approach. Due to this shift the market for investment
analysts and managers with the skills taught in this course is expanding rapidly.

This paper
may also help prepare you for postgraduate study in Sustainable Finance and/or
Business.

Contents:
The module covers the material for one of the three CFA® levels. Standards of practice, detailed finance, accounting, and security valuation tools are included. The curriculum, in class mock exams and the final exam resemble a portion of the respective CFA® level exam. Each level is offered triennially, for detailed information please have a look at the chair homepage.

Contents:
In this course, students acquire knowledge about

current economic challenges for financial institutions due to the low interest rate environment, digitalization-driven innovations such as cryptocurrencies and smart contracts as well as social transformation processes with regard to sustainability.

current regulatory challenges for financial institutions such as Basel IV, IFRS 9 and 13, MARisk, EMIR and MiFID

the impact of these challenges on business models, corporate governance, processes and methods.

Contents:
This module analyzes the decision-facilitating and strategic role of managerial accounting. Managers have the responsibility and authority for making decisions with respect to the acquisition and the use of an organization’s resources. To effectivley do this, they must identify the actions or strategies available to them, predict the relevant consequences of those actions, and then choose the action that has the most preferred predicted outcome. Management accounting systems can be effective tools in providing information that is useful in predicting the possible consequences of alternative actions and in presenting a description of those consequences.

Contents:
Firms need to react to recent developments in corporate governance, global competition, and continuous technological change by adjusting their organizational structure. This module provides a multidisciplinary approach to managerial and organization economics, with a special focus on accounting information and the internal organization of firms. After a general introduction to organizational architecture as a management device, the module topics relate to allocating tasks within organizations, rewarding managerial performance, and measuring managerial performance.

Comment:
formerly known as: Managerial Economics and Organizational Architecture - Lecture

Learning target:
Students learn how to use and implement accounting information for efficiently designing and operating an organization. They understand the role of incentive and performance management systems for firms and are able to critically evaluate the use of these systems. The goal in this module is to develop rigorous frameworks to enable students to apply them to real‐life problems. In the accompanying practice course, students will develop solutions to these problems and apply them to organizational problem settings.

Contents:

1. Data Collection

This course will be held in Room 111, Wilhelmstrasse 26.

The course introduces Buddhism in India and Japan through close reading and discussion of a curated selection of primary sources in English translation. Rather than offering a comprehensive historical survey, the course uses original texts—canonical excerpts, medieval Japanese writings, and modern reflections—to explore how Buddhist authors and communities articulated key ideas and negotiated practice across time and place.

Across the semester we will read texts connected to the Buddha’s life narratives, core teachings (such as impermanence and no-self), and the formation of Buddhist communities (sangha and vinaya). We will then trace how Buddhism took root and transformed in Japan, focusing on early Japanese Buddhism and its relationship to the State, and on major currents such as Zen and Pure Land. We will also examine modern and contemporary debates, including the legalization of clerical marriage in the late nineteenth century and its impact on temple life.

The first two sessions explicitly frame our approach: we will reflect on different ways of studying Buddhism and on the place of texts within Buddhist traditions. We will also critically discuss the history of Buddhist Studies and its tendency to treat texts as the sole—or “most original”—access point to Buddhism. In other words, while our main material will be primary texts in translation, we will read them with methodological self-awareness, attending to genre, audience, historical context, and the limits of textual sources for understanding lived religion.

Contents:
This course offers an in-depth discussion of Christianity in India. With approximately 27.5 million followers, Christianity is the third-largest religion in India. We begin with an overview of the major denominations of Christianity in the different regions of India. After this, the course will look at three major epochs of Christianity in India.

Tradition places Christianity in India to Apostolic times. “Thomas Christians”, as they are called now, amalgamated themselves into the Hindu Caste System, developing their own distinct pollution rules.

The first part of the course will look at the “Thomas Christians”, and their cultural and social presence in South India.

The second part of the course gives a detailed overview of the advent of Catholicism in “Colonial” India—pre and post Portuguese “Patronage” missionaries, the Protestant activities under the Dutch Colonial era, and the evangelical activities under the British rule.

The third part of the course discusses the status of Christians in post-independent India.

Contents:
The analytical frameworks presented in this lecture provide a deeper understanding of the role of global interdependency on economic development in emerging economies: “What are the main drivers behind economic growth and what is the role of globalization for growth potentials in developing countries?”

A natural starting point for the analysis of these questions is a discussion of economic growth. Hence, Part 1 provides a theoretical background based upon the Solow model of economic growth and an illustration of related empirical growth studies. First, we tackle the question, "Why do countries grow?" Capital formation is one potential source of economic growth, but its growth potential is limited without technological change.

Based on the understanding of this model, we will ask why some nations failed to grow by focusing on the middle income trap.

Besides growth and trade, the other face of globalization is international migration, which constitutes the subject of part two of this course. The “loss” of individuals due to migration away from developing countries has been a crucial topic both for academic and policy debates. Hence, the aim of this chapter is to provide an overview of the international migration movements and the interrelated brain drain phenomenon. Specifically, we answer the following question: “Why do people migrate and how does migration affect economic development?" In doing so, we review the theoretical frameworks that provide explanations behind the individual migration decision (that is, at the micro-level). We then proceed by answering the same question from the aggregate perspective. Not all individuals from a given population have the same propensity to migrate. Thus, we inquire about who chooses to migrate, stressing the importance of the issue of the immigrants’ “selectivity” for the study of migration. Finally, we offer a brief overview of the economic effects of immigration on the host country.

The last part will be focusing on the interaction between globalization and economic development. Once we open the economic growth model studied in Part 1 to international trade in goods and factors, i.e. migration and foreign direct investments, the pattern of economic growth is substantially different.

A sound knowledge of the basic models in economic growth and international trade is an advantage, but it is not a prerequisite. The course presents all the models from scratch and detailed explanations of the relevant mathematical and econometric tools will be discussed during the lecture.

Learning target:
Recognize important challenges developing economies are facing in an interdependent world

Understand the consequences of economic development in the South for the North

Develop a sound knowledge in modelling these challenges

Auch die kulturellen Voraussetzungen literarischer Produktion im Mittelalter sind einzubeziehen: Literatur und Medialität (Mündlichkeit, Schriftlichkeit, Buchdruck), Literatur und Gesellschaft (Kloster, Hof, Stadt), Funktionalität von Literatur. Topics to be covered include: Heterogeneous-agent macroeconomic models. Search, matching and equilibrium unemployment. Dynamic programming. Solution Methods of General Equilibrium models.

Outline

1. Tools for Studying Dynamic Economies

(a) Dynamic Programming

(b) Numerical Dynamic Programming

(c) Applications to Neoclassical Growth and Search, Matching and Unemployment

2. Self Insurance and Incomplete Markets Models (Theory)

(a) Self Insurance (partial equilibrium)

(b) Bewley Models

3. Heterogeneous-agents in Macroeconomics (Applications)

(a) Household heterogeneity

(b) Firm heterogeneity

4. Equilibrium Unemployment Theory

(a) Theory

(b) Applications

• Numerical problem sets, solved on a computer

– Neoclassical growth model – using the social planner’s problem

– Stochastic growth model (RBC) – planner’s problem

– Neoclassical growth model – competitive equilibrium

– Incomplete markets model (Huggett-Aiyagari)

– Basic McCall job search model

• Analytical problem sets, pen and paper

– some full analytical solutions

– some characterizations of the problem and describing an algorithm to solve it on a computer

Objectives

Students get acquainted with two major features of modern economies. The first is the large dispersion across households and firms in income and wealth, the second is the existence of persistent unemployment. Students will understand the causes and consequences of dispersion or, put differently, economic inequality. They will do so by learning the models and tools that macroeconomists have developed to represent these phenomena. With the help of these models, students will then analyse the welfare implications of various government interventions aimed at reducing inequality.

One goal of the course is to give students the opportunity to learn how to use a computer to solve economic models that may not have a “pen and paper” solution. This will allow students to consider richer models of economic behaviour and will hopefully inspire them to be ambitious in research ideas.

Contents:
The course "Microbial Glycobiology & Cell Wall" deals with the compound class of carbohydrates (sugars). The emphasis lies on the metabolism of bacterial carbohydrates and glycoconjugates including the bacterial cell wall (peptidoglycan, teichoic acids) and analytic techniques for carbohydrates such as high-performance liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (HPLC-MS). The theoretical part will cover the chemical and biological basics of carbohydrates, glycoconjugates and polysaccharides, the physiology of bacterial carbohydrates and the enzymology of carbohydrate acting enzymes. Moreover, the theory behind techniques for carbohydrates analysis will be addressed. In the practical part different lab methods will be applied including hands-on training in mass spectrometry.

Learning target:
In this 4-week practical course you will learn about sugars (carbohydrates), how they react, how they can be analyzed, how they are metabolized and you have the opportunity to work on a topic closely related to a PhD-project conducted in the lab that will be supervised by a PhD student. The first week starts with lectures and basic experimental work (block course) that will provide the theoretical background and experiments introducing sugars. The second and third week is dedicated to practical work related to our own research topics in the lab. In the last week you will present your work and will get time to prepare a protocol.

Qualification objective:
You will learn about the compound class of carbohydrates (sugars) which constitute important polymers in bacteria.

The course will provide you with a detailled knowledge about how carbohydrates react and how they can be analyzed.

State of the art information will be provided on how carbohydrates are metabolised by bacteria, how carbohydrate polymers

of the bacterial cell wall are synthesized, and how these pathways are regulated.

You will practically work on a current research topic of the group, related to the understanding the action of antibiotics targeting the bacterial cell wall.

Keywords:
bacterial carbohydrate metabolism, mechanism of cell wall-targeting antibiotics, peptidoglycan, teichoic acids, capsular polysaccharides, mass spectrometry

Contemporary Muslim Theology and Interfaith Engagement in the West seminar examines key debates shaping Muslim theological discourses and interfaith engagements in European and North American contexts, introducing students to contemporary approaches to scripture, tradition, and reason as they intersect with pluralistic societies. The course foregrounds Muslim relations with other faith and non-faith communities; explores purpose, vocation, and service as theological practices; and critically reflects on violence and nonviolence, human dignity, justice, peace-building, and stewardship of the earth. By the end, students will: (1) map major currents and interlocutors in contemporary Muslim theology; (2) analyze case studies of interfaith, and non-religious engagements and public theology; (3) evaluate theological arguments regarding ethics of violence, rights, and environmental responsibility; and AI ethics (4) articulate a values-grounded personal stance on service and civic contribution; and (5) practice constructive theological writing for diverse publics.

Beginning with scriptural texts it will further analyse theological, spiritual and philosophical texts focusing on death, life in the hereafter, resurrection, heaven and hell, and other relevant themes that fall under the category of Sam'iyyat. Contents:
This seminar offers a close reading of Abū al-ʿAbbās al-Qurṭubī’s al-Iʿlām, a key text of Muslim responses to Christian critique in medieval al-Andalus. Focusing on the 13th-century context, the course examines how Christian arguments are presented, reformulated, and systematically refuted.

Students will work directly with selected passages from the Arabic text. The seminar develops skills in reading complex theological prose, with particular attention to argumentative structure, key concepts, and strategies of refutation. Central topics include the Trinity, the Incarnation, and questions of scriptural authority.

After a brief introduction to the historical and intellectual context, the main part of the course is devoted to guided close reading sessions. Students will also engage with questions of textual analysis, focusing on the identification of argumentative structures and strategies of refutation, and explore the use of AI-based tools to support the study of premodern Arabic texts.

Contents:
Dieser Kurs ist speziell als Übersetzungsübung für Nicht-Muttersprachler konzipiert (wobei alle Interessierten herzlich willkommen sind!).

Warum dieser Kurs?

Ich denke jeder kennt das Gefühl: Man beherrscht die Grammatik eigentlich ganz gut, aber sobald man vor einer ganzen Seite voller Schriftzeichen steht, wirkt der Text überwältigend. Das Hauptziel dieses Kurses ist es daher, die „Angst vor dem großen Text“ abzubauen. Wir wollen gemeinsam die Hemmschwelle senken, flüssiger in größere Textmengen einzutauchen und dabei die fortgeschrittenen Strukturen aus unserem Lehrbuch in der Praxis wiederzuerkennen.

Kursinhalt: Die Welt der Chinese Webnovels

In diesem Semester nutzen wir das populäre Format der Webnovels als Material. Der Kurs ist in drei Phasen unterteilt:

1. Hintergrund & Kontext: Wir lesen Texte über die gesellschaftspolitische Bedeutung von Online-Literatur in China.

2. Genre-Einblicke: Wir schauen uns kurze Ausschnitte aus unterschiedlichen Webnovel Genres an. Die können beispielweise sein:

Xianxia (仙侠): „High Fantasy“, die tief in daoistischer Mythologie und Kultivierung verwurzelt ist.

System-Novels / LitRPG (系统流): Ein modernes Genre, in dem Charaktere wie in einem Videospiel agieren (mit Level-ups, Quests und Statusanzeigen).

Danmei (耽美): Das populäre „Boy’s Love“-Genre und seine kulturellen Nischen.

3. Gemeinsame Lektüre: Als Kurs entscheiden wir uns für eines dieser Bücher, das uns am meisten interessiert, und lesen es gemeinsam über den Rest des Semesters hinweg.

Das Ziel: Am Ende des Kurses sollen Sie sich einfach „dran trauen“, wenn Sie ein längeres chinesisches Kapitel aufschlagen. Es geht nicht um perfekte Übersetzung, sondern um das Vertrauen, auch umfangreiche Texte bewältigen zu können.

Contents:
This class introduces students to the history of anatomical and pathological collections in China. It first discusses the historical background of the introduction of anatomy to China in the early 20th century, and then focuses on the role visual sources and material specimens played in the production of epistemological cathegories, such as the "normal" and the "pathological". The theoretical foundation of the discussion of these materials is Focault's teacher Canguilhem, who discussed the normativity behind the normal and the patholgoical. Students will further be informed about ethical debates discussed around the preparation and display of anatomical and pathological displays. Primary sources from the 1950s, 1960s, and 1970s further introduce how anatomical specimens (jieoou biaoben) were crafted in China. Comparative approaches further shed light on the histories of pathological collections in the USA and Germany. Students are also encouraged ot understand their own university's collection, learning about the exhibition on Entgrenzte Anatomy and the current exhibition practices of the anatomy department of the University of Tübingen.

This class is open to all students, Chinenese language skills are not required. Text provided in Chinese for students of Sinology can be substituted by texts in English or German, if students join from other disciplines.

The class is taught in English.

Contents:
This class introduces students to the history of Biomedicine or "Western" medicine in China.

It first introduces the origins of clinical medicine in Paris of the early 18th century, and discusses the role missionaries played in transmitting anatomical knowledge to China in the 18th and 19th centuries. We then continue to focus on the establishment of hospitals in China in the early 20th centuries, discussing the role of individual actors (from doctors to nurses), as well as the relationship between medicine and the state. The class highlights that various competing schools of medicine existed in the first half of the 20th century, that are often subsumed under the umbrella term "Western medicine".

Practice-oriented sessions will further introduce students to a range of primary sources, with the help of which they can develop their own research projects (for example term papers), including the anatomy laws (e.g. from 1913/14-1979) as well a resources portal on "The History of Western Medicine in China", which guides students through collections in the USA, Canada, Europe and China.

The class is open to all students, Chinese language skills are not required. Texts provided in Chinese for students of Sinology can be substituted by texts in English or German, if students join from other disciplines.

The class is taught in English.

The first class session will take place Tuesday April 21, 2026.

Contents:
The drive for modernisation has been a persistent issue in China for the past 150 years. China’s defeat by Western powers prompted the launch of the Self-Strengthening Movement between 1860 and 1890. Japan’s rapid “modernisation” enabled it to defeat not only China, the erstwhile teacher, in 1895, but also Russia in 1905. This opened China’s eyes to the idea that being a “modern” and thus a strong nation also meant transforming its political, educational, and economic subsystems. The failure of successive and parallel governments during the Republican era urged Chinese intellectuals to call ever more radically for modernisation. With the foundation of the People’s Republic, all obstacles to future development seemed to have been removed, yet a veritable “modernisation” of the state, economy, society, and culture did not come until the 1980s. After 40 years, China seems to have, in many respects, reached and even surpassed Western competitors, though it still lacks (or has even lost) some colours in the panoply that constitutes “modernity”.

The seminar will build on differing theories of modernisation as an analytical tool to evaluate trends and policies of modernisation from the late 19th to the early 21st century. Based on various modernisation theories, the students will study individual cases and phases in China’s modern and contemporary history to identify core problems and central issues in attempts to modernise the country. They will understand the difficulties of definition, evaluate the standpoints of participants in the historical debates, point out contradictions and lacunae in the political strategies adapted over time, and explain why certain aspects of modernity are less significant in a Sinitic society.

Case studies:

Self-strengthening movement; resilience of culture and social norms; modernisation under the KMT; was Mao modern?; schooling system; Deng Xiaoping’s Four Modernisations; China’s modernisation in a global environment; technical steering of societies (social engineering); reduction of absolute poverty; ways of life; national security; state-funded high technologies;

Contents:
This seminar introduces the "developmental state" as one of the most influential paradigms for explaining East Asia's postwar transformation. The core puzzle is how economies such as Japan, South Korea, and Taiwan achieved rapid industrial growth while, for significant periods, maintaining comparatively broad-based gains that are often framed as "growth with equity". We will reconstruct the classic arguments in developmental state scholarship to clarify the concept's core claims about state capacity, industrial policy, and state-business relations, and to understand why the East Asian experience became a global reference point in debates about development strategy.

Building on the canonical cases, the seminar then asks two larger questions: how far does the paradigm travel, and how useful is it today? We will examine contested applications of the developmental state framework to China and engage major critiques, especially those that bring social forces, class relations, and labour back into the picture and challenge overly state-centric accounts. Finally, we assess contemporary relevance under conditions of globalization and democratization, and in light of newer challenges such as financialization and ecological transition. Has the developmental state adapted, transformed, or lost explanatory power? The seminar is intended for students with different regional specializations in Japan, Korea, Taiwan, and China.

The course consists of 3 components:

(1) A test of your knowledge of common Red Sea reef fishes, which you can acquire by using the Reef Fish Trainer for the Red Sea.

(https://uni-tuebingen.de/de/251585)

(2) 21-day field course to Mangrove Bay, 30 km south of El Quseir, Red Sea (Egypt). During the first week, participants familiarize themselves with the coral reef ecosystem and its inhabitants at the species-rich house reef. The area includes the full gradient from exposed reef slopes to shallow mangrove forests within snorkeling distance. As a central course component, students develop small independent research projects. After formulating a working hypothesis, they use the remaining 1.5-2 weeks for data collection. All projects will be extensively supported, discussed and evaluated during meetings. Projects take place in teams of two students. In between, we offer at least one full-day boat trip to a distant reef. All projects are presented in short talks to the hotel guests and dive base staff. The focus of the projects is on reef walks and snorkelling. A dive certificate is not required, but diving is possible for those who are already certified. Diving conditions are very safe and ideal for people with little diving experience. Both course leaders are professional level divers (Divemaster and Instructor) and can help you further your diving skills. Diving is not included in the course price and needs to be covered by the participants.

(3) Brief report about the findings from the research project in Mangrove Bay, including the classic components of a scientific paper i.e. Introduction, Materials & Methods, Results, Discussion. To be written in Tübingen, after returning from Egypt.

Contents:
An improved understanding of viruses and their host interactions, as well as recent biotechnological methods, have led to a paradigm shift: Once thought to be dangerous threats, viruses are now increasingly being used to develop new therapies. In addition to viruses for gene therapy, virus-based vaccines and oncolytic viruses for the therapy of tumors represent important and promising approaches or even approved drugs. In this seminar, different virus-based therapy approaches to combat cancer will be studied, and various issues in this context discussed. These include challenges in the development of effective therapeutic approaches in the field, the mode of action of different technologies, new developments and the resulting opportunities for their application, as well as the influence of the immune system.

Beyond the sole transfer of knowledge, the critical handling of scientific literature represents a major objective of this seminar.

Contents:
The focus of this course is the identification and isolation of new antibiotics from actinomycetes using modern methods in genomics (genome mining) and analytics (HPLC/MS; MS/MS).

In the theoretical part, the biosynthesis of the major antibiotic classes, the fundamentals of regulation and engineering of antibiotic biosynthetic gene clusters, as well as chemical methods for antibiotic identification, are covered. Additionally, the basics of key sequencing techniques, genome analysis, sequence assembly, and annotation are addressed.

In the practical part, the genomes of selected actinomycetes are sequenced using Oxford Nanopore technology and analyzed bioinformatically. Subsequently, the genome sequences are screened with genome-mining tools to identify new biosynthetic gene clusters in the producer strains. To isolate the antibiotics encoded by these gene clusters, the strains are cultured, and the biologically active substances are purified chromatographically.

Contents:
PCM12A - Optical Spectroscopy of Conjugated Organic Materials

Optical Spectroscopy of Conjugated Organic Materials

PD Dr. Johannes Gierschner, IMDEA Nanoscience, Madrid, and IPTC, University of Tübingen

Chromophores, based on -conjugated organic molecules, are of eminent importance in chemistry, materials science, biology and pharmacy as dyes, pigments and functional components in opto-electronic devices, such as optical switches, sensors, lasers, organic LEDs and solar cells. Analysis of the working principles and design of novel compounds requires however a deep understanding of structure-property relationships in solution and - more challenging - in the solid state, ideally at a predictive level.

The lecture series - given in two block courses (16 h each) - chromophores in solution (WS), and in the solid state (SS) - will give a thorough introduction to this subject. This combines spectroscopy, photophysics, quantum chemistry, (physical) chemistry, and materials science, to complement the existing local lectures in physical chemistry in this important and interdisciplinary field of research.

Part A "Chromophores in Solution" (WS) will discuss the basics of light-matter interaction (classical & quantum-chemical description), electronic excitations of single organic chromophores (MO description, configuration interaction), selection rules, chemical constitution & absorption (chainlength dependence, substitution, solvent shifts), vibronic coupling, line broadening, excited state deactivation; experimental techniques (absorption spectroscopy)

Part B "Chromophores in the Solid State" (SS) will deal with interacting chromophores from the weak coupling regime (supramolecular host-guest systems) to the medium/strong coupling regime (nanoparticles, films and single crystals), addressing generation of molecular excitons (H/J-aggregates, CT complexes, and its proper theoretical description), energy/exciton transport (exchange/Coulomb mechanism), and deactivation (emission, trapping etc.); techniques (fluorescence, light scattering, reflection, refraction).

Contents:
This lecture comprises different areas of Medical Data Science. Data Science or statistical machine learning methods have the potential to transform personal health care over the coming years. Advances in the technologies have generated large biological data sets. In order to gain insights that can then be used to improve preventive care or treatment of patients, these big data have to be stored in a way that enables fast querying of relevant characteristics of the data and consequently building statistical models that represent the dependencies between variables. These models can then be utilized to derive new biomedical principals, provide evidence for or against certain hypotheses, and to assist medical professionals in their decision process.

Specific topics are:

Gaining new insights from medical data

Modeling uncertainty in medical data science models

Making medical findings available through interpretable decision support systems

Method-wise, the lecture will introduce methods for GWAS analyses (e.g., LMMs), methods for sequence analysis (e.g., kernel methods), methods for ”small n problems” (e.g., domain adaptation, transfer learning, and multitask learning), methods for data integration (advanced unsupervised learning methods), methods for learning probabilistic Machine Learning models (e.g., graphical models), methods for large data sets (e.g., deep learning models)

Contents:
Algorithmic systems are tools of governance when they are used to determine how social roles are assigned and how social goods are distributed. They influence the support unemployed receive; how health care resources are allocated among patients; and whether prisoners are released or detained before trial. As companies and public administrations entrust increasingly significant predictions and decisions to algorithmic systems, data scientists and machine learning practitioners are empowered to determine aspects of the structure of our societies. Attending their rise in power and prestige is a growing chorus of critics calling for fairness, justice, and democratic accountability in algorithmic decision-making. These developments are, in their technological aspect, unprecedented. At the same time, the questions they raise concerning the just distribution of social goods and roles belong to the most traditional areas of philosophical inquiry.

This course introduces students to (1) recent technical literature in algorithmic fairness, (2) empirical evaluations of allocation mechanisms, and (3) classic philosophical work on the just distribution of social roles and goods. We stress the continuity between contemporary problems in algorithmic fairness and similar difficulties that predate machine learning. Engaging with literature drawn from a wide range of disciplines will present significant challenges but, we hope, yield equally significant rewards.

The seminar will be held in English.

Contents:
This course examines the teaching of philosophy in Late Antiquity and Early Byzantium, with particular attention to pedagogical practices in logic, ontology, and ethics. The course explores several case studies drawn from historical educational contexts, illustrating how logical puzzles were taught to be solved, how coherent ontological systems were trained to be constructed, and how ethical dilemmas were learned to be addressed. Students will analyze weekly short excerpts from primary sources. Knowledge of Latin or Greek is useful but not required, as all texts will be provided in English. Assignments include either an oral presentation or a written essay. Comparative perspectives are welcome, such as modern philosophical curricula in various countries or historical examples of different educational programs.

Contents:
Recent decades have witnessed an explosion of studies on the lived experiences and agency of women of the past. The debate that surrounds this flourishing of gender studies and women’s studies reminds us of the urgency and importance of reintegrating female histories in historical narratives in order to have a fuller, deeper, and more meaningful comprehension of past societies. Ancient history has been a vital part of this momentous trend: accordingly, this course will provide the students with an introduction to the history of women in the Roman world, with a focus on female condition(s) in the Roman Mediterranean empire (1st-3rd centuries CE). We will explore a wide range of themes related to female presence, representation, and agency in the Imperial world. After an introduction on the prodromes of these phenomena in Republican Rome and Hellenistic Greece, the classes will extensively deal with the impact that the unifying yet flexible imperial framework had on the social, political, cultural, and economic lives of women both in the Eastern and Western parts of the Roman empire. This will be possible thanks to the examination of a wide-ranging selection of sources – from theatre to poetry, from medical texts to rhetoric and historiographical works, from inscriptions to papyri, all the while integrating insights from material culture, iconography, and numismatics. With this course, students will learn how to approach diverse sources from a critical perspective and to engage with far-reaching international debates and the possibility to use theorical frameworks to investigate ancient women’s lives. By learning to see through Roman women’s eyes, I aim at bringing the students in contact with new exciting and innovative ways to tell the history of the past in all its complex, vibrant, and manifold expressions

Lesson Plan

The course is divided in two main parts. Part 1 (lessons 1-4) will provide an overview on the sources to reconstruct the history of women during the Roman empire, and an introduction on the female condition during the Hellenistic and Republican periods. Part 2 (lessons 5-14) presents a thematic structure: in each lesson, we will discuss the role of Graeco-Roman women in specific societal contexts and/or roles, in order to situate them in their political, cultural, and social milieu and to reconstruct a polycentric history of the ancient world. 1. Lesson 1, 13.04.2026: Introduction to the subject; ancient women in modern scholarship, catalogues and repertoires of sources Lesson 2, 20.04.2026: Women in the Hellenistic world Lesson 3, 27.04.2026: Women in Republican Rome Lesson 4, 04.05.2026: The emergence of the imperial framework; female condition under the Roman empire 2. Lesson 5, 11.05.2026: Female representation in the Roman West: written sources and iconography Lesson 6, 18.05.2026: Female representation in the Roman East: written sources and iconography Lesson 7, 01.06.2026: Imitatio Augustae: empresses as models and trendsetters Lesson 8, 08.06.2026: Pious women: religion and the role of priestesses Lesson 9, 15.06.2026: Women in politics: crowdfunding and magistracy-holding Lesson 10, 22.06.2026: Literate women as authors Lesson 11, 29.06.2026: All about family: roles of women in family law, social reproduction, and glocalism Lesson 12, 06.07.2026: Women as donors: euergetism as an economic and political tool Lesson 13, 13.07.2026: Working women: businesswomen, merchants, prostitutes, artisans, slaves… Lesson 14, 20.07.2026: The private sphere

Contents:
This course introduces students to the ways in which the New Deal reconciled democracy and capitalism in the face of major economic, diplomatic, and military crises throughout the 1930s and 1940s. Rather than give life to yet another nation-centered interpretation of the New Deal, this course invites students to consider both the domestic and international reach of the democratic administration which redefined the American experience by regulating business and agriculture, recalibrating foreign policy, introducing labor protections, and eventually mobilizing the American population for a second world war. But to what extent were certain New Deal policies distinct, national variations of a larger, transnational pattern of adaptive governance? How can the Roosevelt administration’s emphasis on cultural production and identity help us make sense of the New Deal’s ultimate goals? By the end of the course, students will be prepared to weigh in on the current historiographic debates surrounding the New Deal order and present their findings in the form of a final paper. The class will be held in English.

Contents:
This course intends to bring together students of History and American Studies from the University of Tübingen and the LMU Munich to explore documentary filmmaking as both an evolving cinematic genre and a powerful form of public history. Rather than treating documentaries as neutral records of the past, we will analyze them within broader debates in American historiography and deliberate on their potential function as interventions in public discourse as well as their impact on civic knowledge and collective memory.

Central to the course are key questions concerning the aesthetics and narrative strategies of documentary film: How do elements such as music, editing, and visual composition shape our perception of historical events? What roles do historians play in the making and reception of documentaries? And to what extent can documentary films themselves be understood as historical sources?

The seminar will be structured in two introductory sessions on April 14 and April 28, as well as two block sessions (May 15-17 in Tübingen, June 19-21 in Munich). During these sessions, we will screen and discuss seminal documentary films and engage in discussions with prominent US documentary filmmakers and historians.

Funding is being sought to cover travel costs and accommodation in Munich. However, partial costs may still arise.

Contents:
This five-week course highlights the relevance of disability in American history writ large. Focusing on selected historical periods, it shows how disability has shaped social, political, and cultural developments in the United States. Topics include fitness and citizenship in early America; disability and enslaved life in the antebellum South; scientific racism and ableism in the age of eugenics; the disability rights movement; and representations of disability.

Each week consists of a three-hour session. Each sessions begins with an overview lecture that introduces the historical context and key issues of the period under study. The second hour is devoted to discussion of an assigned article- or chapter-length reading by an early-career scholar in disability history or disability studies, who will usually join the class via Zoom. In the third hour, students work with a selection of primary sources in a workshop format. This component introduces them to the challenges disability historians face in working with the historical record and to the strategies used to make disability and disabled people legible in the archive.

The course concludes with a mini-symposium on representations of disability, addressing both ableist and empowering portrayals. Using the course’s lecture, discussion, and primary-source workshop format, students compare ableist depictions of disability and disabled people in nineteenth-century “freak shows” and twentieth-century environmentalist rhetoric. They will also watch the award-winning documentary Crip Camp: A Disability Revolution (2020) and close with a discussion of the significance of more realistic and empowering representations of disabled people.

Readings, lectures and discussion will be in English

Contents:
In this course, which covers developments in the 19th, 20th, and early 21st century, we will examine the fraught relationship humans have had with automated technologies, and artificial intelligence. What has motivated the drive toward making automated technologies and AI? And how have these initiatives reshaped how humans see themselves and how they work? Are we losing our freedom and self-reliance as machines become more autonomous? Are we becoming more mechanized or are our machines becoming more human? We will examine how these worries and concerns have been addressed by past and present-day Anglo-American scholars, fiction writers, and film-makers.

Topics include the plausibility of technological determinism, the historical relationship between human and machine autonomy, embodiment -- or the separation of thinking from doing and mind from matter, the computer metaphor and the promise and perils of anthropomorphizing machines and mechanizing humans, and the past and present battles that have been fought in the drive to automate physical and intellectual labor.

Contents:
This course examines the daily lives of diverse Americans in the 19th and 20th centuries, focusing on such topics as the history of birth, marriage, death, food, bathing, and communication. Such activities of everyday life sometimes appear “natural,” inevitable, and outside the purview of historical analysis. In reality, however, they can be deeply revealing subjects of investigation, opening a window onto private lives and at the same time demonstrating their public implications, for these quotidian practices reflect and affect power relations and social order.

The course will combine the techniques and approaches of social history, the history of emotions, and the history of experience, focusing particular attention on the ways that capitalism, individualism, and industrialization affected daily rituals and practices. To trace this history, the course readings will cover a wide range of sources—from gravestones to love letters, soap ads to lunch menus.

Contents:
The project of women’s history and gender history does not simply “add” women and gender to existing historical narratives. Instead, practitioners in these distinct but related fields have revolutionized historical methods to better study their subjects, and transformed our idea of what history is and how we should approach it. This course presents the study and use of historical methods through the methodological issues that have arisen in women’s and gender history. We will tackle key questions in the field, many still unresolved, such as: what is the relationship between women’s history and gender history? How can we approach historical actors who left no, or few, written records? At each turn, we will consider how historians have used different kinds of historical witnesses to study women and gender (including texts, material culture, and oral history), and how these methods can inform historiography more generally. This approach provides two things at once: an overview of key topics in women’s and gender history, and an in-depth look at the methodologies that inform the scholarly study of history. This course is therefore suitable for all students, regardless of their prior knowledge of women’s and/or gender history. The course will be given in English and is discussion-based.

Contents:
The Middle Ages is a concept designed to describe European history, specifically the thousand years (from the fifth to the fifteenth centuries) separating the end of the ancient world, marked by the fall of Rome, from the birth of the modern world with its cultural and religious transformations, such as the Renaissance and the Reformation. Although assessments of the European Middle Ages may vary, the shared idea is that a period of general regression in the seventh to the tenth centuries was followed by a slow and gradual recovery after the year 1000.

But did the other continents have a Middle Ages? Can we imagine, for instance, an African Middle Ages similar to the European one? This course shows that Middle Ages is a useful concept to describe African history; however, it looks at the African Middle Ages from a global perspective as a vibrant age of transformation rather than as a mere interlude between ‘The World that had been Rome’ and the Early Modern Era. This course explores the economic and social changes occurring in the Maghreb, Sub-Saharan Africa, Egypt, and Ethiopia between 500 and 1400 CE, drawing emphasis on African centrality in interregional trade and cultural exchanges. It also offers a microhistorical approach through examining the transformation of the agrarian economy and peasants’ vicissitudes at the local level.

Contents:
Medieval marriages were arranged, loveless, and violent? Members of the aristocracy only ever married their own cousins? Women were married off as teenagers and died shortly thereafter in childbirth? Knights in shining armour rescued their ladies from dragons, and true love’s kiss could wake sleeping beauties? Medieval marriages were not like today’s unions and there were few fairytale weddings, but neither were marriages as repressive, forced, and violent as they are often represented today. In this course, we will discuss the development and function of marriages in the European Middle Ages, predominantly from c. 1000–1300, a period of immense change. We will consider marriages from different angles: their cultural, social, and political importance, the arrangement of aristocratic marriages on the one hand, and the rise of love poetry and emphasis on freely given consent on the other, as well as the connection between love, sexuality, and marriages. We will also talk about ‘alternative’ forms of marriages, including divorces/annulments, marriages between religions, variant sexualities and sexual identities, the rejection of marriage, and relationships outside traditional marriages. We will talk about case studies, both ‘positive’ and ‘negative’, but also consider what married everyday life looked like, and what normative sources, court cases, theological treatises, and Romances had to say about love, sexuality, and marriages. You will gain an overview over some of the political and cultural developments between 1000–1300, and what we can learn about them from one of the most important cultural institutions of any given society.
