Contents:
Recent scholarship has moved beyond viewing
the medieval papacy as a monolithic administrative organisation, instead
emphasising its dependence on people, social networks, personal connections,
and local influences. This course engages students with these evolving
interpretations, by uncovering the agents and instruments through which the
papacy communicated its authority. Rather than approaching the papacy as a
top-down institution, students will investigate the individuals: cardinals,
legates, papal subdeacons, judges delegate, mendicant friars, notaries,
collectors etc., who implemented papal governance at ground level. The course
also considers how their personal backgrounds and connections affected their
function as papal agents. In doing so, it highlights the fundamentally adaptive
nature of the medieval papacy, which was continuously shaped by external
pressures and interference.

Contents:
In the eighth century, the Iberian Peninsula was almost entirely conquered by Muslims, with just a small area in the north remaining under Christian control. This course will be concerned with the Christian kingdom of Asturias-León, which emerged in the aftermath of that devastating defeat. More precisely, it will explore how the Asturian-Leonese chronicles interpreted the kingdom’s creation, envisaged its place in the world, and constructed a new political identity by claiming continuity with its Visigothic heritage. In addition to the ideology, these sources offer various insights into Asturian-Leonese political history, including all sorts of plots, military campaigns, and interreligious relations. Depending on your interests, we could discuss any of these aspects and so much more. On successful completion of this course, you will receive 4 credit points, and a grade will be available on demand to exchange students. If you have any questions, please do not hesitate to get in touch by email: daria.safronova@uni-tuebingen.de. I am really looking forward to getting your inquiries and meeting you in class!

Contents:
The majority of the knowledge we have for Late Antiquity and the Early Middle Ages comes from textual sources. For centuries, they were read again and again to uncover as much “factually correct” information as possible so that we could better understand this period that was so different from our own. Following the linguistic turn, scholars began to realise that these texts require a different approach. No longer was it important to look only at what was said, but also how it was said.

From this perspective, information that was previously thought to be factually incorrect or an author who was thought to be uneducated or naïve was seen as conveying a different kind of truth; maybe not “historical” truth, but the “truth” the author wanted their audience to see. In this Übung, we will first explore modern developments in historical studies, such as the linguistic turn and post-structuralism. With this baseline established, each week will focus on a different rhetorical or narratological technique that we will use to examine short episodes from chronicles, hagiography, and historiography from Late Antiquity and the Early Middle Ages.

Literature:
von Contzen, Eva & Stefan Tilg (eds.) 2019. Handbuch Historische Narratologie. Berlin.

Fafinski, Mateusz & Jakob Riemenschneide (eds). 2022. The Past Through Narratology: New Approaches to Late Antiquity and the Early Middle Ages. Heidelberg.

Kempshall, Matthew. 2011. Rhetoric and the Writing of History. Manchester.

Pizarro, Joaquín Martínez. 1989. A Rhetoric of the Scene: Dramatic Narrative in the Early Middle Ages. Toronto.

Contents:
Die Lehrveranstaltung befasst sich mit der Spannung zwischen der Materialität von Quellen und ihrer Digitalisierung. Die jüngsten Fortschritte der digitalen Technologie haben neue Reproduktions- und Konsumformen hervorgebracht, die das Konzept des „Objekts“ und der „Sammlung“ im Zentrum kultureller Institutionen wie Bibliotheken und Museen grundlegend verändert haben. Der Kurs befasst sich mit zentralen Fragen, die sich aus dem Studium der Vergangenheit im digitalen Zeitalter ergeben. Zu diesen Fragen gehören die sich verändernde Natur von Objekten wie Büchern und wissenschaftlichen Instrumenten als Quellenmaterial, die Geschichte und Praxis von Sammlungen und Sammeln, die Digitalisierung und ihre Herausforderungen, sowohl technologischer als auch geistiger Art.

Das Hauptseminar zeigt die Möglichkeiten und Herausforderungen auf, die das digitale Zeitalter für Forscher mit sich bringt. Der fortschreitende Prozess der Digitalisierung macht Quellen der Vergangenheit in einem bisher unbekannten Ausmaß zugänglich: aber was bedeutet das für die Forscher?

Wir werden auch die Rolle von Objekten in der Public History diskutieren. Wie geht die Gesellschaft mit dem Erbe der „Dinge“ in Museen und Kultureinrichtungen um? Welche Objekte sind „bewahrenswert“, warum und wann? Wer bestimmt den Auswahlprozess und was sind die Auswahlkriterien für Kuratoren, Archivare und andere Akteure in diesem Bereich? Welche Sammlungen werden digitalisiert und warum diese? Wer trifft die Auswahl? Wie werden wir den wissenschaftlichen Anforderungen an Systematik und Transparenz gerecht, wenn wir mit Online-Suchmaschinen und unterschiedlichen (und manchmal inkompatiblen) Designs von Datenbanken arbeiten?

Die Veranstaltung findet in Verbindung mit den Universitäten Bern, Durham, Groningen und Uppsala statt. Die Lehrsprache ist Englisch.

Der erste Teil der Lehrveranstaltung ist digital und findet vom 24. April bis 4. Juni jeweils von 13.45 bis 16.45 statt. Der zweite Teil der Lehrveranstaltung findet in Form einer Summerschool vom 22. bis 26.6. in Uppsala statt. Für die Reisekosten wird es eine Förderung in erheblichem Umfang geben.

Contents:
Public history does not emerge in a vacuum — it is shaped, constrained, and continually reinterpreted through political climates, cultural debates, and struggles over national identity. This course examines how politics influences the creation, presentation, and contestation of public history in two distinct but interconnected contexts: the United States and Germany.

Through a comparative lens, students will explore how each nation’s political culture, historical ruptures, and public debates have shaped museums, monuments, archives, commemorative practices, and popular narratives about the past. We will analyze topics such as the politics of race and civil rights in the U.S., Germany’s memory culture after 1945, debates over national myths, the role of federal and state governments in shaping public history institutions, and the impact of contemporary political polarization on historical interpretation.

Students will develop critical tools for analyzing public history as a political act, reflect on the responsibilities of public historians in democratic societies, and consider how transnational perspectives can enrich public-facing historical work.

Contents:

Contents:
Historians of emotions have long documented the ways in which emotions can form a useful lens of investigation within the field. By suggesting that emotions—as words, expressions, practices, and social structures—have a history, one can uncover a significant amount about how people in the past lived. But how can the history of emotions provide insights about the fields of migration and mobility? How does the mobility of individuals for different purposes—under exile, as a refugee, an economic migrant, or as a tourist—present new ways of understanding emotions historically?

This Übung provides an overview of the history of emotions in relation to histories of migration and mobility. The course outlines the basics of the history of emotions, providing analytical and methodological approaches, while applying them to different case studies in the history of mobility. Beginning from the 19th century, the course will explore different forms of involuntary and voluntary mobility into the 20th century from a global perspective.

Students in this course will develop their critical comprehension and thinking skills through discussion and analysis of primary and secondary sources in-class. In addition, students will develop their writing skills in two writing assignments over the course of the semester.

Literature:
Recommended Introductory Literature:

Jan Plamper, The History of Emotions: An Introduction (Cambridge 2017); Rob Boddice, The History of Emotions (Manchester 2018); Ute Frevert, Emotions in History: Lost and Found (Budapest 2011); Thomas Dixon, The History of Emotions: A Very Short Introduction (Oxford 2023); Colin G. Pooley, Mobility, Migration, and Transport: Historical Perspectives (Cham 2017).

Contents:
Like hardly any other historical perspective, “Global History” has experienced an international boom over the past 20 years. Global History is less a finished program or paradigm than a field of methodological and thematic reorientations, loosely connected by common starting points such as the departure from the nation state as a natural frame of reference and a critique of Eurocentrism. Fierce theoretical and methodological positioning battles that other approaches (such as Social History and Women and Gender History) went through during their establishment were largely absent in the case of Global History. Rather, Global History long found open doors and was carried by a vague understanding that this was what historical research “in tune with the present” had to look like.

This situation has changed dramatically in recent years. Neo-nationalist movements, economic policy shifts away from global market integration, neo-imperialist great power thinking, but also the experience of a global standstill due to the COVID-19 pandemic have put pressure on historical research that puts emphasis on global entanglements and mobility. But even within the Global History community, there has been discontent for several years about certain conceptual shortcomings and biases in their own subdiscipline. This crisis-ridden coming-of-age of Global History has given rise to productive reflections on the conceptual foundations and unresolved methodological challenges of Global History. This involves, for example, how we deal with the problem of positionality (who writes Global History from what point of view and in which language?) or how time and periodization are organized differently from a global history perspective. It is about how to make sure that materiality and socio-economic stratification do not disappear in a global history view and what place methods of explanation and quantification have. In short, Global History’s “crisis” is also a moment to rethink and solidify its foundations and potential.

The course builds on this ongoing debate about the state of Global History and new approaches to it. After a brief introduction into the Global History and some of its critics, we will turn to a selected range of topics and specific case studies through which the concepts, methods, and methodological pitfalls of Global History can be rethought.

Literature:
Jeremy Adelman, “What is Global History Now?,” Aeon, 2 March 2017, https://aeon.co/essays/is-global-historystill-possible-or-has-it-had-its-moment; Sebastian Conrad, What Is Global History? (Princeton: Princeton University Press, 2016); Richard Drayton, and David Motadel. “Discussion: The Futures of Global History,” Journal of Global History 13, no. 1 (2018): 1–21; Stefanie Gänger and Jürgen Osterhammel (eds.), Rethinking Global History (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2024).

Contents:
First Part: Index theory with application to condensed matter systems,

mostly Integer Quantum Hall Effect

1. Recap of functional analysis: bounded operators on Hilbert spaces, with emphasis on compact and trace class. Paragraphs 4,5,6 of Chapter VI of Reed-Simon vol I.

2. Fredholm index theory, as in the first part of chapter 27 and 30.7 of Lax, Functional Analysis. In particular emphasizing the existence of a finite rank pseudo inverse for every Fredholm operator that allows to write its index as a difference among traces, as proven by Murphy in “Fredholm Index Theory and the Trace” https://www.jstor.org/stable/20489482?origin=JSTOR-pdf. All the statements with full proofs.

3. Example (with proof) of a Fredholm operator: (1 − P ) + P U P , with P a projection and U a unitary. Later on in the course P will be a Fermi projection of a Hamiltonian modelling an insulator in two dimensions, and U will be the “flux insertion” operator.

4. Introduction to the physics of the Integer Quantum Hall Effect. Sections I and II of “The noncommutative geometry of the quantum Hall effect” http://dx.doi.org/10.1063/1.530758.

5. Stating (without proof) the index theorem: Index((1-P) + PUP) = 2πiTr[P Λ_x P, P Λ_y P]

6. Index of a pair of projections, as in the Les Houches lecture notes of Avron, section 13.5 of https://phsites.technion.ac.il/avron/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2013/08/leshouches.pdf Here Avron provides a simplified approach with respect to the original papers “The index of a pair of projections” and “Charge Deficiency, Charge Transport and Comparison of Dimensions” with Seiler and SImon.

7. Index of a pair of unitaries: the Bott index, as introduced by Hastings and Loring, is introduced to prove an index theorem in the context of insulators in two dimensions (with periodic boundary conditions) described within finite dimensional Hilbert spaces.

• Definition and properties of the Bott index, with proofs.

• Index theorem: proof of the equality with the transverse conductance.

Proofs are given following https://arxiv.org/abs/1708.05912.

8. Bulk-boundary correspondence for a finite 1-dimensional system with chiral symmetry: https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.17099. This paper establishes the equality of edge and bulk indices for the same finite system, while traditionally edge and bulk are treated for different geometries. Explaining the main ideas and results.

Second Part: Finite spin systems, introduction to the main models (Ising, XY and XXZ), proof of Lieb-Robinson bounds

1. Tensor product of finitely many Hilbert spaces: definition of partial traces and proof of its relation with Haar-averaging.

2. Discussion (at the level of theoretical physics) of the spin 1/2 system: Ising, XY and XXZ, with their phase diagrams.

3. Proof of the Lieb-Robinson bounds in the simplest setting of nearest neighbor one-dimensional spin Hamiltonian following appendix B of https://arxiv.org/pdf/2408.00743 and appendix B of https://arxiv.org/pdf/2509.02383.

Contents:
This seminar explores extreme astrophysical phenomena and the physical limits that become apparent in such systems. The focus is on white dwarfs, compact objects, massive stars, as well as high-energy and transient phenomena. Using a selection of accessible research articles, we discuss how observations and simple physical arguments can be used to infer properties that are not directly observable.

The emphasis is on conceptual understanding, critical reading of astrophysical literature, and discussion of assumptions, validity ranges, and limitations of common interpretations. Detailed modeling, numerical simulations, or computationally intensive methods are explicitly not the focus.

Extrasolar System planets

Objects and structures in our Universe. The physics aspects of the Universe.

Moreover, they can evaluate, compare, and contrast different modeling approaches as well as modeling results. In particular, they can use also statistical methods to quantitatively compare different cognitive models.

Content information:

Approximately ¼ of the course will be devoted to background training of visual psychophysics, and ¾ to an individual practical project.

The topics of the individual projects include human visual psychophysics experiments (e.g., visual illusions, visual attention) and zebrafish behavioral experiments. Each student will meet with the lecturer to agree on a custom designed project topic based on the student’s skills, interests, and training goals.

During the semester, each student should spend at least 10 hours/week of the workload at the Dept. of Sensory and Sensorimotor Systems in MPI, where they will have access to computers, office space, lab equipment for projects, and advice and assistance from the lecturer and her colleagues for their course learning and projects.

Students will be required to write weekly progress reports, which will form the basis of their final project report. The final project report should be in the style of a research article that fully documents the project, consisting of an abstract, background/introduction, methods, results, discussion and conclusions. Students will also need to make an oral presentation summarizing their project and findings.

Each week there will be formal lectures and/or project report presentation practices, TBD.

For further information see the website of Prof. Zhaoping Li.

To be able to do research and background reading necessary to approach a scientific problem.

To understand the relationship between computational questions and experimental investigations.

To learn project management with a timetable of intermediate goals.

To program an experiment using computer code that is organized, clear, and debugged/verifiable.

To carry out data collection, and debug software and hardware problems in the process.

To learn and practice basic techniques in data analysis, statistics and plotting.

To be able to communicate scientific material clearly, in both a written paper and oral presentation format.

Contents:
The lecture "Neurobiology of Language" provides an overview of the neural mechanisms underlying human language and communication.

Topics covered include the neural basis for speech perception and production; reading and writing; semantics and syntax; sign language and multilingualism. The lecture takes an in-depth look at these topics, and will cover both foundational findings and current debates in the field.

Contents:
Das Seminar behandelt „Sound Symbolism“ – ikonische und lautmalerische Zeichen. Stimme, Gesten und sprachliche Laute können dem ähneln, was sie bezeichnen, und so den Verstehensprozess in der Kommunikation unterstützen. Im Seminar wird untersucht, wie Menschen sensorische, motorische und affektive Erfahrungen über solche Ausdrucksformen vermitteln. Dabei stehen die Entstehung und Funktion dieser Laute im Fokus, insbesondere im Hinblick auf Evolution, Entwicklung und ihre neuronale Verarbeitung.

Learning target:
Die Teilnehmer lernen den Umgang mit Forschungsliteratur, indem sie wissenschaftliche Publikationen analysieren und deren Inhalte erarbeiten. Durch Präsentationen und Diskussionen wird zudem die wissenschaftliche Kommunikationsfähigkeit geschult.

Darüber hinaus bietet das Seminar eine interdisziplinäre Perspektive auf das Thema „Sprachverarbeitung“. Behandelt werden unter anderem linguistische Studien, kulturübergreifende Untersuchungen sowie neurowissenschaftliche Ansätze.

Contents:
Approximately 1/3 of the course will be devoted to guided reading and learning of a focus topic (details below) of computational vision, and ¾ to a practical project. The practical project can be a replication, or a modified/extended version, of a previous visual psychophysics experiment or a previous computational vision model contained in the reading materials.

There are three choices of the focus topic mentioned in (1): Encoding, Selection, or Decoding, which are based mainly on, respectively, chapter 3, chapter 5, or chapter 6 of the textbook “Understanding Vision: Theory, models, and data”, see https://zhaoping.thinkific.com/. For each of this topic, students should also read the two short introductory chapters 1 and 2 (unless the student has taken previous courses on vision science). This book is available in the library of University of Tuebingen, and its content can be viewed here https://www.lizhaoping.org/zhaoping/prints/TableOfContents.pdf. There are also online videos to assist reading and learning, see http://www.lizhaoping.org/zhaoping/PlayList_VisionBook.html

Each student should start with a consultation with the lecturer to agree on which of the three focus topics in (2) to do the internship on. The choice of the practical project based on the choice of the focus topic can be decided at the beginning of the internship, or during the internship after some initial reading and learning on the focus topic.

Examples of practical projects (depending on the focus topic) include: visual psychophysics projects to replicate or extend an experiment described in the textbook (e.g., sections 3.5.8, 5.3, 5.5, 6.4), implement and simulate the neural circuit model of the primary visual cortex (section 5.4) for a saliency map, or data analysis of existing experimental data related to the focus topic. The practical project will be custom suited to the training needs and interests of the student. If needed, the practical project can also be an experiment (or data analysis on the experimental data from ) on zebrafish or mice as a modified version of human psychophysics experiments for the focus topic.

During the course (or semester), students are encouraged to spend as much time as they like at the Dept. of Sensory and Sensorimotor Systems in MPI, where they will have access to computers, office space, lab equipment for projects, advice and assistance from the lecturer and her colleagues for their course learning and projects, and an environment where they can be exposed to view or visit other research projects by members of Prof. Zhaoping’s group. According to the number of the course credits, and under the conditions allowed by covid restrictions, there will be a minimum number of hours, e.g., 5 hours/week, required for the students to spend in the department.

Students will be required to write weekly progress reports (between 100 to 1000 words per week), which will form the basis of their final project report. The final project report should be in the style of a research article that fully documents the project, consisting of an abstract, background/introduction of the focus and project topic, methods, results, discussion and conclusions. Depends on the requirement or workload of the course, students may also need to make an oral presentation summarizing their project, materials learned, and findings.

Learning target:
Students will learn skills necessary to conduct a scientific study from beginning to end, including:

To be able to do research and background reading necessary to learn a focus topic and approach a scientific problem.

To understand the relationship between computational/theoretical questions and experimental investigations.

To learn project management with a timetable of intermediate goals.

To program an experiment or a model using computer code that is organized, clear, and debugged/verifiable.

To carry out data collection or model simulation, or data analysis, depending on the project topic, and debug software and hardware problems in the process.

To learn and practice basic techniques in data analysis, statistics and plotting.

To be able to communicate scientific material clearly, in both a written paper and oral presentation format.

Contents:
Expanding on the theories and ideas discussed in the ‘What can task switching tell us about cognitive control?’ FS Seminar, we will choose an interesting research question within this topic and will work together to design and carry out the experiment. The module will focus on practical skills such as data analysis, experiment design and report writing. Together we will work step-by-step through the stages of an experiment, from conceptualisation to completion.

Contents:
In this seminar, we delve into a useful tool for understanding cognitive control: mixing costs. These occur when performance declines in blocks where more than one task is possible—even on task repetition trials—revealing how the brain manages task ambiguity, coordinates competing task sets, and handles increased working‑memory demands.

We will explore the key theories behind mixing costs and discuss what they reveal about how people flexibly control their thoughts and actions in everyday multitasking situations. Students will not only learn the foundational research but also apply it: part of the seminar allows for application of mixing costs and related cognitive control processes in different developmental and clinical situations.

By the end of the seminar, students will be able to evaluate theories of the mixing cost, apply task switching tools to assess performance and ask questions about how alterations in control processes might contribute to clinical symptoms. This seminar is also an opportunity to bridge a thorough comprehension of executive functions with more applied domains in psychology —ideal for students interested in how laboratory findings help us understand the mind in these different contexts.

Contents:

At the beginning of the semester, we will develop a schedule based on participants' interests, needs, and requirements. During our sessions, we focus on issues related to the formulation of a research question, the writing process, current research in Fachdidaktik Englisch – TEFL – TESOL and its related fields, writing techniques and methods, time management and research methodology, and, most importantly, the discussion or analysis of the participants' writing plans, text samples/drafts, data samples, or presentations.

Contents:
Foreign language teaching goes beyond language proficiency, cultural knowledge, literary competence, and teaching strategies. It requires a profound understanding of the concepts, variables, and processes involved in language acquisition as well as in learning about and with literature, culture, and media. This introductory lecture provides an overview of various aspects and principles relevant to foreign language teaching and learning, including historical and political perspectives, psychological and neurological considerations, individual differences among learners, classroom interaction, and approaches to foreign language teaching. Although held in the lecture format, frequent interactive sequences require student participation.

Contents:
This course will be co-taught by Bernd Wick from the "Gymnasium" in Metzingen and the Tübingen "Staatliches Seminar für Ausbildung und Fortbildung der Lehrkräfte" as well as Stefan Hofstetter from Tübingen University, and it essentially comes in two parts: In the first part, we shall look at how unknown vocabulary can be taught at school. In this context, we'll consider questions such as the following: Which kinds of vocab have to be pre-taught at all and which different teaching strategies can be used for introducing new vocab (depending for example on your students' age)? What options are there for checking vocab afterwards and which of these lend themselves particularly well to a given age group or a specific type of vocab? In the second part of this course, we'll then focus on the four basic skills, i. e. speaking, writing, listening and reading, and we'll see how these skills can effectively be trained at school on the basis of classical teaching manuals, establishing e. g. reading and listening comprehensions, creative writing exercises and the like. We'd also like to stress that while the theoretical background of teaching vocab and working with schoolbook texts will of course be taken into account, this class will also put a strong emphasis on actually putting things into practice.

Contents:
This course will be co-taught by Bernd Wick from the "Gymnasium" in Metzingen and the Tübingen "Staatliches Seminar für Ausbildung und Fortbildung der Lehrkräfte" as well as Stefan Hofstetter from Tübingen University, and it primarily has the following two goals: First of all, it aims at looking at a wide variety of English-speaking countries around the world such as the UK, the US, Canada, South Africa or India, but also others, the exact choice ultimately also depending on the participants' own interests. For each country, we'll then focus on some core facts about geography, economy, politics or history intended for cultural teaching at school, but we'll also take a closer look at certain language features of the English variety spoken in the corresponding countries. At the same time, a second intention of this class is to provide participants with a basic introduction to lesson planning, that is the question of how a lesson should be structured as an adequate sequence of individual subparts, the ordering and relative length of which are considered to be vital for successful teaching. While the theoretical background of teaching language and culture and that of lesson planning will of course be taken into account, this class will also put a strong emphasis on actually putting things into practice.

Contents:
The short story is one of the most widely used and most versatile literary genres in the EFL literature classroom. This is small wonder given that short stories can readily be aligned with the objectives of foreign language learning/teaching and also lend themselves to a wide range of approaches and methods.

In this seminar, we will explore ways of integrating short stories into the advanced EFL classroom (Sekundarstufe II). Covering a broad spectrum of short stories selected around regional and thematic criteria, we will investigate into their significance for the coverage of curricular topics and for intercultural learning. Furthermore, we will cover the basics of lessong planning and discuss curricular requirements in this context. Finally, we will also critically evaluate samples of preexisting teaching material. Students will be required to analyze short stories and to develop and present approaches to teaching (via) short stories in the advanced EFL classroom on the basis of their own lesson plans.

Contents:
Teachers must think about several aspects when planning to teach reading, writing,

speaking, listening or even mediation in the EFL-classroom. The vehicle of any foreign

language teaching is most often a “short text” that can be covered in a single 45- or 90-

minute session. In the context of the EFL classroom, it is not necessarily the pure

analysis of a text that is in the foreground, but texts are the root from whence language

acquisition and production sprouts.

This seminar will take various forms of “short texts” (fictional and non-fictional) into

consideration and will explore how different focuses can be set, depending on the

methods and learning goals, the personality of the teacher and the target student

audience. We will work on lesson planning and critically investigate how to incorporate

curricular and competence requirements into your own approaches to teaching.

Contents:
In this class, you are going to learn how to:

name, explain and apply the main criteria for effective teaching

define and explain terminology, theoretical concepts, approaches and models with regards to the teaching of literature in the EFL classroom

apply and develop techniques, exercises and models of teaching literature in the EFL classroom (focus: teaching poetry, drama, short stories and novels)

apply your analytical and methodological knowledge to plan a literature-based lesson

Contents:
What should English lessons ultimately achieve? In an age shaped by competence frameworks, standardized testing, and packed curricula, this question can feel unnecessary or even overwhelming. Yet, current debates in foreign language education show the opposite: Clarifying the goals and deeper purposes of EFL teaching is more important than ever.

This seminar invites future teachers to explore how foreign language education and critical literacy intersect and why this intersection matters deeply for today's classrooms. Together, we will unpack questions such as:

What does it mean to be critically literate?

Is critical literacy and critical thinking the same?

What can and should we as educators aspire to when it comes to the critical literacy of our students?

We will address all of these questions and discuss how critical literacy as an educational goal fits comfortably or uncomfortably within the scope(s) of the foreign language classroom. Throughout the course, we will discuss whether and how the aims of education for critical literacy can be put into dialogue with curricular frameworks, how they challenge traditional EFL practices, and how teachers can balance critical literacy with the goals of EFL learning and teaching. By the end of the seminar, you will be equipped with both theoretical understanding of critical literacy and practical strategies to foster responsible, reflective, and empowered students.

Literature:
Gerlach, David, Hrsg. Kritische Fremdsprachendidaktik: Grundlagen, Ziele, Beispiele. Tübingen: Narr, 2020.

Contents:
Drawing from the experience of the Schulpraxissemester, this seminar integrates teaching practice and classroom interaction with concepts, theories, models, and methods of foreign language education — with a particular focus on the role of media in the EFL classroom. We will discuss and reflect on your projects, observations, and explorations at schools and contextualize them in light of current theoretical insights. The media landscape is shifting at an unprecedented pace: artificial intelligence, generative tools, and new forms of networked communication are reshaping not only how texts are produced and consumed, but also what it means to be literate in a language. This makes a critical, reflective engagement with media more important — and more complex — than ever. The overarching question of the seminar is therefore:

How can observation, experience, and critical reflection be processed and transformed into (empirical, theoretical, or instructional) insights into media use in the EFL classroom?

To develop knowledge of current research approaches, studies in the field, and an individual repertoire of methodologies, three aspects are particularly relevant:

Reflecting on practice: Examine and thoughtfully reflect on your personal observations and experiences during the Schulpraxis phase.

Exploring frameworks: Explore and considerably expand your knowledge of theoretical concepts in media-focused TEFL/TESOL.

Navigating the present: Work from practice to theory and then back to practice: use your school experience as an opportunity to gain deeper theoretical insights into media knowledge — and then consider pathways to reintegrate these into classroom practice.

Therefore, we will reflect on your topics in groups and in the plenum, using TESOL and English/American Studies discourses on media, literacy, and language learning.

Learning target:
By reflecting on and exploring the Schulpraxisphase alongside your questions, readings, and group work, completing the seminar should enable you to:

Analyze your classroom experience with media, reflect on it critically, and articulate your observations in relation to theoretical frameworks in TEFL.

Develop your professional portfolio (Lehramtsportfolio) and situate your findings within current debates on media, digitality, and language education.

Analyze, apply, and reason about concepts, theories, and approaches to teaching and learning with various media — including AI-powered tools — particularly in the areas of teaching languages, cultures, and literacies.

Define, discuss, and critically evaluate research methodologies and theoretical studies of media in teaching contexts, drawing on your readings, lectures, and seminar discussions.

Work and participate cooperatively in groups, engage with academic literature, develop research-informed teaching ideas, and communicate your findings effectively.

Reflect critically on the ethical dimensions of media use in education, including questions of data privacy, algorithmic literacy, and the responsible integration of AI in the EFL classroom.

Contents:
Marking and assessing your students' work is undoubtedly one the most controversial and delicate parts of a teacher's job at school. This is why I'd like to spend a whole seminar on this rather complex issue: We'll start out by having a quick look at the legal basis of marking to give you an idea of what can and should be done in this domain, but also of what is to be avoided by all means. We'll then look at various forms of written tests and exams (simple vocab tests, class tests, etc.) in different years (5 to 7, 8 to 10 and finally the 'Kursstufe') and with different focuses (grammar, free writing and so on), until we'll ultimately reach the official A level exam. Moreover, we'll also deal with oral marks, marking oral presentations or even groupwork in some detail. While we'll of course take a look at theoretical aspects underlying the marking process, this seminar will also put a strong emphasis on the practical side of matters and ideally, we'll discuss your experiences from your 'Schulpraktikum' in the context of marking. I'd thus highly appreciate it if people were willing to share their own experiences/ideas on the subject and maybe to even bring along own material they encountered at school (dating either from this 'Schulpraktikum' or from their own days back at school), which would certainly contribute to making this course more interesting.

Contents:
Building on the concrete experience of your school internships, this lecture offers a structured survey of selected current concepts, theories, and research methodologies in the field of Teaching English as a Foreign Language. Where the accompanying seminar focuses on your own projects and teaching experience, this lecture broadens the theoretical horizon by introducing key research topics, ongoing debates, and methodological approaches shaping the field today. The aim is to provide an academically grounded perspective that enriches your reflection on practice and prepares you to engage critically with scholarly literature in foreign language education.

Learning target:
With the completion of this class, you should be able to

outline key research topics, methodological approaches, and current debates in foreign language education,

analyze research studies and their claims, relating findings to relevant theoretical frameworks and methodological considerations,

assess current developments in the field, including possible trends and shortcomings, from an academically informed standpoint,

argue for or against current research claims using disciplinary terminology, core concepts, and established theoretical references

Contents:
'Scriptural Reasoning (SR) is a tool for inter-faith dialogue whereby people of different faiths come together to read and reflect on their scriptures. Unlike some forms of inter-faith engagement, it is not about seeking agreement but rather exploring the texts and their possible interpretations across faith boundaries, and learning to ‘disagree better’. The result is often a deeper understanding of others' and one’s own scriptures, as well as the development of strong bonds across faith communities.' (http://www.scripturalreasoning.org/). The Tübingen Scriptural Reasoning seminars build on this tradition and develop it further in the German context. Over ten years now, the SR seminars have proven to be a fruitful and very accessible method for students to enter into inter-faith dialogue.

This year's seminar will focus on 'pluralities'. Examining relevant Biblical and Qur'anic passages, we will explore how Christians and Muslims understand, conceputalize and deal with plurality. What are the similarities and differences between the two faith traditions on 'plurality'? How do Christians and Muslims read their own scriptures and the scriptures of the other, especially the verses dealing with plurality and difference? Questions such as these will be discussed by engaging with the Bible and the Qur’an, following the method of Scriptural Reasoning. The conversation will be enriched with the participation of a number of internationally renowned scholars and guest speakers.

Contents:
This unit provides a first and basic introduction to the use of git for project-focused and collaborative data management.

Here, git (and other file versioning systems) enable a detailed tracking of file changes (history) tailored for collaborative use cases, i.e. sharing and shared working on files and projects. To this end, it provides efficient methods that support concurrent changes of files and their automated merging where possible. Git-based project management goes well beyond collaborative word processing (e.g. using Google Docs or MS365) or cloud storage solutions (e.g. MS OneDrive) with a strong focus on file management and versioning. Therefore, git is well placed as soon as "projects" are defined and files and information have to be aggregated, shared and maintained.

GitHub is a cloud service that serves as an online hub to store, share and communicate (data/coding/..) projects using git-based workflows. It is one of the leading platforms in the field and offers much more than git functionality.

GitHub Desktop is an app provided by GitHub to perform git-related tasks with an intuitive user interface (UI). Since developed by GitHub, it is tailored for the latter but not exclusive and works with any git server.

Within the course, participants will understand why working with git-controlled projects is a good idea in any study/research context and how to manage and share data using git. We will mainly use the GitHub Desktop app for this but also discuss git integrations into programming tools like Visual Studio Code or RStudio.

Learning target:
Awareness of advantages and use cases for git-based data management

Understanding git-based workflows

Creation and management of data repositories using git

Understanding Branching, Pull Requests und Merging

Being able to handle conflicts in git workflows

Familiarity with GitHub Desktop UI

Using git within IDEs like Visual Studio Code or RStudio or from the command line interface (CLI)

Contents:
This colloquium will help students prepare for their final oral exam in the MEd Programme and support them, for example, in compiling the mandatory reading list. It will be partly based on directed reading, reading logs and other written activities as well as oral presentations and discussion activities related to specific texts, literary analysis and interpretation etc. The colloquium will also provide a thorough revision of terminology, close reading skills etc. and will take into account the chances and challenges introduced by ChatGPT etc. It will reflect on the need of Fachwissenschaft for secondary school teaching and pay particular attention to the new Abitur in English.

Contents:
The Kolloquium will allow you to communally workshop the material you have selected for the final oral exam in the MEd degree scheme. Students will take turns to present excerpts from their exam reading lists, with the discussion serving to improve and focus the mode of working with the respective texts. The approach we wil be using will be that of close reading with an emphasis upon the literariness of the literary text (what are the specific formal characteristics that make a text "literature"), against a background of generic and historical knowledge of the literatures of the English-speaking world. These discussions will be framed by an ongoing inquiry into the relevance of such questions for the EFL classroom that the candidates will be steered towards after their VBJ/Referendariat. Students will be expected to be able to talk about a broad selection genres and historical epochs via exemplary texts. You will be required to have at least 2 texts by William Shakespeare among your selection.

**It is ESSENTIAL that you register on the relevant moodle platform, as material will be made available week for week on that platform. Without access to the platform you will be unable to participate in the weekly discussions.

Contents:
This colloquium is aimed at MA candidates who wish to present their theses.

Contents:
This lecture course will be an introduction to the literature and culture of Shakespeare’s time by focusing on the range of textual practises characteristic of the period. To a large extent, it was a world of the word: what to say and how to say it was a key issue in people's lives. We will try and reconstruct this world by considering the many ways in which words became texts. Particular attention will be given to the specific material manifestations of these texts as books, manuscripts, single-print sheets etc. The material addressed will include play-texts, royal entertainments, dialogues, storybooks, pamphlets, treatises, broadside ballads, sermons, prayer books, bibles, classical texts and translations, verse miscellanies, chapbooks, commonplace books, grammar books, recipe collections, manuals, court depositions, letters, contracts, diaries, account books, etc. Most of these texts will be introduced in the course of the lecture series but everyone should read two plays in which different kinds of texts and their production are thematized: William Shakespeare’s Love’s Labour’s Lost and Ben Jonson’s Bartholomew Fair.

Contents:
This courses will examine 3 African genres in contemporary fiction: science fiction (South African Lauren Beukes' Zoo City, 2010), detective fiction (Kenyan/American Mukoma wa Ngugi's Nairobi Heat, 2011), and auto/biography (Kenyan Wangari Maathai's Unbowed, 2008). The course will ask about the way these genres are deployed to confront and process African histories, contemporary African realities, and African futures - sometimes head-on, sometimes in indirect and tangential ways. It will also address the nature of these genres themselves, as imports from European cultures that have been retooled to serve specifically African purposes, asking how they have been transformed under the influence of the respective source cultures, but how residual generic components may sit uneasily with the African contexts in which they are employed. .

Literature:
Beukes, Lauren. Zoo City, Penguin, 2010.

Mukoma wa Ngugi. Nairobi Heat, Melville House, 2011.

Maathai, Wangari. Unbowed, Penguin, 2008.

Contents:
This course provides an overview of oral literature as a field of study and exposes students to its major genres as well as to theories of oral performance. It stresses the importance of the spoken word as an art form. The course also discusses the cultural, historical, and socio-political relevance of specific genres of literature such as folktales, proverbs, riddles, tongue twisters, and songs. It further reflects on how artists exploit oral literature in their work. It concludes with a brief introduction to research methods in oral literature.

Contents:
African Queer Literature encapsulates a paradox in continental literary canon because it is often decontextualized and discussed as if it is devoid of a history. This course proposes to historicise this sub-genre of African Literature by tracing the evolution of its representations and criticism over a period of 60 years. It will foreground three questions in its deconstruction of the anatomy of African queer fiction: What are the primary canonical African queer fictional texts? Who are the leading writers and critics of this fiction? How has representations or criticism of this sub-canon evolved over the last 60 years? These and related questions will guide an exploration of the evolution of a genre from pathology, Western corruption, imperial hypocrisy or humanised ‘coming out’ narratives that resonate with the three generations of African writing. The pedagogical anchoring of the course is that while earlier continental representations and/or debates of unorthodox sexuality — often laced with racist sentiments — demonised and exoticized non-orthodox sexuality to justify African singular heterosexuality, contemporary discourses are characterised either with queer denialism or sexuality rights activism.

Contents:
This seminar will provide you with the possibility to engage with a range of cultural studies questions and approaches and their applicability beyond academic discussions. We will take a combined approach of condensed reading and discussion sessions and sessions in which guests from a variety of job backgrounds (library, publishing, museum, journalism, international relations and culture exchange...) will discuss what they do and how intruduce cutural studies approaches and questions from their humanities degrees which they use in their current line of work. You will be able to engage in critical discussions, ask questions and explore possible applications of cultural studies concepts and approaches (in the form of reading and discussion questions, writing projects, portfolios, or term papers - based on the requirements of your specific course of studies).

Contents:
Please note that this is a 'Blockseminar'!

In this course, we will deal with the way board games operate on spatial concepts - the very term "board" points towards their spatial dimension on the tabletop. The places we encounter in board games, however, are neither 'given' nor 'neutral'. Board games create place and convey certain notions about these places. The world created in Risk, for instance, is one of global military opportunity.

The course will we hinge on three interrelated topics:

First, we will explore why board games are worth investigating academically in the first place. Here, our focus will be on how board games reflect and shape the contexts they are created in and how they produce cultural meaning.

Second, we will delve into the different aspects that can be studied. These include notions of spatial representation in board games (maps, boards, areas...), material culture (tokens, cards, tiles) and how the shaping of experience, social and cultural context (e.g. reflection of dominant norms and related worldmaking capabilities), and narrative/theme.

Third, we will engage with diferent ways of how to study board games, ranging from Huizinga's "magic circle" (the way game rules create an artificial reality that - temporarily - overwrites actual-world reality/rules) to place as a humanised/emotional/social concept, as well as different ways of modelling ideologies.

Literature:
Edler, Dennis, Olaf Kühne, and Corinna Jenal, eds. (2022). The Social Construction of Landscapes in Games. Springer.

Mochocki, Michal, ed. (2024). Heritage, Memory and Identity in Postcolonial Board Games. London and New York: Routledge/Taylor and Francis.

Randl, Chad and D. Medina Lasansky, eds. (2023). Playing Place: Board Games, Popular Culture, Space. The MIT Press.

Contents:
This module explores a significant range of George Gordon Byron and Percy Bysshe Shelley’s poetry, focusing on critical themes such as loss, love, the imagination, nature, politics, and the language and form of their poetics. The module will be structured thematically with some seminars focusing on one poet (or one particular poem) whilst other seminars offer a comparative analysis of the poetry and thought of Byron and Shelley. The poems include a selection of major works by both poets such as Childe Harold’s Pilgrimage, Don Juan, The Sensitive Plant, ‘Mont Blanc’ and The Mask of Anarchy, among others.

Literature:
Required texts:

Percy Bysshe Shelley, The Major Works, ed. by Zachary Leader and Michael O’Neill (Oxford

University Press, 2003)

George Gordon Byron, The Major Works, ed. by Jerome J. McGann (Oxford University Press, 2008)

Contents:
Romantic fiction has emerged as one of the thriving genres in contemporary literature, particularly within the burgeoning digital book market. This seminar will explore the prevalent trend of “feminist” love narratives, a genre historically pioneered by female authors who intricately wove their own stories of love while negotiating societal gender norms. Notably, Jane Austen’s works have left an indelible mark on both literature and modern fan fiction, highlighting the enduring relevance of female perspectives on romance.

In an era characterized by increased feminist consciousness, we observe a paradox: the visibility of female subjectivity appears to be diminishing. This is particularly striking in light of the self-assured depictions of women in both everyday life and literary works. Our inquiry will delve into the nature of this perceived disappearance. Are contemporary narratives genuinely feminist, or do they merely masquerade as such? What are the implications for women's self-perception and agency within these narratives?

This seminar aims to critically assess the intersection of feminism and female subjectivity in today’s cultural landscape, questioning the authenticity of the narratives that shape women’s experiences and identities. Through this lens, we seek to redefine what it means to be a woman in contemporary society or a heroine in literature.

Contents:
Common ground is a key concept for the study of human interaction and communication. It denotes what is required for these joint activities to be carried out successfully. Literary communication is an especially rewarding object of study in this respect, since literary texts both represent communication (e.g. between characters) and are part of it (e.g. between author and reader). In this course, we will study the relationship between these two levels of communication with a view to learning more about how common ground is established (or not) and how the management of common ground is essential for the meaning of a literary text. Misunderstanding and dramatic/narrative irony are key phenomena in this respect. Besides some poems, we will read a corpus of particularly illuminating texts: William Shakespeare’s Comedy of Errors (1594), Charlotte Lennox’s The Female Quixote (1752), Jane Austen’s Emma (1816), and Alan Bennett’s The Uncommon Reader (2007).

Literature:

William Shakespeare, The Comedy of Errors, ed. Kent Cartwright, The Arden Shakespeare, ISBN ‎ 978-1904271246

Charlotte Lennox, The Female Quixote, ed. Margaret Dalziel, Oxford World’s Classics, ISBN ‎ 978-0199540242
