Contents:
This course explores the role(s) and significance of dreams and dreaming in literature in English from Geoffrey Chaucer to William Shakespeare (1370s–1610s). From Chaucer's vision of a parliament of birds to Prospero's 'We are such stuff as dreams are made on', the dream is a much utilised framing device for Renaissance imaginative fiction and a vehicle for reflections on poetry, drama, love, nature, and the divine. What is the connection between dreaming and writing? Why does the dream have such longevity in English literature? We will set out to answer these questions first with an introduction to pre-modern dream theory and the dream as a narrative device, with reference to Chaucer’s Parliament of Fowls. Then, we will follow the (Chaucerian) dream vision through Stewart Scotland and early Tudor England, including some early examples of dream visions in print, demonstrating the surprising adaptability of the form. Finally we will turn to Shakespeare and his use of dreams 1) as otherworldly warnings and 2) for metatheatrical reflection in selected extracts from the plays.

Most texts will be made available as electronic versions on Moodle; but please in advance of the course purchase Geoffrey Chaucer, Dream Visions and Other Poems, ed. Kathryn L. Lynch (New York 2007), which includes the Parliament and good contexts and criticism sections. To prepare, please study the section ‘A Quick Course in Chaucer’s Language’, have a go at reading the Parliament, and look over the extracts (at the back of the volume) from Cicero, Macrobius, The Romance of the Rose, and A. C. Spearing’s Medieval Dream Poetry.

Contents:
This course approaches the literature and culture of the age of Queen Elizabeth I and Shakespeare through one of the great long poems in the English language: Edmund Spenser’s Faerie Queene (1590, 1596). On a literal level, this a collection of stories of knights on exciting adventures; but each knight is also an examination of a different moral virtue; and the whole poem is a sophisticated allegory of England’s past and ambitions for its future. Accordingly, this course will begin with an overview of The Faerie Queene and its relevant backgrounds: the literary, intellectual, and political contexts that informed Spenser’s subject and approach. Subsequent classes will be a guide through the poem, read first in extracts from a supportive reading guide – Andrew Zircher, Edmund Spenser’s ‘The Faerie Queene’: A Reading Guide (Edinburgh: Edinburgh University Press, 2011) – then advancing to the Longman Annotated edition. Further points for discussion will be gradually introduced: sixteenth-century preoccupations with literary allusiveness and imitation, history, theology and philosophy, as well as more modern responses to Spenser’s work – from criticism focusing on gender and sexuality to political concerns such as law and empire. The aim is to be able to understand, and to enjoy understanding, Spenser’s early modern epic, not only for the pleasures that it affords in itself, but as an important point of reference for further study of English Literature and/or the Elizabethan period.

An electronic version of the Zurcher reading guide is available via Katalog plus; but please in advance of the course purchase the Longman Annotated edition: Edmund Spenser, The Faerie Queene, ed. A. C. Hamilton, 2nd edn (Harlow: Longman, 2001). Read as much of the poem as you can; especially beneficial will be the ‘Letter to Raleigh’ (at the back of the volume) and Book 1: ‘The Legend of the Knight of the Red Crosse, or of Holinesse’.

Contents:
This seminar will explore the gendered and political aspects of modern women's literature. Recently, women authors have presented a wide range of embodied narratives highlighting women’s experiences. We will analyse the gendered politics in contemporary fiction, focusing on feminist narratological aspects and embodied narratives. Our goal is to uncover narratological and gendered portrayals of women’s embodied experiences that challenge social norms and cultural expectations. To promote meaningful discussions on current gender roles, we will highlight writers who develop innovative, subversive, and ambiguous narratives about women. Key works include Ottessa Moshfegh’s My Year of Rest and Relaxation (2018), and Sally Rooney’s Normal People.

Literature:
Preliminary List of Texts:

Ottessa Moshfegh, My Year of Rest and Relaxation (2018)

Sally Rooney, Normal People (2018)

Lauren Groff, The Vaster Wilds (2023)

Contents:
"Why were the things that were closest so often the hardest to see?" (Keegan, Small Things Like These, p. 104)

This seminar explores how Irish literature represents and creates “small worlds” - microcosms ranging from domestic interiors and village communities to island spaces and coastal landscapes, to think through belonging and identity. We will examine contemporary and modern texts that use rooms, hearths, townlands and shorelines as miniture worlds of social, political and emotional life. Paying close attention to scale, care, kinship and everyday practices, we will ask how Irish writing turns miniature settings into sites of tension and transformation.

Readings include works by Claire Keegan, Audrey Magee, Claire Lynch, John McGahern and others. Students will conduct a short micro-ethnography of a “small world” of their choice, hold a presentation and further develop analytical and writing skills through close reading, discussion and reflective research.

A highlight of the course will be a guest lecture by Claire Lynch, author of A Family Matter and Small: On Motherhood, on Friday, 19 June from 14-16. Attendance is mandatory.

Literature:
Required reading includes the following titles:

Claire Keegan: Small Things Like These (Faber, 2021)

Audrey Magee: The Colony (Faber, 2022)

John McGahern: That They May Face the Rising Sun (Faber, 2003)

Claire Lynch: A Family Matter (Chatto & Windus, 2025)

Doireann Ni Ghriofa: A Ghost In The Throat (Tramp, 2021)

Contents:
This Blockseminar explores how Anglophone literature and film imagine the creation of life and how “created beings” function as cultural figures through which societies negotiate questions of identity, humanity, technology, and power. From Mary Shelley’s Frankenstein to contemporary science-fiction cinema, narratives of artificial or engineered life have repeatedly been used to reflect anxieties about modernity, scientific responsibility, embodiment, and the boundaries of the human.

Through close readings of literary texts and films — including Frankenstein, Never Let Me Go, Blade Runner, Blade Runner 2049, Ex Machina, and Moon — students will examine how monsters, clones, replicants, and artificial intelligences are constructed as both “other” and deeply human. These primary materials will be read alongside influential theoretical texts from posthumanism, feminist theory, and monster studies in order to analyze how modern cultures imagine technology, agency, and ethical responsibility.

The course combines literary analysis, film studies, and cultural theory and treats popular culture as a serious site of ideological and cultural meaning.

Literature:
Literary Texts

• Mary Shelley — Frankenstein (1818)

• Kazuo Ishiguro — Never Let Me Go (2005)

Films

• Ridley Scott — Blade Runner (1982)

• Duncan Jones — Moon (2009)

• Alex Garland — Ex Machina (2014)

Contents:
This course is concerned with how recipes and festivals brought people together in early modern England.

Or put differently: we seek to explore how pragmatic and literary texts (recipe collections and royal festival entertainments, respectively) are collaboratively created by communities while simultaneously acting as de facto links between community networks as well as material manifestations of the very same. Network(ing) is understood as 1) the establishment or extension of a community (or the linking of two separate communities) through the sharing and co-creating of these texts and 2) as a feature of the texts themselves: how they are connected to one another or changed because of the networks they represent and (co-)create. The communities we examine range from private households to the court of Queen Elizabeth I: the texts we will discuss reflect that range, including, for example, the Recipe Book of Mrs. Deborah Haddock and recipes from Queen Elizabeth I’s court, as well as the royal entertainments at Bisham Abbey and Cowdray.

Literature:
Given that the reading is uncommon and unique, all texts will be made available through moodle.

Contents:
The course fundamentally questions the spurious distinction between space (physical, i.e. nature) and place (social, cultural, conveyed via language) by addressing poetry as a vibrant, existential mode of being in and making place. In German, for instance, we have the notion of a “Kulturlandschaft”, and even to name such a landscape is to situate oneself in it in a particular way. Since the Anthropocene, we know that there is no place on the planet that hasn’t been transformed by human technology and culture. The natural world is always already cultural from the very moment we cast eyes upon it and see it through culturally-inflected lenses. Just as Butler in Gender Trouble (1990) claimed that there was no biological “sex” that wasn’t always already inflected by the cultural conventions of “gender”, so to there is no “space” that is not always already “formed” by the cultural and in particular the artistic and philosophical articulations of “place”. Following these intimations, we will experiment with three levels of methodological approaches to the poetry of place: first, the notion of poetry as a mode of description of place (often in the pastoral mode of the early Early Modern or Enlightenment periods, or the picturesque mode that arises around the Romantic period), frequently connected to personal affect and spatial atmosphere or mood; then, the idea that poetry is a particular form of intervention in discourses about landscape, i.e. literature engages with other linguistic modes of portraying, understanding, articulating the landscape; and finally, the more speculative but epistemologically radical sense of poetry as an ontological exploration at the interface between the creativity of language and the creativity of place, seeing them at an intertwined space of unfurling complexity and environmental agency. The course will explore landscape poetry from the Book of Genesis to contemporary verse (e.g. Tomlinson, Lucie, Kinsella), from works of the Augustans (Pope) via classics of British Romanticism (Wordsworth, Keats, Coleridge) through to Modernism (Stevens). All the poetry will be made available on moodle, along with a portfolio of theoretical texts. 60 minutes of close readings of poems will be followed by 30 minutes of discussion.

Assessment: 4000-word essay for BA students, 5000-word essay for MA students (or other modalities should your degree scheme specifically demands them), based on a close reading of one poem, due at the end of the summer semester (i.e. end of September 2026).

Contents:
This course will discuss the notion of the Popular in African Literature as a product of everyday life which highlights the divide between high and low culture. It will explore how the dichotomy between high and low culture draws attention to emergent hybrid forms that focus on the relationships between texts, their producers and audiences. This course will introduce students to the major concepts, trends, theories and aspects of African Popular Literature as a part of the trends in literary and popular culture that have emerged over the course of African literature

Contents:
In the winter semester 24/25, but also in the winter semester 25/26, my seminars touched on topics that could be considered part of the post-feminist sensibility. This is a crude mixture of feminist rhetoric and patriarchal stereotypes of female gender imagery. In a way, post-feminist sensibility (Gill, 2007) has already become standard in media theory. Building upon the foundational work of Gill regarding post-feminist sensibility—characterized by a complex amalgamation of feminist discourse and entrenched patriarchal stereotypes—we aim to explore whether similar dynamics apply to the evolving landscape of queer identities. As myriad self-identifying categories emerge within digital spheres, queer representation has increasingly become a prominent facet of modern culture. Nevertheless, it is crucial to interrogate whether these representations escape traditional frameworks that reinforce rather than subvert binary gender norms. Indeed, certain expressions of queerness now serve as cultural capital, potentially diluting the radical potential inherent in queer activism. This seminar posits that while societal recognition of diverse sexual identities is imperative, it simultaneously invites scrutiny into the commercialization of queerness. We will critically examine how queerness, when commodified, can inadvertently align with and uphold heteropatriarchal and capitalist structures rather than challenge them. Through an academic lens, participants will engage with contemporary texts, media, and theories to unpack these complex intersections and their implications for cultural production and identity. The seminar does not question that heteronormativity is a code that is both outdated and mostly useless. Here, however, we are concerned with a different phenomenon, namely how queerness can be sold in a market-compatible way and thus does not attack heteropatriarchal and capitalist structures but rather embraces them.

Contents:
On the topic of women writers in the Romantic period, Anne K. Mellor says that 'there is no "Romantic period" in women's writing. But is this truly the case? This module challenges the notion of Romantic Women Writers as peripheral and shows, instead, that women writers played an important role in how we read, study and think about Romantic literature and how they actively participated within cultural, political, literary and philosophical debates around Europe. In this module we will read women writers from Germany (Karoline von Günderrode, Bettina von Arnim, Annette von Droste-Hülshoff), England (Mary Shelley, Mary Robinson, Charlotte Smith) and France (Mme de Staël, George Sand, Marceline Desborde-Valmore).

Depending on the study programme, academic papers can be written in German, English or French, likewise Oral Exams can also in German, English or French.

German and French course description below.

Über das Thema der romantische Frauen, schlagt Anne K. Mellor vor, dass es tatsächlich keine romantische Literatur für Schriftstellerinnen des 19. Jahrhunderts gibt. Aber ist das wirklich so? Dieses Seminar fordert zur Kritik das Verständnis von romantischen Frauen als "peripher" heraus und weist stattdessen auf, dass romantische Frauen eine notwendige Rolle in unseren allgemeinen Verständnis der romantischen Literatur spielt und wie sie in der Tat an den kulturellen, politischen, literarischen sowie philosophischen Debatten in Europe teilnahmen. In diesem Seminar wird man Schriftstellerinnen aus Deutschland (Karoline von Günderrode, Bettina von Arnim, Annette von Droste-Hülshoff), England (Mary Shelley, Mary Robinson, Charlotte Smith) und Frankreich (Mme de Staël, George Sand, Marceline Desborde-Valmore) lesen.

Je nach Studiengang, können Hausarbeiten bei mir auf Deutsch, Englisch oder Französisch geschrieben werden, ebenso mündliche Prüfungen können auf Deutsch, Englisch oder Französisch absolviert werden.

Au sujet des femmes romantiques, Anne K. Mellor suggère qu'il n'y pas de tout un romantisme au féminin dans la littérature européenne du 19ème siècle. Mais, est-ce vraiment le cas ? Pendant ce séminaire on redécouvrira le rôle des femmes romantiques dans le contexte culturel, politique, littéraire et philosophique du romantisme en Europe, mais surtout de quelle façon les femmes romantiques nous aident à comprendre les liaisons interculturelles et internationales qui ont établi la dynamique comparée du romantisme. Dans ce séminaire on lira des écrivaines de l’Allemagne ((Karoline von Günderrode, Bettina von Arnim, Annette von Droste-Hülshoff), de l’Angleterre (Mary Shelley, Mary Robinson, Charlotte Smith) et de la France (Mme de Staël, George Sand, Marceline Desborde-Valmore).

En fonction du cours d’étude, ‘Hausarbeiten’ peuvent être écrits en allemand, anglais or français et ‘Prüfungen’ peuvent être aussi effectuées en allemand, anglais or français.

Contents:
In this seminar, we will examine Shakespeare’s works as dynamic sites for engaging with the social and political divisions that shape both early modern England and our contemporary world. Rather than treating Shakespeare as a literary icon, the course situates his plays and poems within contexts of polarisation—power and resistance, sovereignty and rebellion, and gender and sexuality—and explores how these tensions resonate in modern debates across the globe. Students will analyse tragedies, histories, and comedies alongside critical theory, historical documents, and modern adaptations to discuss how Shakespeare’s plays help develop a sensitive reading of authority, challenge injustice, and examine cultural conflict.

Literature:
Preliminary List of Texts:

William Shakespeare, Richard III

William Shakespeare, Macbeth

William Shakespeare, Measure fore Measure

Contents:
Since its emergence in the early nineteenth century, the historical novel has been a form that navigates productive tensions between narrative, historiography, and ideology. Focusing on three landmark texts – Sir Walter Scott's Waverley (1814), John Fowles' The French Lieutenant’s Woman (1969), and Hilary Mantel's Wolf Hall (2009) – this course traces the genre's development from its foundational realist model through its postmodern disruption and contemporary reinvention. We will explore how historical novels construct the past, negotiate questions of agency and causation, and reflect changing assumptions about historical knowledge itself. Aspects such as narrative voice, temporal distance, political interpretation, and the ethics of representing the past will play key roles in our readings and analyses. Read alongside key theoretical and critical texts, these novels allow us to ask what kinds of historical understanding fiction can produce, and why the historical novel remains a vital literary form in contemporary culture.

Literature:
Please buy and read in advance:

Sir Walter Scott. Waverley (Recommended edition: Penguin Classics)

John Fowles. The French Lieutenant’s Woman (Recommended edition: Vintage Classics)

Hilary Mantel. Wolf Hall (Recommended edition: Fourth Estate)

Further texts will be provided at the beginning of term.

Contents:
In this seminar we will shift our gaze beyond dominant human-centric discourses and engage with a variety of approaches to the non-human as well as literary and cultural texts which de-center the concept of the human from various angles - including posthumanist and materialist approaches, intersectional feminist approaches, critical disability studies, queer studies and indigenous approaches.

If you would like to get a headstart, you could begin reading Ursula Le Guin's short story "Vaster than empires and more slow" and Nnedi Okorafor's novel Death of the Author. All critical texts will be made available via Moodle.

Throughout the semester you will be asked to engage with a range of theoretical texts, as well as examples of non-human perspectives in different literary genres and other media (here you will also be free to add your own examples, which you can explore further in writing, for instance in a writing project or your term paper at the end of the semester).

Contents:
If one were to believe some of the early 20th-century modernists, one would expect "Victorian Poetry" to be conventional in content and form, moralizing, sentimental, prudish, the very opposite of "avant garde". The 19th-century witnessed massive and also disruptive developments in the economic, social, and political realm, including major shifts in the fields of religion, science, and philosophical thought, and one would expect to see these also in the poetry of the period in terms of sheer content. Obviously, this course will also concern itself with such contents. However, our approach will be directed mainly through the perspective of poetic forms and techniques which will demonstrate that Victorian poets were, in fact, highly experimental in their writing, pushing the boundaries of what poetry and language could do.

Each session we will be dedicated to a specific poet with a selection of their poetry provided at the beginning of term. In additon, there will be sessions dedicated to specific forms and poetic inventions. Poets studied will be, for example: Gerard Manley Hopkins, Alfred, Lord Tennyson, Algernon Swinburne, Christina Rossetti, Elizabeth Barrett-Browning, Emily Bronte, Robert Browing, "Michael Field", George Meredith, Augusta Webster.

Contents:
This seminar explores how contemporary fiction and film adaptation give voice to those omitted, obscured, or silenced by official histories. Rather than focusing on national canons, the course examines transnational and diasporic texts that trace the afterlives of empire across multiple geographies. Through works by Anuk Arudpragasam, Bama, Michael Ondaatje, and Oisín Fagan, we investigate how memory, the body, landscape, and narrative function as counter-archives in the aftermath of empire, caste oppression, war, and displacement. Moving between South Asia (Arudpragasam, Bama, Ondaatje) Europe (Fagan/Ondaatje), and the Americas (Fagan), the seminar asks how literary and cultural texts speak into silences left by violence and how storytelling itself can become an act of resistance.

Learning target:
We will try to find answers to the following questions:

1. What happens when history forgets or is designed to forget?

2. How do landscapes, bodies, and sensory experiences function as alternative forms of record?

3. Who gets to speak, and in what language or form?

4. What roles do race, caste, gender, and nation play in shaping whose stories survive?

Literature:
Students may use electronic versions. But print copies are highly recommended.

Reading list (in order of classroom discussions)

The Story of a Brief Marriage by Anuk Arudpragasam – a very short narrative that is set over 24 hours during the final stages of the Sri Lankan civil war, Arudpragasan’s debut novel traces the fragile interior life of a displaced Tamil man. It explores trauma, impermanence, and how the body becomes both archive and refuge when history fails.

Karukku by Bama - A Dalit Christian woman’s very short autobiographical account of growing up in Tamil Nadu, navigating caste discrimination, religion and resistance. Written in a bold, non-linear style, it defies both literary and societal silences.

The English Patient by Michael Ondaatje - winner of the Booker Prize (1992) and later the Golden Booker (2018). The novel’s fragmented narrative reflects on identity, loss and the blurred lines between cartography, colonialism and desire. We will explore the complexities behind national identity and the problems relating to narrating personal stories and historical events.

Eden's Shore by Oisín Fagan - follows an Irish colonial expedition to South America, revealing how utopian ambition, violence, and ambivalent imperial roles create erasure and fractured memory.

• We will also allocate one session for a discussion on the 1997 film adaptation of Ondaatje’s The English Patient which was nominated for 12 Academy Awards (won 9) and find out what makes adapting a novel to a film “prizeworthy”.

Recommended editions: (other editions are also fine as long as they help you to follow the sections read in class.

Arudpragasam, Anuk. The Story of a Brief Marriage. Granta Books, 2017. ISBN 9781783782383.

Bama, Karukku. Translated from Tamil by Lakshmi Holmström, edited by Mini Krishnan, Oxford University Press, 2014. ISBN 0199450412.

Fagan, Oisín. Eden’s Shore. John Murray Press, 2025. ISBN 9781399815918.

Ondaatje, Michael. The English Patient. Everyman’s Library, 2011. ISBN 1841593397

Oisín Fagan will join the seminar on 27.07 (final session; attendance mandatory as part of the regular seminar schedule) to discuss the text. This will be followed by a public reading on 29.07 (attendance optional)

Contents:
In this class, we will approach Old English from the perspectives of linguistics and literary studies, focusing on grammar, morphology, phonetics, semantics as well as poetic language, stylistic means, text structures. We wish to explore how this language works and how texts in the language work. No knowledge of the language is required to take this class, as we will start with the basics and take our approaches from there, to get to know the language and have fun while doing so!

Contents:
Colonialism is not only a theft of space but a theft of time as well.
Through this course, we will delve into how clocks and timekeeping, much like maps, are imbricated in coloniality. Historian Giordano Nanni argues that European colonial expansion was not only propelled by the “geographic extension of its clocks and calendars” but was foundationally anchored in a discourse of time. Colonisers deployed time as an instrument of discipline and reform. The imposition of the colonial temporal order led to the suppression of temporal imaginaries and practices of the colonised. This imposition is also inextricably linked to imperial capital and settler control over land and labour. These colonial temporal constructions very much defined, as Johannes Fabian has shown, the discipline of anthropology, and its “denial of coevalness” or production of “allochronic” discourse —through which the time of the white anthropologist was constituted as different from that of the Other—anthropology’s object of study. In this course, we will not only look at the forms of temporal control in our contemporary world and engage with concepts such as waiting, futurism, linearity and homogeneity, but we will also delve into
decolonial refusals. We will explore how people reclaim and take control of their own time. We will delve into enactments of alternate temporal imaginaries and unpack how liberation is also rooted in a discourse of time.

The course is designed around several thought-provoking interventions and exercises. Some of these interventions include (but are not limited to) investigating colonial continuities by engaging with the museum as a crime scene with a focus on Ethnologische Sammlung at the University of Tübingen; ‘disassembly’ as a critical practice aimed at foregrounding questions of labor and extraction with a focus on the supermarket as a site of inquiry, among other engagements such as workshops and film screenings.

Seeking to decenter dominant scholarship, the course is a call for attentiveness towards citational politics and acknowledging the intellectual debt of scholars writing from the margins. Critical pedagogy is foundational to the course: through collaborative and participatory pedagogical interventions, the classroom is reimagined as a space of unlearning and learning.

Furthermore, in the hope of forging multiway learning, participants are encouraged to share articles, stories, music, poems, podcasts, films, drawings, and a range of other works they feel connected to or influenced by. At the heart of the course is reimagining anthropology as a site of refusal, hope and liberation, and enabling participants to tell stories that matter the most to them.

Contents:
Is the body a biological ‘fact’ or is it a cultural ‘artifact’? While we often experience our bodies as natural, bounded, and unchanging, medical systems profoundly influence the way we see, heal, and understand them. In this seminar, we move beyond the clinical definition of health to explore the body as a site of historical, political, and sociocultural negotiation.
Drawing on medical anthropology and Science and Technology Studies (STS), we will dissect the ways in which medical systems have historically mapped, fragmented, and governed the human form. In doing so, we will explore how biology intersects with culture, power, gender, race, technology, class, and globalization in shaping medical knowledge and bodily experience.

Contents:
Awakenings. Auto-biographical accounts of radical self-transformation

Tuesdays, 10:15-11:45, roof chamber, Barthel-Zimmer [Ethnologie] 220.

Through autobiographical accounts of radical self transformation framed in terms of ‘awakening’, this course invites students to explore the interplay between individual and collective change. Religious, gender, ethno-racial, conspiracist, or other awakenings are commonly narrated in the first person as experiences of radical change, marking a decisive break between past and present. These, in turn, are often contrasted as states of darkness and ignorance versus light and consciousness respectively. Through close discussion of autobiographical accounts in dialogue with the emerging literature on awakenings, the course examines how change takes place. A guiding question throughout will be: How do personal experiences inform broader social transformations and, conversely, how do collective events reverberate in individual perceptions of truth, identity, and belonging? Meetings will be structured around the analysis of textual and/or visual materials, and active participation is expected. Students are welcome to bring additional material for discussion in class.

Contents:
WICHTIG

DER KLASSIK KURS VON DR C BUBLATZKY BEGINNT AM MITTWOCH 22.4

ANMELDUNG PER EMAIL IST ERBETEN FÜR BESSERE PLANBARKEIT!

Die Ethnologie arbeitet empirisch, praxisnah und feldforschungsbasiert. Ihre Erkenntnisse und Methoden finden daher auch außerhalb der Universität Anwendung – etwa in der Entwicklungszusammenarbeit, in Museen, NGOs, in der Politikberatung, in Medien, Bildungsinstitutionen sowie im Gesundheits- oder Umweltbereich.
Um diesen Praxisbezug näher kennenzulernen, beschäftigen wir uns in diesem Seminar mit unterschiedlichen Ansätzen und Strömungen der applied, public und engaged anthropology sowie mit zentralen Vertreter:innen dieser Perspektiven. Anhand konkreter Fallstudien und weiterer Themenfelder – etwa der politischen Ethnologie oder der dark anthropology – vertiefen wir unser Wissen über unterschiedliche Traditionen, strategische Positionierungen und analytische Perspektiven innerhalb der Ethnologie.

Folgende Fragen bilden einen guten Ausgangspunkt für das Seminar:
Wie können sich Ethnolog:innen in öffentlichen Diskursen positionieren und mit ihren Erkenntnissen zu politischen Entscheidungsprozessen oder gesellschaftlichen Herausforderungen beitragen? Wann und wie können ethnologische Forschungsprojekte, Forschungsdesigns und Methoden sowie verschiedene Formen der Wissensvermittlung – etwa wissenschaftliche Publikationen, Blogs oder journalistische Texte – dazu beitragen, komplexe gesellschaftliche Zusammenhänge sichtbar zu machen und marginalisierte Perspektiven zu stärken?
Wie kann es dabei gelingen, die kritische Distanz der Ethnologie zu bewahren? Und welche Möglichkeiten eröffnet das Fach für außeruniversitäre Arbeitsfelder? Welche ethischen Fragen stellen sich in solchen Kontexten?

Oder anders formuliert: Wann wird ethnologisches Wissen politisch wirksam – und wann kann es problematisch werden?

Learning target:
Ziel des Seminars ist es, zentrale Konzepte der öffentlichen, engagierten und angewandten Ethnologie kennenzulernen und erklären zu können. Darüber hinaus sollen ethnologische Forschungspraktiken in öffentlichen Kontexten kritisch eingeordnet sowie ethische Dilemmata ethnologischer Forschung analysiert werden. Ein weiterer Fokus liegt darauf, unterschiedliche Möglichkeiten kennenzulernen, ethnologisches Wissen für nicht-akademische Öffentlichkeiten aufzubereiten und zugänglich zu machen.

Anhand konkreter Fallbeispiele und zentraler Vertreter:innen der öffentlichen, engagierten und angewandten Ethnologie erhalten die Studierenden Einblicke in die Verbindungen zwischen Theorie, Methodik und Praxis. Gleichzeitig eröffnet das Seminar Perspektiven auf mögliche außeruniversitäre Tätigkeitsfelder und die gesellschaftliche Relevanz ethnologischer Forschung.

Contents:
This seminar explores how belonging is constructed, negotiated, and contested in various cultural, social, and political contexts. Drawing from anthropological theories, interdisciplinary perspectives, and contemporary case studies, we will examine the ways in which belonging is shaped by factors such as nationality, migration, race, gender, class, and religion.

Key questions include: What does it mean to belong? How is belonging performed, experienced, and institutionalized? How do exclusion and marginalization shape different forms of belonging? Through weekly readings, discussions, and critical reflections, students will engage with both classical and contemporary texts, developing a nuanced understanding of the politics of belonging in a globalized world.
The first session will be held on the 14th of April!

Contents:
Whatever activity we engage in, there is bound to be a thing involved. Things move, things move us and we find things moving. So how do we begin to explore our relationship to things from an anthropological perspective? This seminar is designed to provide some answers to this question collaboratively. Together we will explore through theory and practice, how we relate to things, how things relate to us, and how to find out. Though reading but also through “making” (Ingold 2013) we will explore what materiality could be and how it can helps us in our ethnographic research. In this seminar we will use multi-sensory approaches to foreground objects, which are usually left largely unattended in the background of everyday life. The theory that we will lean on foregrounds the processual and relational and so in the end, there will be no single outcome or finished product that we will produce. We will learn through the process and learn how to describe the process. Therefore, rather than a final single masterpiece, our own learning process will be what we accomplish and showcase in a collaborative exhibition. The anthropologist only has their body as a tool with which to apprehend the world. In the process of making we will hone our senses to become more attentive and attuned to the material things around us and therefore become more sensitive instruments with which to investigate the social world of things.

Contents:
Ethnographic writing

Fridays, 9-12:30 (5 June - 17 July), roof chamber, Barthel-Zimmer [Ethnologie] 220.

This intensive, hands-on course conceived as a workshop, aims to help students hone their ethnographic writing skills through a series of in-class and take-home assignments. Class meetings combine readings on ethnographic methods with collaborative analysis and practical experimentation. Students are supported in refining their observational and narrative skills, and in integrating theory with ethnographic material. Regular feedback and revision are central components of the course, which aims to foster clarity, reflexivity, and stylistic confidence in ethnographic writing.

Contents:
The module Geo-Biosphere Interactions targets the linkage of the Geosphere - comprising various components of the abiotic environment (focus on Lithosphere - but also Atmosphere, Hydrosphere) and its organisms (their sum - i.e. the community - but also individual "ecosystem engineers"). Special focus will be laid on soils - the pedosphere - as by its definition this is a compartment comprised of a magnituded of direct interfaces between organisms and their abiotic environment.

The course will give an introduction into Geo-Biosphere Interactions and start with the linkage of Geo- and Biosphere via the biogeochemistry of some of the main elements living organisms are comprised of - C, N, P, S. As main constitutents of cells, these elements naturally link Geo- and Biosphere - being derived from the first and incorporated into the second by a magnituce of processes under various controls. After a scale-briding view on the biogeochemistry of Geo-Biosphere Interactions, the cellular biochemistry (with special focus on microbial ecology) behind the biotic influence on these element cycles shall be unravelled.

The second part of the course shall focus on the specific look on Geo-Biosphere Interfaces with highest relevance quantitatively for element cycling and matter fluxes in the environemnt - ranging from relevance for processes on geologic timescales up to relevance for causing and/or combating negative impacts of global, specifically climate, change. These interfaces comprise e.g. soil fauna (such as burrowing animals, earthworms, termites and ants), microbial biofilms, lichens, cyanobacteria, the rhizsophere and the mycosphere.

Besides the lecture, the module will have a one-week lab course where specific element fluxes at a geo-biosphere interface will be monitored with a coupling of state-of-the-art isotope labeling and biomarker methods.

Keywords:
Geo-Biosphere interactions

Geo-Biosphere interfaces

Biogeochemistry of element cycles

Key organisms in ecosystems

Organisms and their abiotic environment

Isotopes

Biomarkers

Highlights include climate modelling experiments, analysis of simulated climate outputs, group projects on interesting and relevant processes in the Earth system. Contents:
This course is an elective module in the Geoscience department study program (e.g. Geoscience, AEG, UNW, Geo-Ecology). The course provides the theoretical and practical basics to two geo- and thermochronological methods that have a broad range of applications in Geoscience, such as quantifying Geodynamic and Earth’s surface processes. Participants will date their own rock/mineral and learn the how to interpret their ages. Specific topics addressed in this course include:

Theoretical and practical background of fission track dating

Principles of U-Pb dating

Interpretation of thermo- and geochronological data

Contents:
The Quaternary (spanning the past c. 2.6 My) represents an important period in the earth’s geological, climate and human history. Establishing a timing for these events, not only provides a chronological framework, but also a potential tool for quantifying the rate of geological or geomorphological processes. This course aims to provide an advanced insight as well as practical experience in the luminescence dating for dating Quaternary sediments. The course includes fieldwork and sampling of sediment samples, preparation of feldspar minerals in the laboratory, luminescence measurements, and calculation of equivalent doses and ages.

Keywords:
Geochronology, palaeoclimate, sediment archives, dating, applications

Contents:
Because many materials and complex specimens cannot be sufficiently characterized by surface-sensitive electron microscopy techniques alone, important internal structures often remain inaccessible. Conventional sectioning or polishing methods can lack site specificity, or fail when applied to hard, heterogeneous, or multilayered samples. Focused Ion Beam (FIB) techniques overcome these challenges by enabling controlled, site-specific material removal and high-precision sectioning directly within the electron microscope. However, ion–matter interactions can also lead to beam-induced damage and artefact formation, making a fundamental understanding of these processes essential for reliable experimental design and data interpretation.

This course introduces the basic principles of Focused Ion Beam scanning electron microscopy (FIB-SEM), including theory, instrumentation, and practical application. The course covers FIB-based sample preparation strategies such as simple cross-sectioning and more complex geometries suitable for serial sectioning imaging (SSI). Building on this foundation, students are introduced to volume electron microscopy workflows based on the iterative alternation of FIB milling and electron imaging, enabling three-dimensional reconstruction of samples. The course further provides an introduction to software-based post-processing, visualization, and analysis of image stacks and 3D datasets.

Qualification objective:
Students

- understand the basic theories and applications of FIB-SEM

- get an understanding of how to handle different sample material for FIB-SEM

- get an understanding of workflow processes of working with 3D data sets

- learn to analyse, document and discuss scientific image information

Keywords:
Electron microscopy, Focused Ion Beam, FIB, SEM, sample preparation

Contents:
Course description

What holds societies together when markets are globalised, working conditions are made more flexible and social security becomes fragile? Between economic rationalities and growing inequalities, the concept of solidarity is gaining new relevance. But what does solidarity mean in an economic order characterised by competition?

In this seminar, we will address the question of how solidarity can become effective as a moral principle and practical attitude in business ethics contexts. We will examine historical, philosophical and economic perspectives and analyse current challenges - from social inequality or corporate social responsibility to global crises such as climate change and migration. The aim is to critically reflect on normative principles, practical areas of conflict and the transformative potential of solidarity-based action in business.

Learning outcomes for this seminar:

Students and Participants

• analyse the ethical foundations of solidarity-based action in an economic context

• evaluate the relevance of solidarity in corporate decisions and strategies

• reflect on the practical implications of solidarity-based economic activity in a global and local context,

• develop recommendations for action for managers with regard to ethical and social responsibility

This seminar can be credited as a themed course for the certificate "Ethics in practice".

Contents:
This course begins with a close reading of John Ruskin’s Unto This Last before branching out to tackle a variety of 20th- and 21st-century world authors on the theme of global economic justice. A common humanistic ‘ethos’ – or at least a harmony of humanistic concern for economic justice - will emerge from these diverse voices. Questions of future economic justice – including the role of artificial intelligence in enabling just (and presently unimaginable) outcomes – will also be explored towards the end of the course.
This seminar can be credited as a themed course for the certificate "Ethics in practice".

Qualification objective:
Students:

- learn key concepts
- develop skills to apply learned topics broadly

Contents:
What does the future of education entail? Does traditional learning theories still hold true when learning and instructional technologies (EdTech in short) evolves at a rate greater than ever before? This course is intended to map the present landscape of EdTech, to reflect on their benefits as well as potential drawbacks, and to connect new technology with old ideas.

Specifically, we will examine traditional learning theories from new perspectives, explore best practices for using various EdTech tools, and apply what we have learned in a learning/teaching challenge (use case) you identify. We will cover topics including learning theories behind EdTech, game-based learning, embodied learning (VR/AR/XR), personalized and collaborative learning with AI, and the learning engineering workflow.

Contents:
Projektseminar 2: Talent Development is a two-semester master’s course that combines theoretical foundations with applied research in talent development. In the first semester, students receive structured input on key theories, models, and aspects of talent development, and are introduced to ongoing projects of the Hector Children’s Academies Program.

Building on this theoretical foundation, students work in groups to engage in applied projects. Depending on their choice, groups either analyze existing secondary data from programs such as FIPS+ or actively participate in ongoing talent development projects, designing interventions, planning and implementing evaluation studies, and summarizing scientific findings on their effects. The majority of practical work and study implementation takes place at the end of the first semester and during the second semester, allowing students to apply theory to practice in a research-oriented context.

Contents:
This is a second part of a research-oriented course providing students an opportunity:

to develop their knowledge about how experimental approaches are used in research in education and learning and

to gain practical knowledge about how to design and program experiments to test learning process.

Research in educational psychology often uses survey/observation designs to understand processes of successful learning and teaching in real-world education settings. There are a number of benefits with these approaches. However, it is impossible to control all relevant factors in everyday classrooms, which makes it difficult for researchers to identify causal mechanisms behind successful learning or teaching. Experimental studies are often less relevant to real-life learning but have an advantage over survey/observation designs in its higher levels of control and thus help us to identify the causal mechanisms and completement survey/observation studies. This seminar covers how experimental studies have helped understand mechanisms underlying successful learning and helps students to develop and conduct their own experimental studies.

Building on the part-1 seminar, in this semester, students will learn how to program experiments using existing tools. We will then help students to program their own study. Students will collect data from several participants based on their program and analyze the data.

Literature:

Contents:
Motivation acts as an internal driver that pushes or pulls learners toward their studies. While it is not something we can observe directly, its presence is clearly felt in the classroom. Some students seem to genuinely enjoy and are energized by learning, while others appear frustrated and show no signs of motivation. This raises important questions: where does this motivation originate, and how does it evolve over time?

In this seminar, we will learn the leading theories of motivation within empirical education research. We will also analyze longitudinal survey data to understand how these theoretical frameworks are tested and validated.

In the first half of this term, we will cover a variety of classic and contemporary theories of motivation. We will then examine how these theories have been tested in past empirical education research, with a specific focus on survey methods. We will place particular emphasis on longitudinal survey data (i.e., panel data) as one of the most common methodologies in the field, exploring its unique strengths and weaknesses.

Next term, we will learn how to analyze real panel data using R while addressing practical challenges (e.g., missing data, coding of categorical variables, nested structure of data, etc.). Through hands-on practice, you will gain the technical skills necessary to manage complex datasets.

Learning target:
The learning objective of this seminar is twofold. The first objective is to learn and critically evaluate leading theories of motivation within empirical education research. The second objective is to learn survey methods, with a particular focus on panel data, as a primary tool used to empirically test these theories.

Contents:
How can statistical results and narratives work together to produce convincing empirical evidence? Is it possible that words, lived experiences, and contexts carry explanatory power equal to, or even beyond, statistical results?

This seminar introduces mixed methods research not merely as a combination of two approaches, but as a systematic framework for integrating quantitative and qualitative data. Focusing on empirical research in education and psychology, you will learn what mixed methods are, why they matter, and how they can be used to address complex research questions that cannot be fully captured by a single methodological lens.

This seminar adopts a learning-by-doing approach. We will engage with real research examples and gain hands-on experience by designing and conducting a small mixed methods project. A special feature of this semester’s seminar is that student will have the chance to explore how Generative artificial intelligence (AI) can be used critically and responsibly in thematic analysis. By the end of the course, we will not only understand mixed methods conceptually but also practice key skills in qualitative analysis and learn strategies for integrating them with quantitative data.

Qualification objective:
This course is graded on a pass/fail basis. In order to earn course credits, students will complete two assignments, including:
1. Mid-term Formative Assignment: Write a short reflection on the use of Generative AI in thematic analysis.
2. Final Assignment: Submit a research proposal presenting a self-designed mixed methods study.

For Course Engagement, students are also expected to complete all assigned texts before each session and participate in class discussions during the seminar.

Contents:
‘International Perspectives on Motivation Research and Motivation Interventions’ is a graduate-level course designed to foster students’ international perspectives on motivation theory and motivational interventions. The course examines major theories of academic motivation, cultural influences on motivational processes, and the design and implementation of motivational interventions in diverse cultural contexts.

Learning target:
The learning objective of this seminar is to acquire the critical thinking skills necessary to evaluate information regarding empirical education research.

Contents:
‘Research and Practice’ is
a seminar that investigates the methodological, structural and behavioural
challenges facing the endeavour of ‘evidence-informed practice / evidence-based
practice’ in the UK, Germany and the US. Initially, the seminar looks at key
issues surrounding the use of the ‘best available’ evidence (methodological
issues associated with meta-analysis and systematic reviews, and publication
bias in particular), but also draws out narratives from participating students
around the incentives and disincentives to producing the ‘best available’
evidence they encounter in their own careers. The focus then shifts to look at
structural and behavioural components of evidence-informed practice, and to
review the current ‘state of the art’ in schools, colleges, and the education
systems of the UK, Germany and the US.

Contents:
As artificial intelligence (AI) continues to transform education, conversational agents—such as chatbots and virtual tutors—are becoming increasingly important in shaping how students learn and interact. This course explores the design, development, and evaluation of pedagogical conversational agents (PCAs) that support teaching and learning across diverse contexts. Students will investigate how AI-driven dialogue systems can enhance engagement, provide feedback, and adapt to individual learning needs while considering ethical, social, and pedagogical implications. Through hands-on projects and critical analysis, participants will design, prototype, and test their own conversational agents tailored to specific educational goals. Topics include natural language understanding, instructional design for AI-mediated learning, multimodal interaction, assessment and analytics, and responsible AI in education. By the end of the course, students will be equipped to thoughtfully integrate conversational AI into real or simulated classroom environments and to evaluate its impact on learning outcomes and teaching practices.

Contents:
The goal of this introductory lecture is to provide teacher students with an overview of psychological concepts, theories and research in educational psychology with a focus on successful learning and teaching. Educational psychology aims to explain how to enable and support successful teaching and learning, and other pedagogically significant issues, such assessments of students’ learning. This lecture will cover various issues from educational psychology, such as what learning means, how learning processes take place, what kinds of individual differences influence learning processes, and how learning is assessed. The lecture thus offers basic knowledge to understand learning processes for teacher students. Note that the lecture will be given in English.

Key topics covered in the lecture will include: theories on learning, cognitive foundation of learning, self-regulated learning, motivation, and assessment of learning.

Please note that this lecture will be delivered in English and given by Prof Dr Michiko Sakaki (https://uni-tuebingen.de/de/199450).

Contents:
This research seminar focuses on the contemporary far right in Europe. Over the past decades, support for radical right parties and movements has increased substantially across the European continent, while extreme right ideas have moved from the margins of the political spectrum into the mainstream. What are the reasons behind the renewed surge of the far right? Who joins far-right movements and why? How do far-right leaders mobilise support? What role do women play in far-right movements? What do we know about far-right party organisation? What effect does the rise of the far right have on democracy? And how can mainstream parties respond? This course offers an in-depth study of the history, ideology, organisation, causes and consequences of contemporary far-right politics.

Keywords:
Far Right; Radical Right; Extreme Right; Parties; Movements; Europe

Contents:
Today select buildings in the Weißenhofsiedlung in Stuttgart are recognized as World Heritage by UNESCO, but the entire estate had its origins as part of a housing exhibition organized by the Deutscher Werkbund a century ago, in 1927. Two years after this event, the Werkbund launched another watershed exhibition in the city—Film und Foto—which toured the world and changed the course of photography and graphic design history alike. Our understanding of modern architecture and the photographic image in the age of their mechanical reproducibility remains, in large part, a product of these two exhibitions. What exactly is the relationship between the built environment and mass media, and how did the Werkbund define it? Established in 1907 to improve the quality and artistry of German industrial goods, the Werkbund was a union of architects, artists, designers, and cultural reformers. A study of this organization and its members will introduce students to many of the main tenets of modern architectural history, in particular: the shift from “Jugendstil” to the “International Style”; the transformation of Kunstgewerbe (arts and crafts) into industrial design; and the tensions between the media image and domestic reality of architects’ passionate pursuit of “light, air, and sun.”

Contents:
What does a global approach mean for art history, and how might it look in practice? By introducing students to a series of texts, this course explores some of the most significant theoretical and methodological interventions in art history in the 20th and 21st centuries. Specifically, we will attend to questions about globalisation, transnationality, legacies of imperialism and colonialism, and examine the discipline’s response to contemporary debates in anthropology, feminist theory, and Anthropocene studies. The course also pays attention to the renewed interest in the area studies, particularly in the region of ‘East-Central Europe’, prompted by the urgency to re-assess existing paradigms and canons in the wake of the Russian Federation’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Contents:
This seminar will focus on the archaeology, topography, and history of the city of Rome and its environs from the mid-Republican through to the late imperial period, c. fourth century BCE – fourth century CE. It aims to engage critically with archaeological as well as textual and other sources, offering an up-to-date assessment of current thinking (and controversies) on the development of Rome’s built landscape, society, and culture across these crucial phases of its millenary history. A close look at archaeological and architectural evidence, art and artistic trends, and urban patterns will provide a wealth of information to engage with broader socio-political aspects and to contextualize the Eternal City within the framework of the Italian Peninsula and beyond. For this reason, other important sites in the region such as Ostia, Portus, Praeneste, and Tivoli will be taken into account throughout our sessions. The seminar will feature student-led presentations and class discussion of the assigned topics, allowing students to review past and current scholarship and offer their personal contribution to ongoing debates on these subjects.

Contents:
Location: Archaeological Park of Baratti and Populonia, Tuscany, Italy

Date of field school: 05/07/2026 – 25/07/2026

Max students: 3

Populonia (Tuscany, Italy) was an Etruscan-Roman costal town and a renowned centre for metalworking and trade activities. The site features two main areas: a necropolis with monumental tombs dating to the seventh–fourth centuries BCE; and an acropolis, located on a promontory overlooking the Elba Island, which witnessed a major phase of urban development from the late third to the mid-first century BCE. This ongoing project is investigating a sector of the acropolis where a large public building (known as ‘Le Logge’) and an elite domus are found. The field school provides a training opportunity for students who will thus acquire knowledge of the organization and day-to-day running of an excavation, including: the development of skills in accordance with stratigraphic methodologies; the ability to carry out collaborative tasks; the application of a range of recording tools, such as the total station theodolite (TST) and photogrammetry. Beyond the on-site work, students will take part in the preliminary classification of finds and will be taught the basics of conservation. They will also be trained in the use of AutoCAD and QGIS to create digital records of the data.

They will learn and practice basic conventions of academic reading and essay writing, which includes basic textual organization, close and critical reading skills, and methods of quotation and citation from a text in MLA style. Contents:
As humans, we have remarkable linguistic abilities: we are able to understand an infinite number of sentences, including sentences that we haven't heard before. The knowledge that allows us to accomplish this incredible feat is largely unconscious. In this class, we will aim to model this knowledge by formulating and testing hypotheses about the interpretation of sentences and their parts. This class will suit you if you are interested in linguistic meaning, are keen on analytical thinking and enjoy theory-building.

Keywords:
theoretical linguistics, generative grammar, compositional semantics, formal semantics, syntax-semantics interface

Literature:
Class handouts, notes and readings will be posted in Moodle. The Moodle password will be shared with students on the first day of classes.

Contents:
Most of what people want to communicate spans more than one sentence. In this course we will investigate the usage and interpretation of sentences in a larger discourse context. We will examine how discourse context can make an otherwise marked construction (more) appropriate, and how context can influence the interpretation of a particular sentence. We will evaluate existing theoretical proposals in light of the results of corpus studies and psycholinguistic experiments.

Literature:
Readings will be made available in the course.

Contents:
In this seminar we will look at the grammar and processing effects of word order, known in technical terms as linear precedence.

The sorts of questions we will look at are:

- what factors influence word order between heads and complements. For example,

(1a) English, French, and Italian have the verb and the object after it:

eat pizza, manger de la pizza, mangiare della pizza

(1b) while German, Hindi, and Korean have the object before the verb.

Pizza essen, pizza khaane, piza meoggo

- what factors influence word order between two complements of a verb:

(2a) I sent my mother a letter

(2b) I sent a letter to my mother.

Here we have two nouns. If the receiver comes last, it must have the preposition 'to'. We can't say:

(2c) I sent a letter my mother.

But pronouns are different. People say both of these two:

(3a) I sent it him.

(3b) I sent him it.

- how we might account for the placement of particles such as up. There are some mysterious patterns here:

(4a) I looked the word up in a dictionary.

(4b) I looked it up in a dictionary.

(4c) I looked up the word in a dictionary.

(4d) *I looked up it in a dictionary.

We will look at why we find these patterns. And it turns out that they are quite systematic, but the patterns are just not quite what people expect them to be.

In the first half of the term we will look at issues in word order and some analyses and models of the phenomena observed. In the second half of the term students will build their own experiments and test a sub-question about this issue.

Literature:
This is yet to be finalized, but we will certainly look at

- Hawkins, J. (1994) A Performance Theory of Order and Constituency. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press

- Wasow, T. (2002) Postverbal Behavior.Stanford: CSLI

- Gazdar, G., Klein, E., Pullum, G. & Sag, I. (1985) Generalized Phrase Structure Grammar. Oxford: Blackwell

Contents:
This course provides a systematic analysis of a number of phenomena at the syntax-semantics interface. We will adopt a comparative approach, focusing on contrasts between English and German.

We will address the following topics:

- clause structure in German and English,

- quantifiers and scope,

- polarity items and negation,

- focus and ellipsis.

Beck, S., & Gergel, R. (2014). Contrasting English and German grammar: An introduction to syntax and semantics. Walter de Gruyter GmbH & Co KG.

You can get access to it from the Tübingen library website here:

https://www.degruyter.com/document/doi/10.1515/9783110346190/html

Contents:
In this course, we will look at a range of phenomena related to the structure, meaning and use of negation in English, among others the form and position of negative markers, the distribution of polarity sensitive items like ‘any’ and the interaction of negation with other expressions. Particular emphasis will be on phenomena related to negation and polarity where English contrasts with German, for instance the fact that the English sentence “You must not sing“ does not have the same meaning as the German word-by-word translation “Du musst nicht singen“. To describe and explain these differences, notions and tools from syntactic, semantic and pragmatic analysis will be introduced and applied.

Contents:
The course offers an introduction to current theories of linguistic pragmatics. Topics that will be covered include presupposition, Common Ground, implicatures and Question under Discussion.

A background in formal semantics is useful, but not mandatory.

Contents:
The seminar will provide students with knowledge about bilingualism from a psycholinguistic perspective. Among other things, we will discuss models for language storage and processing, the role of emotion in second language processing, and dive into the topic of heritage language.

Comment:
This course guides you through the final stages of your Masters degree. We discuss thesis work as well as oral exams. You will get input on finding a topic, designing a project and writing the thesis. You will find out about oral exam topics and how to prepare for the exam.

Contents:
This course follows on from the Topics for Candidates course. In oral exams you need to know things but you also need to perform in the oral exam context. Rather than focussing on what you need to know for your exams, these sessions focus on the skills of talking about linguistics in English. We therefore address issues around presentation and discussion in English, so that you appear in the best possible light and sell yourself well.

For example, if you get asked a question that you don't know the answer to, then you don't say "I'm sorry, I don't know." Instead you say "Well that's a very interesting question. I tend to think that it is useful to address the issue by relating it to X" and continue by talking about some X which you do know about. It's easy when you get the hang of it and it is a useful life skill.

For people who wish to do their oral exam in the last week of term, these sessions will take place during the term at times which are arranged between the groups and me. For people who want to do their oral exam in the first week of the following term, the sessions take place during the holiday period, for SS in September/October, for WS in March/April. The precise dates will be discussed with the group in advance.

If this is unclear, don't worry, it will all become clear in the first session of the term.

Contents:
This course is aimed at MEd people doing their Colloquium and Independent Study module (ENG_ME_3).

For this module you need two main topics plus a certain amount of wider knowledge of linguistics. The two topics are tested for about 15 minutes each in the final oral exam. The overview then follows as about 10 minutes discussion.

Topics: I think it is important for English teachers to be able to analyze the pronunciation of (varieties of) English, so I normally expect you to do phonemic and phonetic transcription as your first main topic.

You have greater choice on the second main topic, but it is easiest to do something you have already done in a HS. I'll show you how to prepare for this too. If you come to me it is should have something to do with syntax, syntactic processing, psycholinguistics, or empirical methods in linguistics.

The overview section should go beyond the areas of linguistics covered in the main topics. You have a considerable degree of freedom here, but I can make suggestions.

Learning target:
By the end of the course students will understand:

basic principles for the description of the sounds and sound systems used in languages, and how they can be applied to describe English;

basic principles for the description of syntactic structure and the structure of words, and how they can be applied to describe English;

basic principles for deriving sentence meaning from word meanings, sentence structure, and context, and how they can be applied to English.

Literature:
Materials will be made available on Moodle. The Moodle password will be emailed to registered participants shortly before the beginning of term.

Contents:
This advanced linguistics course focuses on two types of interrogatives whose form – namely, its syntactic and/or prosodic realization – and discourse properties differ from those of canonical questions: (i) biased questions, such as “Didn't you turn the light off?”, and (ii) reprise questions, such as “you did WHAT?!”. We will investigate the formal properties of these questions, analyse the requirements they place on the discourse contexts in which they are expressed, and aim to understand how their non-canonical syntax and prosody contribute to their pragmatic effect. Our broader goal will be to use these phenomena as a probe into the structure of the Common Ground that conversational participants share and construct as they communicate with one another.

Learning target:
Deepen knowledge and understanding of core concepts in the syntax, prosody, and pragmatics of questions.

Practice and refine analytical and critical thinking skills

Increase familarity with primary linguistic literature

Practice and refine presentation and groupwork skills

Develop and refine independent research skills (in the case of "Kolloquium" students)

Contents:
Expand your expertise in semantics!

This class offers a forum for students interested in recent developments in semantic theory. We will explore a topic in current semantic research, discussing recent developments. Students will have the chance to discover a topic for their thesis and pursue their own research questions.

Literature:
The syllabus and a reading list will be distributed in the first session.

Contents:
Native-like pronunciation in a second language is often said to be hard to achieve. Yet, foreign accents have a large inherent variability and are a dynamic aspect of linguistic fluency. In this course, we will consider phonetic and phonological manifestations of foreign accent as well as an accent's impact on language comprehension and the perpetuation of its negative reception through stereotypes. The course takes an inclusive approach with the aim of integrating theoretical and experimental perspectives on sounding 'foreign'.

Literature:
Readings will be announced at the beginning of the semester on Moodle and will be made available online.

Contents:
This linguistics proseminar teaches students the basics of English syntax and syntactic theory.

Comment:
This is a Proseminar, so it can be done as a seminar in the Basic and Advanced Modules of BA and BEd, or as an Übung in the Advanced and Focus Modules. It can also be used as a workgroup/lecture in MEd and MA modules.

Contents:
The goal of the class is to introduce participants to generative syntax. Participants are not expected to have any previous experience of syntax. There are three main aims:

First, students should gain some idea what range of phenomena are described and explained by syntactic theory, and how models of syntactic structures can help us understand them. The focus of the course is on structures in English and German, because they provide a good example of the strengths of generative syntax. While English and German sentence structures look as if they are very different in complicated ways, it turns out that in a model of structure such as generative grammar, the differences can be accounted for very economically as the results of just a couple of parameters.

The second aim is very practical. Students should learn to analyze sentence structures on their own and *do* linguistics themselves.

Thirdly, I'd like to show you how syntax is actually pleasurable. You will spend a lot of time drawing tree structures, which is fun and somehow very satisfying.

Literature:
The course is structured around handouts and exercises which I have produced. I will make them available to you on Moodle.

Contents:
This seminar examines the basic syntactic properties of English sentences. Students will learn how simple sentences of English can be structurally analyzed and how to apply syntactic methods to English sentences. The course covers basic declarative sentences, embedded clauses, as well as various types of interrogatives.

Literature:
Radford, Andrew. 2009. An Introduction to English Sentence Structure. 1 edn. Cambridge: CUP.

The full text PDF is available through the university library; to access it, you need to be connected to the university network or use a VPN (explanations will be made in the first session).

Contents:
Psycholinguistics is the study of mental processes underlying language behavior. Our goal in this course is to use the knowledge of various fields (linguistics, psychology, neuroscience, etc.) to gain a better understanding of these processes. Our focus will be on adult language processing, but we will take a look at language acquisition and language disorders as well. In addition to examining theories of language processing, we will also discuss experiments designed to test the predictions these theories make.

Literature:
Readings will be made available in class.

Contents:
We examine research methods in language science, with a focus on psycholinguistics and phonetics. The course covers research ethics, experimental methods, the design and analysis of quantitative research, and the basics of survey research.

Learning target:
At the end of the course, students should be able to:

define and differentiate between various research designs

critically read and analyze research articles, extracting key information, identifying research methodologies, and interpret the findings

​​​apply ethical guidelines in the design and execution of reserach involving human participants

develop well-defined and testable research questions

understand the principles of designing and analyzing a quantitative study

apply problem-solving strategies to address challenges in the research process

Literature and course materials will be provided on Moodle.

Contents:
This course provides an introduction to the sentence structures of English and to the way these structures are interpreted.

Contents:
We examine the clause structure of earlier stages of English in the context of Present Day English as well as other Germanic languages. Crosslinguistic syntactic and semantic variation will illuminate fundamental building blocks of human language.

Contents:
The assumption that the literature of medieval North-Western Europe was coldly unemotional has been widely debunked: across Old English and Old Norse literature, we see characters being angry and ashamed, joyful and sad, loving and grieving, anxious and fearful. In this seminar, we will focus specifically on grief and sorrow, complex emotions arising from different forms of loss in social, familial, and romantic contexts. Drawing on recent scholarship in emotion studies, and with a sound basis in theoretical and historical discourses, we will trace the depiction, impact, and narrative function of these emotions across a variety of prose and poetic texts, including elegies, riddles, epics, and sagas, and try to reconstruct and compare the emotive scripts of different generic and cultural contexts. Along the way, we will see how emotion intersects with gender, class, age, and other markers of identity, as well as how it is shaped by biology, society, and genre. And we will finally see that medieval literature, despite its apparent alterity, shows us feeling, grieving, characters whose emotions may not ultimately be so different from ours today.

Contents:
DaF/DaZ Sprachlehrmethoden

Trotz aller Kritik (als langweilig, unterfordernd, schnell rückständig, unzureichend an individuellen Lernervoraussetzungen orientiert usw.) spielen Lehrwerke im Fremd- und Zweitsprachenunterricht immer noch eine große Rolle: Sie stellen einen festen Bestandteil des Lehr- und Lernprozesses dar, indem sie für Lernende Übungsmöglichkeiten (auch zum selbstständigen Lernen) bieten und zugleich für Lehrkräfte als eine praktische Orientierung bei der Stundenplanung und der Klassifikation der Lernergebnisse und somit als Hilfe bei der Realisation des Unterrichts dienen.

Im Seminar DaF-/DaZ-Sprachlehrmethoden werden wir uns zunächst einen kurzen Überblick über die Geschichte der Methoden des Fremdsprachenunterrichts verschaffen. Im Anschluss erarbeiten wir einen Kriterienkatalog für die unterrichtspraktische Lehrwerkanalyse und wenden diesen anschließend an. Wir gehen u. a. folgenden Fragen nach: Welche Art von thematischen Inhalten findet sich in den Lehrwerken? Wie authentisch sind sie? Welche Bedeutung wird Grammatik in den Lehrwerken zuteil? Wird sie eher implizit oder explizit behandelt? Welche Themenkomplexe werden wie ausführlich dargestellt? Welche Art von Übungen und Aufgaben findet sich in den Lehrwerken? Welche Lernziele werden mit ihnen verfolgt? Und schließlich: Lassen sich anhand der Lehrwerkanalyse Merkmale von bestimmten Lehrmethoden identifizieren?

Studiumsbegleitend werden die Studierenden über einen Zeitraum von etwa einem Jahr in einer Einrichtung unseres Kooperationsnetzwerkes im Einsatz sein, um dort im Zweierteam eigenverantwortlich eine Gruppe von Kindern oder Erwachsenen mit Sprachförderbedarf in der Sprachentwicklung zu unterstützen.

In der Supervision, die entweder vor Ort in der Einrichtung oder auf Basis einer videographierten Förderstunde erfolgt, erhalten die Praktikums-Teams ein individuelles und ausführliches Feedback zu ihrem Vorgehen sowie Anregungen für das weitere Praktikum.

Interkulturelles Training (DaZ-Praktikum)

Das Seminar bietet DaZ-Studierenden Raum, Erfahrungen aus dem studienbegleitenden Praktikum vor dem Hintergrund von zentralen Annahmen der Interkulturellen Pädagogik bzw. der Migrationspädagogik zu reflektieren. Anhand von Fallbeispielen und Praxisübungen setzen wir uns mit dem Kulturbegriff und seinen Verwendungsweisen auseinander, um die Grundlagen für eine reflexive und vorurteilsbewusste Sprachförderarbeit in der Migrationsgesellschaft zu legen. Um diesbezüglich auch gesellschaftliche Einflussfaktoren in den Blick zu nehmen, wenden wir uns schließlich Themen aus dem Spannungsfeld Bildung und Migration zu.

Die Ziele richten sich nach den individuellen Bedürfnissen der

Contents:
Can grammar be seen in vector space?

This seminar explores the grammatical structure of Ukrainian nouns at the interface of morphology and semantics, with a focus on number, case, and gender. Using both static (semantic) and contextualized word embeddings, we examine how well different models capture the intricate interplay between morphology and meaning in a morphologically complex language such as Ukrainian—and where they reach their limits.

A central question of the seminar is whether embeddings can distinguish between syncretic forms, for example knygy ‘book’, which may correspond to Genitive singular, Nominative plural, Accusative plural, or Vocative plural. By visualizing and analyzing embedding spaces, abstract grammatical categories become empirically observable patterns — or reveal systematic obstacles to computational modeling.

Learning target:
By the end of the seminar, students will be able to analyze grammatical phenomena using distributional and contextualized embeddings, critically assess the ability of computational models to capture morphosyntactic distinctions, and interpret empirical patterns in relation to linguistic theory. Students will also be able to conduct a contrastive grammatical analysis and present their findings in a clear and structured way.

Qualification objective:
The course develops students’ competencies in grammatical analysis, and data-driven research methods, with transferable skills applicable to linguistics, language technology, and related fields.

Keywords:
Ukrainian nouns; morphology; case; number; gender; syncretism; word embeddings; contextualized embeddings.

Literature:

Jurafsky, D. & Martin, J. H. (2023). Speech and Language Processing.
