Contents:
Who causes what — and how do languages encode responsibility and control?

Causation is a typological universal, yet languages encode it in strikingly different ways. Ukrainian verbs often package causation and even multiple caused events through prefixal morphology within a single verb, as in rozsmišyty ‘to make someone laugh’ (first caused event) or zasmišyty, which can further encode an intensified result (do znehomhy ‘to the point of exhaustion’, second caused event). In German, the same meaning is typically expressed analytically (jemanden zum Lachen bringen), distributing causation across several words.

This contrast highlights how languages differ in encoding causation raising fundamental questions about control, agency, and responsibility.

Learning target:
Students will be able to analyze causative verb constructions from a morphosemantic and typological perspective, compare synthetic and analytic strategies of causation across languages, and critically interpret empirical linguistic data. They will also develop the ability to formulate and present independent research questions related to causation, agency, and control.

Qualification objective:
The seminar provides students with analytical competence in morphosemantics and linguistic typology and introduces them to empirical, data-driven approaches in cross-linguistic research.

Keywords:
Causativity; morphosemantics; verb morphology; prefixation; Ukrainian; German; linguistic typology.

This course provides an introduction to the semantics and pragmatics of natural language, two subfields of modern linguistics that focus on meaning: how it is constructed, how it is interpreted, and which parts of it are sensitive (or insensitive) to context.

Students will gain familiarity with a broad range of concepts from semantics and pragmatics, including but not limited to: entailment, presupposition, conversational implicature, ambiguity, scope, indexicality, and much more.

Students will also gain key skills useful for diagnosing and analyzing semantic and pragmatic phenomena, which will be broadly applicable across any number of phenomena.

Contents:
Where do Slavic languages come from—and why do they still matter politically and culturally today?

This seminar explores the Indo-European roots of Slavic languages, from Proto-Slavic and sound change to language contact and competing origin theories. We examine controversial debates such as the Normanist question, key historical concepts (Ukraine, Rus’, Russia), and the role of alphabets in shaping cultural and political identities.

Learning target:
By the end of the seminar, students will be able to:

relate linguistic data to historical, cultural, and political contexts,

critically evaluate competing theories on the origins and development of Slavic languages,

analyze language change and language contact phenomena,

discuss the role of language in processes of cultural and political identity formation.

Keywords:
Slavic languages, Indo-European, Ukraine, Rus’, Russia, writing systems, language and identity, language and politics; cultural identity.

This course is an introductory course where students will develop short explainer videos of complex topics, trying to make them understandable for the general audience. They will learn industry practices and standards. The course will include lectures, screenings, critiques, and practical lessons. The course will cover important topics like script-writing, voice-over, storyboarding, artwork creation, and animation.

Contents:
In this course, we will explore how a large LED wall can be used to augment reality by combining virtual and physical content. We will work with the new LED wall in the television studio of the Zentrum für Medienkompetenz (ZFM). The course will start with an introduction into various ways of how such walls are used in film production, television broadcasts, multimedia art, and live performances. We will analyze visual effects, virtual production, virtual studios, motion graphics, interactivity, optical illusions, and similar hybrid phenomena such as projection mappings. The main part of the course is dedicated to creating student projects, working in smaller groups to experiment with the capabilities of the LED wall according to students’ interests.

Contents:
This media analysis course will investigate the role of new media in political communication with a focus on campaigns. Over the past years, we have all witnessed important campaigns: the COVID-19 immunization campaign, the Global Climate Strikes, the #BlackLivesMatter movement. These efforts affect our understanding of political power, government action, democracy, and cultural issues, to name a few. In this course, you will gain a theoretical background that helps you grasp the complexity of contemporary politics alongside the centrality of media, including (digital) media activism, social media communication, and the formation of digital publics. We will focus on campaigns—electoral campaigns, grassroots/organizational/activist campaigns, public information campaigns, etc.—from across the political spectrum and across geographical contexts, enabling you to study a campaign of your choosing in order to explore how new media and (digital) communication play into the political.

Important note: This course starts on May 6th

Contents:
Digitization has contributed to a surge of new actors producing and disseminating information that resembles traditional journalism, increasingly blurring the margins of journalism, like (political) influencers, new (hyper)partisan media, podcasters. At the same time, longitudinal studies find that some audiences disengage with what we would traditionally consider news. However, this does not mean that audiences in today’s hybrid media systems are less informed. In this class, we will discuss the difficulties to study news consumption outside of traditional news media and engage with empirical work that addresses these questions with diverse and innovative methodological approaches. This includes traditional survey and interview research but also two-sided videoethnography, photo elicitation, and data donations.

Contents:
Have you ever been drawn into a compelling TV show, book, or social media video—so immersed that you lost track of time? Stories have that power. Throughout history, storytelling has helped inspire social movements, political action, revolutions, and, at times, conflict. But how does this happen—and why are stories so influential?

This course explores this question, looking at narrative and storytelling techniques as tools for media advocacy. It examines how advocates, activists, and social movements craft stories that shape public understanding and influence policy outcomes. Through academic readings, case studies, and hands-on projects, students will explore:

Key definitions and concepts related to storytelling and narrative

How movements and advocates build the foundation for effective narratives

Elements of compelling stories for systemic change, including hooks, imagery, characters, and dialogue

Methods for evaluating the impact of narrative persuasion efforts

Students will critically analyze real-world narrative persuasion campaigns and design their own storytelling-based advocacy messages. This course is ideal for students interested in public policy, communications, activism, and anyone seeking to understand how storytelling can be used to influence systems and create meaningful change.

The event will take place in Room 128a in the Brechtbau.

Contents:
Digitization has contributed to a surge of new actors producing and disseminating information that resembles traditional journalism, increasingly blurring the margins of journalism. These can include (political) influencers, new (hyper)partisan media, podcasters and more who (intentionally or not) change public discourse and sometimes attack journalism as a profession and democracy as a societal system. In this class, we will engage with theoretical and empirical work that addresses the question whether journalism is a distinct profession and how we can understand these shifts, what they can mean for journalism’s role for society and how journalism could protect its democratic funtion.

Contents:
Latein gilt oft als „tote Sprache“. Aus den verschiedenen Varietäten der lateinischen Sprache entstanden jedoch die romanischen Sprachen wie Italienisch, Spanisch, Französisch, Portugiesisch und Rumänisch. Die Lehrveranstaltung möchte einen Einblick geben, in welcher Form Latein in diesen Sprachen weiterlebt.

Die Lektüreübung richtet ihren Blick zunächst darauf, die Zusammenhänge zwischen dem Lateinischen und den romanischen Sprachen darzulegen. Dabei stehen die Sprachgeschichte und der lautliche, morphologische sowie syntaktische Wandel im latein-romanischen Übergang im Vordergrund. Einen Schwerpunkt bilden hierbei Vulgär- und Spätlatein.

Als „Mutter” der romanischen Sprachen ist Latein wesentlicher Schlüssel zum Verständnis sprachlicher Strukturen und literarischer Texte der romanischen Sprachen. Anhand der Lektüre und der Analyse ausgewählter Textbeispiele soll aufgezeigt werden, dass und wie die Kenntnis der klassischen lateinischen Sprache für das Verstehen vulgärlateinischer Texte nutzbar gemacht werden kann und wie auch Texte unterschiedlicher romanischer Sprachen mit Hilfe des Lateinischen entschlüsselt werden können.

Contents:
This is a new course designed to introduce you to philosophy, and provide you with a sense of what philosophy is and the range of topics in philosophy.

For the students majoring or minoring in Philosophy (BA, BEd), these lectures are paired with an accompanying course called Philosophische Argumentation, where you will learn and practice various philosophical skills, like arguing, and reading and writing philosophy. All and only students majoring or minoring in Philosophy (BA, BEd) can take the Übung.

The lectures will be given in English. The Übung (Philosophische Argumentation) will be held in German. You can do any of the class assignments, final essay, and exam in either English or German. Together the Vorlesung and the Übung will provide you with a broad introduction to philosophy and the basic philosophical skills you need for the philosophy degree.

The Übung will be given in 6 different time slots which you can sign up for on ILIAS, in a separate folder for the Übung.

Contents:
Dieses Proseminar bietet eine Einführung in zentrale Fragestellungen und Debatten der Sprachphilosophie sowie in ihre historischen Wurzeln. Im Zentrum stehen grundlegende Fragen wie: Wie beziehen sich Eigennamen, Kennzeichnungen und andere sprachliche Ausdrücke auf die Welt? Was ist Bedeutung? Wie kommunizieren wir mit Sprache? Zur Beantwortung dieser Fragen werden wir klassische Texte und Positionen der analytischen Sprachphilosophie erarbeiten und diskutieren. Insbesondere lesen wir Arbeiten von Frege, Russell, Carnap, Wittgenstein, Grice, Kripke, Putnam und Davidson.

Contents:
Do you live your life in harmony with the world around you? Since the dawn of ancient philosophy, this question has stood at the centre of Greek philosophical enquiries. The different answers to it are to be found in the porous boundaries between cosmology, psychology, and ethics. In the Hellenistic period, Stoic philosophers gave a distinctive turn to the problem and offered one of the most ambitious and sophisticated responses: a vision of ethical life grounded in the structure of the cosmos itself. Human happiness depends on living in harmony with a unified, rational, and divinely ordered universe (sympatheia, συμπάθεια). This course explores the emergence of ‘cosmological ethics’ in Stoicism within the broader framework of the Hellenistic schools. We will first make a detour into the philosophical antecedents of this theory in Plato and his fellow pupils, to then delve into the materialist metaphysical principles of Stoic cosmology and the formation of a new form of divine pantheism. Next, we will turn to the individual and the ethical laws governing actions and emotions, in order to understand how it is ultimately possible to achieve a state of blessed life in harmony with the cosmic nature of everything. The final part of the course will place Stoic ethics in conversation with contemporary debates to show its relevance and contribution to environmental ethics and ecologism. You will be able to engage with a range of problems, methods, and arguments in ancient philosophy, strengthening your preparation for advanced studies in the field. In addition, you will have the opportunity to critically share and discuss your views, thereby developing argumentative and presentation skills.

Learning target:
To introduce you to prominent ancient philosophical debates in Platonist philosophy and Hellenistic philosophies, especially Stoicism, with a focus on cosmology and ethics.

To develop further your argumentative and presentation skills to share and present your views and philosophical positions in several types of activities.

To assess, among other things, philosophical arguments and explanations for psychological phenomena, ethical theories, and cosmological questions, with the aim of evaluating the soundness and flaws of these philosophical arguments.

To explore a range of textual sources and develop a methodological approach for their critical reading and interpretation in order to further enhance connections with other areas of philosophy that you are already familiar with.

Keywords:
Ancient Philosophy, Hellenistic Schools, Plato, Ethics, Cosmology, Ecologism.

Literature:
Reading materials will be provided throughout the module. You will also find online the required materials for the seminars’ activities.

(Long, A.A. and Sedley, D. 1987. The Hellenistic Philosophers (2 vols.). Cambridge will be the referred editions for fragments and translations).

Contents:
Wissen wird meistens als gerechtfertigte wahre Meinung definiert (eventuell mit zusätzlichen Bedingungen), die einem Individuum zugesprochen werden kann. Seit einiger Zeit gibt es allerdings eine Richtung in der Erkenntnistheorie, die untersucht, ob man so etwas auch Gruppen von Individuen zusprechen kann, also davon sprechen kann, dass eine Gruppe etwas als Gruppe weiß. Besonderes Augenmerk richtet sich dabei darauf, wie das Wissen der Individuen in der Gruppe mit dem der Gruppe zusammenhängt: Kann das Gruppenwissen auf das Wissen der Mitglieder der Gruppe reduziert werden oder nicht? Ein neuer Ansatz dazu wurde von Jennifer Lackey entwickelt, den sie in dem Buch “The Epistemology of Groups” vorstellt. Ihr Ansatz hat dabei eine spezielle Motivation, nämlich zu erklären ob Gruppen lügen können. Dies sprechen wir Gruppen oft zu wie in der Aussage "Die Tabakindustrie hat lange über die Schädlichkeit des Rauchens gelogen". Sie entwickelt nun einen Ansatz zu Gruppenwissen, der es uns auch möglich macht, das Konzept der "Gruppenlüge" zu definieren.

In diesem Seminar werden wir das Buch von Lackey lesen und diskutieren. Es bietet eine hervorragende Einführung in das Thema und seine Entwicklung in der sozialen Erkenntnistheorie. Ziel des Seminar ist es, tiefer in die Frage von Gruppenwissen, eines der wichtigen Teilgebiete der sozialen Erkenntnistheorie, einzusteigen. Dadurch gewinnt man auch genaueren Einblick in allgemeine erkenntnistheoretische Fragen, wie den Zusammenhang zwischen Meinung und Begründung, oder Wissen und Handeln.

Contents:
This senior seminar is designed for students who already have experience with Kant's system, and would like to devote a semester to the intensive study of Kant's conception of the intuitive intellect, or the mind of God. The goal of the course will be to fill out this conception as much as possible, identify the limits on what we can say about it, and compare it to our own form of mindedness in the hopes of better understanding both. To do so, we will concentrate on passages scattered across Kant's mature works, including all three Critiques.

Dieses Seminar für Fortgeschrittene richtet sich an Studierende, die bereits Erfahrung mit Kants System haben und sich ein Semester lang intensiv mit Kants Konzept des intuitiven Intellekts oder des Geistes Gottes befassen möchten. Ziel des Seminars ist es, diese Vorstellung so weit wie möglich zu konkretisieren, die Grenzen dessen, was wir darüber sagen können, aufzuzeigen und sie mit unserer eigenen Form des Denkens zu vergleichen, in der Hoffnung, beides besser zu verstehen. Dazu konzentrieren wir uns auf Passagen, die über Kants reife Werke verstreut sind, darunter alle drei Kritiken.

Kants Text muss auf Deutsch gelesen werden, aber unsere Diskussionen könnten auf Deutsch oder Englisch führen. Die Lehrerin wird auf Englisch und auf Deutsch sprechen.

Contents:
Ziel dieses Seminars ist es, Kants Auffassung der Moralität und seine Theorie von Freiheit, Unsterblichkeit und Gott zu verstehen. Können wir sicher sein, dass wir frei sind, oder handelt es sich lediglich um eine grundlegende Annahme in Bezug auf menschliches Handeln? Welche Rolle sollten die Konzepte der Seele und Gottes in unserem Leben einnehmen? Um sein Werk angemessen zu interpretieren, müssen wir auch seine Auffassung von Vernunft und die Rolle, die die Glückseligkeit im menschlichen Leben spielt, diskutieren.

Kants Text muss auf Deutsch gelesen werden, aber unsere Diskussionen könnten auf Deutsch oder Englisch führen. Die Lehrerin wird auf Englisch und auf Deutsch sprechen.

Contents:
General Information

This Hauptseminar provides a comprehensive introduction to the study of metainferences within the framework of substructural logics. Traditionally, logic has been understood as a theory of inferences (relations between sentences). However, recent developments suggest that a com plete understanding of logical systems requires analyzing metainferences—inferences between inferences. Based on the recent volume by Teijeiro and Barrio (eds.), Metainferences in Substructural Logics, we will explore how shifting to a metainferential perspective allows for a more nuanced characterization of both classical and non-classical systems. The course will cover technical aspects (sequent calculi, many-valued semantics) and philosophical applications, particularly concerning semantic paradoxes.

Course Schedule (Weekly)

1. Introduction: What are Metainferences? Logic as a theory of theories. Standard inferences vs. metainferences.

2. Classical Logic from a Metainferential Perspective The sequent calculus LK. Deriv ability and admissibility.

3. Validity and Soundness in Classical Logic Global, local, and absolutely global va lidity. Metainferential soundness and completeness.

4. The Role of Cut and its Elimination Cut-elimination theorem and its consequences for substructurality.

5. Non-Transitive Logics: The ST Family (I) Introduction to Strict-Tolerant logic. Proof theory and trivaluations.

6. Non-Transitive Logics: The ST Family (II) Metainferential ST. The ”ST phe nomenon” generalized.

7. Non-Reflexive Logics: The TS Family (I) Tolerant-Strict logics. Duality between ST and TS.

8. Non-Reflexive Logics: The TS Family (II) Metainferential TS. Soundness and com pleteness results.

9. Non-Contractive and Non-Monotonic Logics (I) Classical Linear Logic. Sequent calculus and semantics.

10. Non-Contractive and Non-Monotonic Logics (II) Phase semantics and unexplored metainferential territories.

11. Philosophical Applications: Semantic Paradoxes The Liar and the Validity para doxes in substructural settings.

12. Philosophical Applications: Internalization Internalization of valid metainferences and the limits of classicality.

13. Final Discussion and Student Presentations Review of the substructural landscape.

The May 29th session will be conducted online. Classes originally scheduled for May 22nd and June 19th are postponed until after the semester concludes, with new dates on July 31st and August 7th.

Learning target:
Learning Objectives

By the end of this course, students will be able to:

– Distinguish between inferential and metainferential levels of a logic.

– Understand the role of structural rules (Cut, Identity, Weakening, Contraction) from a metainferential standpoint.

– Analyze non-transitive (ST), non-reflexive (TS), non-contractive and non-monotonic logic families.

– Evaluate the philosophical impact of substructural solutions to the Liar and Validity paradoxes.

Contents:
Course content

This course will give you an overview of the most commonly used qualitative methods and of crucial considerations of research design in political science so that you can pursue studies in political science and further choose the appropriate methodological specializations for your research or future professional interests.

The course will cover the major methodologies used in the discipline, including i.a. case study research, multiple comparative case studies, discourse analysis, interviewing, and ethnographic techniques. We will also discuss the different epistemological traditions in political science.

Together we will analyze the strong and weak points of individual methods and common flaws and pitfalls in research design. We will dissect in detail canonical and recent empirical studies in political science, as well as grey literature (e.g. think tank reports) from a methodological perspective in order to understand the consequences of methodological and design choices for our understanding of politics.

Aims of the course

This is an introductory course designed to give you an overview of the key techniques and debates in political science methodologies. By the end of the course, you will be able to have the background necessary to choose appropriate methodologies for your own undergraduate research and will be able to further choose specialized elective courses in methods according to your research or professional interests.

The course aims at building a critical understanding of the advantages and disadvantages of individual methods and of their appropriate use. To do this, the course relies on critically assessing published scientific and grey literature on a range of topics from political science from a methodological point of view.

An important skill built in this course is the art of giving feedback: in order to avoid the common pitfall of junior scholars (namely showing off by being mean), we will collectively strive to recognize and mention not only the weaknesses but also the strong points of methodological choices and to formulate constructive suggestions for improvement when evaluating scientific work. Interactive elements of the lectures (such as pair- and group work, plenary debates and reflexive writing), which complement frontal lectures, are geared towards the practice of constructive feedback.

Learning outcomes

By the end of the course, you will:

have a critical understanding of different methodologies in Political Science;

be able to critically assess the appropriateness of individual methods in published scientific and grey literature;

be able to choose appropriate research design and methodologies for your own research;

know which methods you want to study further;

know how to formulate constructive criticism of other’s work.

Language

This course is taught in English, although readings in German are provided. The language of the exam is English. You will be assessed based on your substantive mastery of the subject; don’t worry about your grammar or vocabulary.

Assessment
For Politikwissenschaft BA students, this course must be taken in conjunction with Empirical Methods in Political Science 2 (quantitative methods) next semester. There is only one final exam for the two semesters which covers both semesters and is worth 2 ETCS for students following Module Handbook 2024 NF and 5 ETCS for students in 20024 HF and students following earlier MHBs.
For Politikwissenschaft B.Ed. students following Module Handbook 2024, this lecture is linked to a final examination (qualitative only) worth 4 ECTS.

Contents:
This research seminar focuses on the cultural engagement of the contemporary far right. Over the past decades, support for radical right parties and movements has increased substantially, while extreme right ideas have moved from the margins of the political spectrum into the mainstream. Simultaneously, far-right actors have broadened their thematic scope. How do far-right actors interact with everyday themes and practices, such as food and music? What role do women play in far-right movements? What role does body culture play in far-right ideologies? And what effect does their cultural engagement have on the mainstreaming of the far right? This course offers an in-depth study of the cultural, everyday dimensions of contemporary far-right politics.

Learning target:
Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:

Demonstrate Knowledge: Acquire, organise, and apply knowledge about various aspects of far-right politics, particularly regarding far-right political actors and ideologies.

Develop Research Skills: Formulate a research plan with a clearly defined problem statement, utilizing appropriate methods and techniques relevant to the study of far-right extremism.

Exercise Academic Integrity: Conduct independent research on a contentious topic in a scientifically, socially, and ethically responsible manner.

Think Critically: Critically assess both their own research and the research of others, identifying strengths and weaknesses.

Communicate Effectively: Clearly report on research choices and progress in both oral and written formats, using precise and coherent English.

Engage in Scholarly Discourse: Participate actively in academic discussions, demonstrating analytical skills and the ability to construct well-reasoned arguments.

Keywords:
Far Right; Radical Right; Extreme Right; Culture; Mainstreaming

Contents:
The seminar focuses on recent debates in security studies after Russia invaded Ukraine. The core question is how to explain – and hopefully prevent – the escalation of international conflict under conditions of globalization, multi-order politics, and power transition. For this purpose, the seminar will introduce participants to major approaches to international conflict and assess their performance against available evidence from the war in Ukraine. More specifically, we will look into realist approaches on alliance dynamics, power transition and rational deterrence, liberal perspectives on domestic politics, international institutions and transnational democratization, constructivist perspectives on ideologies and feelings of superiority, as well as critical approaches on racism, post-colonial legacies and gender dynamics.

Contents:
The so-called ideational turn in political science and other related social sciences is built on the simple claim that ideas matter. This seminar delves deeper into this claim and asks why and how ideas matter in public policy. We ask, for instance, why some ideas are more successful than others?

In public policy, we can consider a number of ways in which ideas matter. Ideational processes can help to construct the policy problems and issues that we need to consider when shaping our policy agenda. They can also shape the key assumptions informing the policy reform proposals. Furthermore, we can think of ideas as public philosophies that help framing/constructing the interests of the policy actors and the way they interpret the environment in which they exist. In order to open up these debates, we will consider the nature of ideas both as cognitive filters that shape interests of policy actors but also through their performative dimension, i.e. how they are, for instance, communicated in political discourse. So, it’s not only ideas per se but the way in which they shape interests, institutions and power, and how they, in turn, shape ideas, that are the key questions here. In this context, thinking about how ideas are used as strategic tools for knowledge production and maintaining or transforming political institutions and societal power structures is important especially when thinking of how policy change comes about or what are the specific processes that hinder it.

We will consider these questions with the various stages of the policy-cycle in mind and will draw on concrete policy examples when appropriate.

Contents:
Die Seminare " Vergleichende Analyse Politischer Systeme: ..." sind Teil des Moduls 3 "Vergleichende Politikwissenschaft/Comparative Politics". Diese ist eine der drei klassischen Teildisziplinen der Politikwissenschaft. Die begleitende englischsprachige Pflichtvorlesung "I Comparative Politics" bietet einen ersten Überblick über die Teildisziplin mit typischen Fragestellungen, Themen, Theorien und Methoden. Die Seminare dienen der Vertiefung und Erweiterung der theoretischen und methodischen Kenntnisse aus dieser Vorlesung. Die Seminare fokussieren auf die Anwendung der in der Vorlesung erworbenen Kenntnisse in Bezug auf entweder bestimmte Weltregionen (z.B. Europäische Union; Naher Osten; Entwicklungsländer; ...) oder auf bestimmte Themen und Systemelemente (z.B. Parlamentarismus; Staatlichkeit; Regime und Regimewechsel; ...).

The seminar courses "Introduction to Comparative Politics:..." are part of module 3 ("Comparative Politics"). This is one of three classical sub-disciplines of Political Science. The accompanying mandatory lecture "Introduction to Comparative Politics" offers a first overview of the sub-discipline with typical questions, issues, theories and methods. The seminar courses serve to deepen and expand the theoretical and methodological knowledge of that lecture. The seminars, in their application of the knowledge gained in the lecture, focus on either specific world regions (e.g., European Union; Middle East; developing countries;...) or focus on specific themes (e.g., parliamentarianism; statehood; regimes and regime change;...).

Learning target:
Die Studierenden sollen in den Seminaren lernen, theoretische und methodische Instrumente der Vergleichenden Politikwissenschaft anzuwenden. Sie verstehen die Logik und Methodik des Vergleichs. Sie kennen zentrale Theorie und können diese einordnen. Sie können selber, unter Einbezug einschlägiger Literatur, ein vergleichendes Untersuchungsdesign entwickeln. In the seminar courses, students learn how to use theoretical and methodological instruments of Comparative Politics. This is essential as these tools are also used in the other sub-disciplines of Political Science. Students understand the logic and method of comparison. They need to know core theoretical approaches and know how to locate them in the broader landscape of contemporary theories. They can apply these and establish a comparative research design, including the research question and appropriate use of academic literature pertaining to their research question.

Comment:
To say that the field of policy studies, and even more so theories of the policy process, are Western-centric would be an understatement. Foundational theories about policymaking have been developed in two countries (US and UK) and most are applicable to the study of a handful of countries at best: Germany, the Netherlands, Scandinavia, and maybe France; i.e. full-marks democracies with zero corruption, clientelism, sectarianism or other “aberrations” from the Westminster norm. Such theoretical prism influences what phenomena scholars and students of public policy can observe, describe, analyze, and evaluate. In this course, we will look beyond Westminster and examine theoretical and empirical literature on policymaking in imperfect democracies, autocracies, and authoritarian and hybrid regimes. We (students and the lecturer) will design the syllabus for the course together during the first sessions, including setting our own learning outcomes, topics, readings, and agreeing on assessment (within the limits of the program accreditation). This course is suitable for students with basic prior knowledge of public policy theories.

Contents:
European welfare states face hard choices as they have to address newly emerging social risks and challenges. Key policy challenges include: low fertility rates, ageing populations, child poverty, youth unemployment, reconciliation of work-life balance, social risks of migrants and the increase of atypical and precarious work. This seminar provides participants with insights into the main social policy challenges faced by policy makers at the beginning of the 21st century and introduces them to different policy approaches. Each session focuses on one set of policy challenges and will draw on the experiences of one or more country cases.

Contents:
This research seminar examines the rise and dynamics of populism in Europe and beyond. In 2017, the Cambridge Dictionary named “populism” its word of the year. The term now appears constantly in the media and has become almost unavoidable in contemporary political debate. But what exactly is populism, and how does it work? How do populist leaders and movements mobilise support? What role do media, culture, and social identity play in shaping populist appeal? What connections exist between populism, conspiracy theories, and gender? Is populism a problem, or can it serve as a powerful political corrective? The course offers an in-depth study of the causes, expressions, and consequences of contemporary populist politics.

Keywords:
Populism; movements; parties; media; culture

The Significance of Trade Unions and Labour
Relations for National Models of Capitalism: A European and International

The seminar focuses on the question of how
trade unions and national labour relations regimes (including different forms
of workplace representation and collective bargaining) influence the political
economy of different models of capitalism in and outside of Europe. The seminar will start with an introduction to
different theoretical approaches on the “varieties of capitalism”. Afterwards, the

globalization on the development of national industrial relations regimes by asking

Contents:
Energy supply encompasses the provision of energy for households, industry, and transportation. It is provided in the form of electricity, heat, and fuels and has various sources such as fossil fuels, renewable energies (e.g., solar, wind, water), or nuclear power. A sufficient and stable energy supply enables economic growth, social development, and a high quality of life for the population. At the same time, energy supply is at the center of current transformation processes: First, it forms the basis of the digital transformation, which requires ever-increasing amounts of energy. Second, the question of which sources are used to generate energy has a significant impact on the global carbon footprint.

Some aspects are key to understanding political economy of energy supply. As reflected in the World Economic Forum's Global Risks Report 2026, geoeconomic confrontation is perceived as the most severe near-term risk while climate change related issues recede to the background. In this seminar, we will explore these dimensions along with the global and regional developments. In the first part of the seminar, we cover the basics of the political organization of energy supply. In the second part, we delve into the developments and challenges of EU energy policy. In the next part, we examine historical and current developments in selected member states. In the fourth part, we combine these national and regional dynamics and processes within the global political economy.

Contents:
This seminar explores the European Union’s relations with countries in its immediate neighbourhood, focusing on three regions: the Eastern neighbourhood (Eastern Europe), the Southern neighbourhood (the Middle East and North Africa), and the Western Balkans.

While the EU’s relations with the Eastern and Southern neighbourhoods are primarily framed by the European Neighbourhood Policy (ENP), its engagement with the Western Balkans and Turkey has traditionally taken place within the framework of enlargement policy. Since the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022, however, the distinction between neighbourhood and enlargement policies has become increasingly blurred, with enlargement policy now extending to parts of the Eastern neighbourhood.

The course examines the historical evolution of EU relations with these regions, as well as the institutional and legal foundations of neighbourhood and enlargement policies. It also addresses recent political developments that have reshaped these relationships and policy frameworks.

Keywords:
Legitimacy, Legitimation, Autocracies, Autocracization

Comment:
This course examines the contemporary international relations and foreign policies of Middle Eastern states, and developments in regional politics and regional order in the last decades. The goal of the seminar is to provide students with the conceptual and theoretical tools, and the empirical evidence, to identify, assess, and explain patterns and variation in the behavior of states in the Middle East. The focus of the seminar is on the dynamics of inter-state relations in the Middle East and North Africa. It discusses a wide range of themes and cases in light of theoretical IR approaches. The course is divided into two main parts: In the first part, we will study key developments in the contemporary history of the Middle East (from the 1950s to the 2020s). The Middle East post-independence regional political order has shaped much of the intra-regional and international relations of Middle Eastern states. In the second part of the course, we will analyze several current issues in international and regional politics of the Middle East, such as Iran-Saudi relations, the effects of tectonic shifts in global order, and recent state collapse. In addition to a discussion of the weekly mandatory readings, group presentations are held in the first part of the course which provide a summary and analysis of key historical developments. In the second part of the course, we shed light on current issues with the help of various theoretical perspectives of IR. To this end, students provide position papers which each formulate a concise argument building on a specific theoretical perspective.

This course is designed for MA students and advanced BA students. Students should have previous knowledge on either IR theories or the Middle East. Otherwise, they need to catch up in the beginning of the course by doing some extra readings that will be provided by the lecturer.

Course assignments (4 ECTS)

- Regular presence, mandatory readings, and active participation

- Briefing on theoretical IR perspective + position paper

- Group presentation

Additionally, students can earn 2, 3 or 4 extra ECTS by submitting a term paper until 15 September.

Contents:
International relations are inherently ethical and moral: Should states intervene militarily when international law is violated? Are human rights universal? Is terrorism ever justified? Do wealthy nations have an obligation to help poorer ones? Should we protect animals from harm and preserve nature? Why should states ban, or even destroy, weapons of mass destruction? What can, should, and must be done to create a more peaceful and just world? Questions of war and peace, sovereignty and the protection of minorities, democracy and political participation, human rights, the fight against poverty and discrimination, and the protection of the earth cannot be studied without discussing ethics and morality.

Ethical and moral foundations, however, are neither given nor uncontested. While institutions that shape and regulate international relations have increased, a diversity of critical voices is rising: they claim that the world order is dominated by “Western-liberal values,” is “racist,” “post-colonial,” and inherently “gendered,” or serves only the “interests of the powerful and wealthy 1%.” How does the unequal distribution of power and authority affect the formulation of ethics and morality? Who has the right and legitimacy to define and implement ethical principles at global, regional, and local sites? How can we evaluate contemporary challenges, for example, the use of force, the rise of nationalism, and the persistence of global inequality, based on accounts of peace, justice, and responsibility?

Contents:
Most armed conflicts do not take place between states, but within states. Today, the loss of life and treasures in these conflicts is significantly higher than in international wars. In the first part of the seminar, we will look at the conditions under which political conflicts escalate into civil wars. For this purpose, we will study approaches looking into the dynamics of political competition, state repression, ethnic discrimination, and postcolonial legacies. The focus will not be on quantitative analyses but on causal mechanisms that can help us to better understand civil war onset. In the second part of the seminar, we will use this theoretical knowledge to analyze armed conflicts in Africa and beyond

Keywords:
Civil War; Conflict Analysis; Conflict Escalation; Political Mobilization; Case Studie

Learning target:
Having completed the course, the students will have a comprehensive overview of central themes linked to gender, peace and conflict; they will have knowledge of central concepts used in analyzing gender, peace and conflict, as well as of challenges and outcomes linked to different methodological approaches within relevant fields of scholarship. Through these efforts, the students will learn what interdisciplinary scholarship entails; i.e. how gender is conceptualized as a social and political construction within different disciplines, with an emphasis on the social sciences. The students will also be able to analyze and identify the relevance of gender in relation to peace and conflict matters; they will be able to discuss the implication of gender analyses to the understandings of peace and conflict; they will be able to work independently and critically with central issues in the research literature; and, finally, they will be able to translate theoretical knowledge into policy and practice.

Contents:
This seminar provides an in-depth exploration of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO), its historical evolution, institutional structure, strategic objectives, and contemporary challenges. It examines NATO’s role in global security, its decision-making processes, military capabilities, and its relationships with member and partner states.

NATO's transformation and policies will be discussed from a selection of theoretical lenses, including realism, institutionalism, constructivism, feminism, post-structuralism, and de-colonial perspectives.

Contents:
In this seminar we will be consulting literature related to climate security and migration to understand the intersection of the two concepts. We will start with Diez et al (2016) on the securitisation of climate change and Diez et al (2021) on the EU’s contribution to the development of the global climate regime, to gain knowledge on climate security discourses. We will then consult Boas (2015) and White (2011) to understand how and why climate migration has been presented in terms of security. We will consolidate our understandings from these four key books with journal articles focusing on contemporary issues in climate security and migration.

Contents:
Not all conflicts between parties turn violent. Negotiations supported by third parties help de-escalate and transform interpersonal, societal, and international conflicts. Mediation is a key mechanism of conflict management and transformation and, under specific conditions, can enable solutions and prevent violence. This seminar introduces students to concepts and approaches in international conflict management and transformation, as well as to the practices of mediating a conflict between political actors. The seminar comprises a simulation and role-play, where students can test their knowledge and competencies in managing and transforming a current conflict. This role-play is designed as an on-site event requiring physical presence in Bad Urach.

Learning target:
To provide students with a deeper understanding of conflict analysis and contemporary research on mediation and conflict transformation

To foster critical engagement with a wide range of literature on conflict transformation and resolution

To discuss, assess, formulate, and evaluate mediation strategies

To present and perform the positions of conflict parties and mediators in a role-play

Contents:
This seminar discusses the EU's role in International Politics through the lens of different theoretical perspectives and themes and in light of current crises, including the Middle East and Russia's invasion of Ukraine. It introduces participants to the main concepts of the debate about EU foreign policy, including "civilian" and "normative power", or the "capability-expectations gap". At the same time, we will cover different areas of EU engagement, both thematically (democracy promotion, regionalisation, trade, climate change) and geographically (transatlantic relations, EU-Africa relations, ASEAN, etc.). Note that the seminar is NOT an introduction to EU foreign policy, and some basic background knowledge about the development and institutions of EU foreign policy will be required. Likewise, while we will encourage debates about current issues, we will do so on the basis of existing scholarship and our knowledge of institutional structures and histories.

Learning target:
After successfully completing this seminar, students should be able to

Elaborate the key concepts of the analytical debate about EU foreign policy;

Critically assess the role of the EU in international relations;

Analyse different aspects of EU foreign policy from the angle of different theoretical approaches;

Provide guidance in relation to possible reforms of EU foreign policy practice.

Keywords:
EU; foreign policy; normative power; geopolitics; regional integration

Literature:

Diez, Thomas (ed.) (2014) A Different Kind of Power? The EU’s Role in International Politics (New York: IDebate/Budapest: Central European University Press).

Contents:
Security has become of the most important topics on EU’s political
agenda. Regularly updated security policies outline those issues that are
perceived as most pressing, while an ever-growing number of security
institutions is tasked to develop, execute and evaluate security measures. The Russian
invasion in Ukraine, but also the COVID-19 pandemic and Trump’s presidency in
the US have been shaping a move towards more autonomy of the EU in security. While
cooperation appears as a necessity, EU member states are still far away from military
integration. However, security cooperation exceeds the realm of the military
and encompasses topics such as cyber security, civil protection, migration and police
cooperation. European Security politics has thus evolved as a multi-faceted
political field with a growing number of actors. The seminar seeks to shed
light on these developments as well as to structure this complex field. It does
so by approaching security politics from different angles (e.g. strategic
cultures, gender, normative power, epistemic politics) before it applies these
different angles to various actors (mainly agencies) and aspects of European security
politics.

Keywords:
Security, EU, politics, institutions

Contents:
Resource extraction fuels conflict in Latin America, especially in the Andes and the Amazon. Conflicts range from symbolic protests to the formation of influential civil society movements and violent clashes between local populations, companies, state and other (armed) actors. Among the manifold reasons for these conflicts are struggles for land rights, competing claims to use resources, contestation about the distribution of benefits and protests against social, environmental and cultural impacts of extractive projects.

Resource conflicts in Latin America are historically embedded into global, regional, and national dynamics. For Europe, Latin America has been a source of natural resources since colonial times. For the world market, main production sites for lithium, copper, soya, ect. are situated in the Andes and the Amazon where they cause major damages to fragile ecosystems. However, for most Latin American countries the export of these resources is a central economic pillar, and a regional “commodities consensus” (Svampa 2015) exists, even though governments have different political orientations. At the same time, national, regional, and international institutions promote legal frameworks to make extractive industries more sustainable.

This seminar focuses on the multi-scalar entanglements of conflicts over resource extraction in Latin America. Central topics are the economic, social, and political dynamics of extracting different types of natural resources; legal frameworks to protect local populations and mechanisms of participatory environmental governance; underlying development models and questions of “environmental justice”.

Contents:
This course examines peace not only as the absence of war, but as a set of everyday social practices, political struggles, and normative contestations that shape life in Latin America. De-spite the relative absence of interstate wars, Latin America remains one of the most violent regions in the world, marked by legacies of civil war, organized crime, inequality, environmen-tal conflict, and structural violence.

How, then, is peace lived, practiced, and contested? Drawing on peace studies, political ecology, anthropology, and Latin American studies, the course introduces the concept of conviviality to analyze how individuals and communities co-exist under conditions of chronic insecurity and inequalities. After conceptually introducing peace and conviviality, we will explore case studies from the region and learn about ap-proaches such as territorial peace, grassroots peacebuilding, gendered and indigenous per-spectives on peace, urban violence, environmental conflicts, as well as post-liberal critiques of peacebuilding.

Focus is set on contextualised understandings of peace and critical evaluations of the limits of liberal, state-centered peace frame-works. Students will engage closely with ethnographic and empirical research, linking theory to lived experience across diverse Latin American contexts.

Contents:
This workshop is an in-depth study of one of the most widely utilized methods in social science research. Throughout the workshop, students will learn about various branches and types of discourse analysis used in political science and international relations, will become familiarized with the underlying methodological assumptions of the various types and applications of discourse analysis, will get accustomed to practical applications of the various branches, and will learn to apply these methods themselves.

Five different branches of discourse analysis will be studied in-depth throughout the workshop: Social Constructivist, Discursive Institutionalist, Post-structuralist, Critical DA, and Discourse-Historical DA. Required readings will be composed of one scholarly work that directly pertains to the specific type of discourse analysis and another that applies the method.

There will, in total, 7 sessions, meaning the workshop will last for the half of the semester, composed of weekly sessions. For coursework, the students (formed into groups if necessary) are expected submit two questions before each session about the readings and the method, to be discussed by all in the approximately first half of each session in conjunction with the discussion about the readings themselves, all of which should take up to 45 minutes. The second half of the session will be devoted to reading and analyzing specific texts that will be distributed by me and possibly suggested by you. As part of the practicing application of the methods, students are encouraged to suggest or bring texts they find interesting or that pertain to their research, which we will then discuss in class. Students will get to actively apply the method on their own to the given text and ask questions as they come up, and then the class will discuss their applications, the difficulties they encountered during the application, etc.

In summary, this seminar aims to provide students with a comprehensive overview of discourse analysis as a method, including its various branches and the differences between these branches, their application in scholarly works, and, crucially, hands-on practice on how to apply them.

Contents:
This seminar examines the relationship between public opinion, political misinformation, and democratic governance, while introducing students to the principles of survey research. In the first part of the course, we discuss how mis- and disinformation shape political attitudes and democratic decision-making. The second part focuses on survey methodology, including questionnaire design, measurement challenges, and survey experiments. A central component of the course is the collaborative development of a survey on political mis- and disinformation. The course jointly designs questionnaire items that will be fielded both among the student body and in a representative sample of the German population. The course therefore combines conceptual debates about democracy and misinformation with practical training in survey research. Students will also be invited to participate in writing a collaborative journal article based on the survey results, although participation in this publication project is voluntary and not required for completing the course.

Contents:
The seminar is aimed at all students who are at any stage of their thesis process, from BA to MA. Dr. Kuisma is relatively open with regard to the topics you work with - if in doubt, do contact him via email to discuss your ideas.

Generally topics that always work are substantive topics that correspond broadly with Dr. Kuisma's research interests and/or theoretical and methodological focus. These include, for instance, comparative political economy and public policy in general, but especially comparative social policy, social rights and social citizenship in Europe, populism and welfare chauvinism, and Nordic and British politics. Even if the substantive focus of the projects was beyond these topics, there could be a match with theory and/or methods. In terms of theory and methodology, projects that concentrate on institutionalist and interpretivist political science could always be of interest. In terms of method, Dr. Kuisma is a specialist on qualitative methods but mixed methods could also fit.

The seminar is built around structured discussions on the individual research projects but it will also feature discussions about the research process in general - from identifying research questions to the writing up of research outcomes. The schedule for the semester will be discussed and fixed in the first sessions. The seminar is also available in hybrid format and the working language will be English.

Contents:
If you are interested in writing your BA or MA thesis under my supervision or just need general input, this is the course for you. Academic writing is my passion, so we will focus a lot on how to read and write effectively to produce a good thesis.

Substantively, I am happy to supervise theses on the following topics: general public policy; health policy; expertise and experts in policy and politics; policymaking in non-democracies. Email me for other topics.

Contents:
This seminar is designed for undergraduate and graduate students who are writing their theses. Participants present short papers of planned BA or MA theses, which are discussed together.

Contents:
International relations are an inherently normative field: Should states intervene militarily when international law is violated? Are human rights universal? Can terrorism be ever justified? What can, should and must be done to create a more peaceful and just world? Questions of war and peace, sovereignty and the protection of minorities, democracy and political participation, human rights, the fight against poverty and discrimination and the protection of the earth cannot be studied without reflecting the normative fabric of political debates. Ethical and moral foundations, however, are neither a given nor are they uncontested. While institutions that shape and regulate international relations have increased, a diversity of critical voices are on the rise.

Starting from reflections on security, justice and responsibility as key concepts for engaging with ethics in the international realm, the seminar revisits several critical debates in the field to normatively reflect global political issues, such as war and peace, climate change, migration and the global economic system.

Learning target:
After finishing this course, students should be able to:

Understand key normative debates in International Relations

Formulate normative arguments based on ethical considerations

Reflect the role of normative considerations in International Relations

Apply normative categories to empirical cases

Keywords:
Ethics, International Relations, Power, Justice, Norms, Peace, Terrorism, Violence

This course is designed as an introduction to the study of Ancient Near Eastern Religions, approached through a focused examination of Anatolian goddesses within their broader historical and cultural context. During the second and first millennia BC, Anatolia (Asia Minor) formed part of the wider cuneiform culture, which also encompassed Mesopotamia, Syria, and Canaan. The course begins with an overview of the region’s geography and history, introducing the major peoples, languages, and civilizations of this part of the ancient world. It then explores the relationship between writing and religion, followed by an examination of key types of religious texts, including myths and sacred narratives, as well as prayers, hymns, and incantations. Further sections of the course address recurring features of religious thought and religious practice, with particular attention to concepts of deities and demons. In the second half of the course, students engage in a detailed study of five Anatolian goddesses, considering what these figures reveal about the beliefs, values, and societies of the communities that worshipped them. The course is open to students from other departments and to anyone with a general interest in mythology, history and religious studies.

Contents:
This seminar offers an interdisciplinary introduction to caste in South Asia and diasporas, treating caste not only as a system of social hierarchy but as a historically produced and continuously reworked field of embodied practices, affects, materialities, and institutions. We examine classical debates on what caste is (and how it has been theorized), while also focusing on how caste is lived, contested, and represented in law, religion, politics, diaspora communities, and popular culture. Alongside scholarly texts, we will work with novels, songs, documentary films, and selected cinematic case studies.

The course is organized in five units that move from foundations to contemporary debates and representation: (1) We begin by introducing caste as a social, historical, embodied, and political formation, working through key terms and texts, genealogies, and everyday practices. (2) We then turn to caste, politics, and law, from colonial knowledge-making and nationalist debates to Ambedkar, Gandhi, and contemporary legal frameworks in India and the diaspora. (3) The third unit focuses on caste across religious boundaries, asking how caste is reproduced or contested in Hindu, Christian, Muslim, Matua, and Ambedkarite neo-Buddhist contexts. (4) Next, we examine literature, music, and popular culture, with attention to aesthetics, representation, and the politics of invisibilization in fiction, protest music, poetry, documentary, and cinema. (5) The course concludes with your research and synthesis through presentations and collective reflection.

Learning target:
By the end of this course, you will have:

• A solid conceptual vocabulary to analyze caste (jāti/varṇa; purity/pollution; endogamy vs. inter-caste marriage; homo hierarchicus; Dalit and Harijan; caste as power and as practice).

• A critical understanding of key historical transformations (colonialism, modern law and state administrative categories, reservations, post-1990 political economy).

• The ability to analyze caste comparatively across religious contexts (Hindu, Muslim, Christian, Buddhist, etc.)

• Practice in reading diverse sources: scholarship, song lyrics, legal and policy documents, ethnography, literary narrative, documentary film, and popular cinema.

• Skills in discussion-leading, short analytical writing, and research related to the topic of caste in South Asia.

Contents:
Tanzania is a multiethnic and multireligious country that encompasses more than 120 language groups as well as various forms of Christianity, Islam, Hinduism, indigenous and new religions. Taking it as a starting point, we will follow the historical entanglements of these religions, traditions, cosmologies and ritual practices across the Indian Ocean space, continental Africa and Europe (incl. Tübingen). Fields on interest include trade, medicine, socialist politics and individual travel. We shall examine Christian missionary and Islamic sources, contemporary fieldwork studies, and modern representations in the media. How have all of these traditions, structures and international relations contributed to the postcolonial process of nation making in Tanzania? What can the global North perhaps learn from such plural societies in the global South?

Contents:
From the sweat lodge to the ice dips in freezing cold lakes, from singing bowls and sound baths to anti-stress mantra chanting: our surroundings are full of old and new rituals that address people in search of mental, physical and spiritual healing. How do people experience health and illness in a post-secular age? How do class, gender, ethnicity, and education shape the ways people make sense of disease, conceive of the body and immunity, and articulate experiences of distress within specific cultural settings? What happens when biomedicine is not enough to address pain and sorrow?

This course explores the epistemic borderlands between religion, spirituality, and medicine. It focuses on the material dimensions of faith and the embodied experiences of healing, thereby blurring the secular Western epistemological divide between science and religion.

Drawing on ethnographically rich case studies, the course offers an intersectional, postcolonial, and post-secular analysis of medico-religious repertoires, including traditional medicines, biomedicine, ritual healing, paths to immunity, and protection-seeking practices, primarily in contexts from Europe, Asia and Africa.

Finally, the course provides theoretical and methodological tools for engaging with ethnography—including digital ethnography—to examine contemporary issues at the crossroads of ritual, health, and society.

Learning target:
Examine the intersections of ritual and health from the perspectives of medical anthropology, the anthropology of religion, science and technology studies (STS), the history of medicine, and subfields of religious studies concerned with the body, the sensorium, and health.

Develop awareness towards multiple and diverse conceptualizations of body, disease, health, healing, immunity and protection.

Engage with theories on ritual, healing and the sociocultural shaping of medical “science.”

Critically apply class material to understand contemporary issues on alternative medicine, religion and public health initiatives, like vaccine hesitancy, governmental protocols on epidemics, and policies on women’s reproductive health.

Conduct independent research and share research materials during an in-class workshop

Develop academic writing skills, including ethnographic film reviews, conference concept notes and workshop “call for papers.”

Contents:
Room: This seminar will take place in Nauklerstr. 35 in room 3.08.

This course is addressed to graduate students (MA students and doctoral students) as well as third year BA students. In this class, we will discuss current methodological and theoretical issues and debates in the study of religion and culture ranging across various fields including, but not limited to, global history, decolonial methodology, discourse theory/genealogy, material religion/culture, cognitive studies, ritual studies, practice theory, digital humanities etc. The open discussions provide the students with an opportunity to develop argumentative skills as they position themselves with or against such topics as new materialism, artistic research, AI research or undercover ethnography (to name just a few issues with controversial potential).

Readings will be based on current and relevant publications across various disciplines but will also include some classic texts that highlight the history of certain theoretical trajectories. The course will also provide space for students to suggest readings relevant to their research areas and/or to present some of their own graduate or research work.

The course is open to students from all humanities, cultural studies and social sciences. The focus will lie on various aspects of religion with religion understood as part of culture and society. Thus, the methods and theories under discussion always reference interdisciplinary debates across all cultural studies. The language of instruction is English.

Contents:
Social theorists have long been concerned with the practice of argumentation, even if often indirectly. And rightly so – human beings can be found exchanging reasons in a wide range of social contexts. Yet little work has been done to connect social theory with the younger field of argumentation theory, which takes this rich form of social interaction as its object of study. At the same time, argumentation theorists – particularly those of a rhetorical orientation – have come to recognize the complex social dynamics involved in the interpretation and evaluation of any argumentative interaction. There is thus much work to be done here, and exploring the bridges and gaps between these areas of research will be the main aim of the seminar. In the first part, we will introduce argumentation theory as a field of research and discuss key texts that push in the direction of greater engagement with social theory. In the second part, we will read a selection of social theoretical texts with special relevance for contemporary research in rhetoric and argumentation.

Contents:
Im Seminar werden wir begleitend zur Vorlesung zentrale Texte zur Diskursforschung lesen. Das Seminar verbindet dabei linguistische und sozialwissenschaftliche Diskursmodelle mit der philosophischen Diskurstheorie (Apel, Habermas) und verortet die Entstehung des Diskursbegriffs im Kontext von Strukturalismus und Poststrukturalismus. Intensiv diskutiert werden soll darüber hinaus das Potential von Diskursanalyse für die rhetorische Arbeit.

Contents:
Informal logic has developed several original methods for the analysis and evaluation of arguments. In this seminar we will focus on one of the most promising and widely used of these methods in contemporary argumentation studies – argumentation schemes (Walton et al., Argumentation Schemes, 2008). The seminar will begin with an introduction to informal logic as a distinct strand within the wider field of argumentation theory. We will then turn to the basics of scheme theory, idenitfying its advantages and problems. After this theoretical introduction, we will spend several weeks using argumentation schemes to analyze and evaluate and invent arguments. In the final weeks we will return to some of the theoretical problems posed at the beginning and consider the merits of argumentation schemes as a method.

Im Seminar erarbeiten wir Methoden der rhetorischen Textanalyse, die größere Untersuchungskorpora in den Blick nehmen. Im Zentrum soll ein kleines Forschungsprojekt stehen, das in Einzel- oder Gruppenarbeit über das Semester hinweg vorangetrieben wird und anhand dessen die jeweilige Methode nicht nur in der Theorie betrachtet sondern in der Praxis ausprobiert werden soll. Neben den inhaltlichen Ergebnissen, die als Antworten auf die jeweilige Fragestellung erarbeitet werden, interessieren uns insbesondere die Eigenheiten, Fallstricke und Lösungsansätze, die sich bei der jeweiligen Methode theoretisch wie forschungspraktisch zeigen: Welche Anforderungen bringt welcher Gegenstand mit sich? Wie muss sich ein Korpus zusammensetzen? Wie gehen wir in der rhetorischen Forschung mit Gütekriterien um?

Contents:
Die Diskursforschung untersucht Texte in ihren intertextuellen und gesellschaftlichen Kontexten. Im Zentrum steht die Frage, wie sich in sprachlichen Praktiken Machtverhältnisse, Wissensordnungen und Geltungsansprüche konstituieren. Analysiert wird, wie soziale Wirklichkeit durch Sprache hergestellt, stabilisiert oder verändert wird.

In der Vorlesung werden zentrale Texte der Diskursforschung behandelt. Ziel ist es, grundlegende Fragestellungen und Methoden des Feldes kennenzulernen und einzuordnen, das sich mittlerweile stark ausdifferenziert hat. Die Vorlesung verbindet linguistische, literaturwissenschaftliche und sozialwissenschaftliche Diskursmodelle mit der philosophischen Diskurstheorie (Apel, Habermas) und verortet die Entstehung des Diskursbegriffs im Kontext von Strukturalismus und Poststrukturalismus. Durch die Auseinandersetzung mit der Diskursforschung soll dabei die analytische Kompetenz gesteigert werden, um im Bereich der rhetorischen Textanalyse auf ein zeitgemäßes Methodenwissen zurückgreifen zu können. Auch die Verbindungslinien zwischen Diskursanalyse und der Critical Rhetoric werden in der Vorlesung diskutiert.

Contents:
In these times of political disruption and unfettered neoimperialism, Global South Studies have to engage with new or swiftly changing dynamics of precarisation across the South and in North-South Relations. This is why our 2026 ICGSS Spring Academy will take up the challenge of addressing Figurations of the Precarious in the Global South. Inspired by a ‘figurations’-based approach to social and cultural analysis as well as ‘proximity as method,’ we are interested in the ways individual and collective social actors perceive and interpret everyday situations, social conditions, and interactional scenarios as precarious. Which cultural references do they draw upon to make sense of precarity? Which tactics, strategies, navigational capacities, and repertoires of resistance do they mobilize to deal with the precariousness of their existence and the precarisation of their living conditions?

Conceived as a laboratory for interdisciplinary, international and intercultural dialogue on theory, methodology and practice, the academic programme of our Spring Academy is offered by diverse disciplines at the interstices of humanities and social sciences. Our international teaching staff comprises the RTG staff as well as visiting researchers, activists, artists and public intellectuals from Brazil, Colombia, India, Mexico, Senegal, South Africa, and Australia. A student project will explore the contribution of sound studies to decolonial thinking as it is our principal to think theory through praxis and research praxis through theory.

The Spring Academy is open to doctoral and master's students from the humanities and social sciences interested in trans-area studies of Latin America, Africa, and Asia.

Im Verlauf des Semesters werden die von den Studierenden im Unterricht sowie eigenständig erarbeiteten Übersetzungen ausgewählter Text- und Filmausschnitte gemeinsam analysiert und diskutiert. Die Arbeit erfolgt in Gruppen von mindestens drei Personen. Die Zusammensetzung der Gruppen berücksichtigt unterschiedliche Vorkenntnisse im Katalanischen, um kooperative Lernprozesse zu fördern. Empfohlen wird ein Mindestniveau von A1 im Katalanischen. Eine Teilnahme ist jedoch auch mit passiven Sprachkenntnissen oder mit Kenntnissen einer anderen romanischen Sprache möglich.

Aquest és un curs pràctic de traducció audiovisual, concretament de la modalitat de subtitulació. Ens ocuparem de dos projectes: en primer lloc, un recull de poemes i, en segon lloc, una *pel·lícula (que serà anunciada la primera setmana de classe). Al llarg del semestre es revisaran les traduccions dels diferents fragments que els estudiants han anat traduint a l’aula i a casa. Es treballarà en grups de mínim 3 persones que no tindran necessàriament el mateix coneixement de català per afavorir un ambient de treball profitós. Es recomana tenir un nivell mínim d’A1 de català, malgrat que s’hi pot participar amb un coneixement passiu o amb el coneixement d’una altra llengua romànica.

Contents:
Welche Rolle haben Frauen in der europäischen Geschichte und Kultur gespielt? Diese Frage zu beantworten ist heute schwierig, da die Geschichten von Frauen oft nicht erzählt wurden oder mit Vorurteilen erzählt wurden. Zeitgenössische Wissenschaftler versuchen, den Frauen ihre Stimme zurückzugeben, was oft mühsam ist, da sie mit einem Mangel an Daten konfrontiert sind. Dennoch erleben wir eine Blüte von Biografien und Ausstellungen, die Frauen gewidmet sind, an die man sich noch in historischen Dokumenten erinnern kann.

Im Jahr 1361 begann Giovanni Boccaccio mit der Arbeit an einem Werk, das berühmten Frauen der Vergangenheit und Gegenwart gewidmet war: De mulieribus claris. Mythologische und biblische Figuren, Göttinnen, Königinnen, Malerinnen und römische Matronen werden einem Publikum vorgestellt, das daran gewöhnt ist, Biografien berühmter Männer zu lesen, wie sie Petrarca in De viris illustribus gesammelt hat. In der Einleitung an die Leser stellt Boccaccio sein Buch als das erste Werk vor, das jemals Frauen gewidmet wurde. Welche Gründe haben Boccaccio dazu bewogen, De mulieribus claris zu schreiben? Wie wählt er die berühmten Frauen aus? Wie werden die verschiedenen weiblichen Figuren beschrieben?

Nachdem wir das Werk in seinem kulturellen Kontext verstanden haben, werden wir auch über seinen Erfolg in den folgenden Jahrhunderten nachdenken: De mulieribus claris wurde nicht nur in viele moderne Sprachen übersetzt, darunter auch ins Deutsche, sondern diente auch als Vorbild für Werke, die die Liste berühmter Frauen zu der Zeit, in der sie verfasst wurden, aktualisierten. Wer sind die Frauen, die es auf den „Walk of Fame” nach Boccaccio geschafft haben? Und wenn wir heute eine „aktualisierte” Ausgabe erstellen würden, wen würden wir hinzufügen oder wie würden wir die Frauen von Boccaccio anders darstellen?

Contents:
Este seminario examina la construcción discursiva de fenómenos políticos latinoamericanos en medios de comunicación internacionales, con énfasis en el análisis de Deutsche Welle como caso de estudio. A través de herramientas del Análisis Sociológico del Discurso (Wissenssoziologische Diskursanalyse) de la Escuela de Duisburg y del Análisis Crítico del Discurso, los estudiantes desarrollarán competencias para identificar cómo se producen regímenes de conocimiento sobre América Latina en contextos mediáticos transnacionales.

El seminario parte del reconocimiento de que el periodismo, aun cuando se presenta bajo criterios de neutralidad y objetividad, participa en la construcción social de realidades políticas mediante selección de fuentes, encuadres narrativos, y dispositivos discursivos específicos. Los estudiantes analizarán crisis políticas recientes en la región (Venezuela, protestas sociales, procesos electorales) para identificar patrones discursivos, estructuras fenoménicas, y articulaciones geopolíticas en la producción informativa.

Contenidos temáticos:

Módulo 1: Fundamentos teórico-metodológicos

Módulo 2: Medios públicos transnacionales y producción informativa

Módulo 3: Crisis políticas contemporáneas en América Latina

Módulo 4: Síntesis y producción académica

Contents:
We are
living in a period when human rights are under renewed and constant attack.
Rights that were once taken for granted are now back on the agenda (the right
to safe and accessible abortion, for example). In this context, literature has
emerged as a powerful tool against a dark narrative that seeks to silence
people and their right to exist. Writers around the world have been politically
engaged and have spoken out against power, showing through their work the
brutality of oppression, but also the comfort of hope. The aim of this course
is to introduce students to the broader context of literature and human rights.
Through the analysis of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, students
will link some of the most relevant rights to a work of literature that
explores the theme in depth. The aim is also to help the students to obtain a
better understanding of contemporary events and to elicit a critical thought
that could foster a connection between literature and real life.

It is
composed by 30 articles, we will focus on 5 with the possibility to further
expand our analysis

For each of
the 5 articles we will pick one work of literature

We will
read the work (autonomously) and discuss it during classes

English, Italian, Spanish, and French translations of specific passages will be provided

materials will be uploaded on ILIAS

Contents:
Même si personne n’est capable de témoigner d’une expérience directe de sa propre fin, la représentation et la méditation de la mort hantent la culture du Moyen Âge et du début de la période moderne. Ce cours se propose d’étudier les représentations de la mort dans la littérature française du Moyen Age jusqu’au siècle classique sous une perspective en même temps littéraire et anthropologique. Nous étudierons la mort du guerrier dans la Chanson de Roland, les danses macabres, la fiction testamentaire de François Villon, la réflexion philosophique sur la mort chez Montaigne, la mort du martyr dans Polyeucte de Corneille et les sermons funéraires de Bossuet. Les textes médiévaux seront étudiés dans des éditions bilingues offrant une traduction en français moderne. Il est recommandé d’acquérir les éditions citées dessous et de les lire pendant les vacances ; les autres textes seront disponibles sur la plateforme ILIAS.
